en: The Sub-commentary on the *Sūtra of Reverence for the Buddhist Community* (Śāsana-namaskāra-vidhi):

This *Sūtra of Reverence for the Buddhist Community* is the grand paradigm for reverence toward both the ultimate and conventional truths, and the guiding line for the contemplation of phenomena and principles and the practice of cultivation.
For this reason, successive generations have esteemed it as a model for emulation. Yet, why is it that in the present age it is not practiced with such fervor?
One might also consider that while the literary style and meaning of this work are lofty and extraordinary, they are even more difficult to comprehend;
it is like a mosquito biting an iron ox—one ultimately gains nothing. Therefore, those of shallow learning and mediocre capacity have not found much nourishment therein.

In the past, the Vinaya Master Tianshan composed a topical outline (*ke-wen*) as well as the *Tongzhen ji* (Record of Penetrating the Truth) in three fascicles, probing the profound depths and revealing the hidden meanings. However, that book has suffered from errors in transcription and copying.
The principles of the texts are now so disordered that those who aspire to learning cannot help but lament it.

Among them is the Bhikṣu Huimen Guang of Mount Chaori to the north of Luoyang, a preeminent talent within the garden of the Vinaya. Whenever he encounters ancient classics, he reverently proclaims them;
his efforts to restore what has been obscured or lost by former sages are not merely one or two instances. His vow to uphold the Dharma reaches its ultimate limit, and having recently obtained—

Tongzhenji Shanben leaped for joy and prostrated himself in incense-burning reverence; he collated and corrected errors, savoring the text through repeated readings, and appended notes beneath the main text while marking its topical divisions.
He compiled these into three volumes, providing phonetic glosses alongside the characters to facilitate the study of future generations.
Once the carving of the printing blocks was completed, he requested me to write a preface. Although I fear the reproach of being a mere imitation of others, I cannot but rejoice in this undertaking.
How could one fail to see that which is good and fail to proclaim it? This is what our Buddha established, and the gentlemen of the Confucian school likewise warn against its neglect.
Thus, I have composed these redundant and humble words. Written on the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment in the year of Gekushi (1709) of the Genroku era.
At the Guhyasamāja Vajra Seat (Miyan Daochang) in Western Luo, the unworthy bhikṣu Miaobian respectfully records this preface to the newly carved annotated edition of the *Śramaṇa-praṇāma-vidhi*.
Regarding the *Śramaṇa-praṇāma-vidhi*, it was [composed by] our Patriarch...
This was composed by Master Zhengzhao of the Southern Mountains. As for this work, its prose is lofty and its principles profound;
its language is concise yet its meaning is vast. It is not something that those of shallow learning and superficial understanding can pursue with refined investigation.
Alas, there was the Vinaya Master Qili of Yongjia, who authored the *Fahufa ji* (Record on Protecting the Dharma) in two fascicles to elucidate its hidden depths. I regret... [text ends].
Among scholars who have sought to view this complete work, it has remained unattainable; truly, it is a deficiency in the canon.
However, the *Tongzhen ji* (Record of Penetrating Truth) in three fascicles, compiled by the Venerable Bukong, along with its categorized text, was previously carved for printing;
yet the wording was inconsistent and scribal errors were frequent, causing distress to readers. I once searched for several copies and collated them.

I have corrected the errors therein—supplementing what was omitted, excising what remained, rectifying what was erroneous, and clarifying what was doubtful—generally returning it to the ultimate correctness before reading it.
After several readings, I closed the volume and reflected deeply: the *sui-zhu* pearl and the *zhao-bi* jade are the supreme treasures of the world;
yet if they were merely wrapped in their caskets and kept hidden away, who would be able to share them with others? Thus it is said.
In the intervals between my studies and recitations, I diligently collated the original texts with their commentaries, recording the annotations directly beneath them.

Arranging these chapter by chapter, I compiled them into a single work divided into three fascicles, titled *The Ritual of Reverence for the Buddhist Community with Interlinear Notes* (*Jiejuzhi Shimen Guijingyi*).
I then commissioned artisans to carve woodblocks so that it might be distributed far and wide. One day, a guest said to me: "The Vinaya Master Liao Ran composed [this work]..."
In composing this text, I have sought to illuminate the ancestral teachings; my intent to propagate the fundamental tenets and support the doctrine has been exhaustive and complete.

Yet, in reaching a definitive discernment regarding the proper methods for circumambulating the Buddha and the stupa, and in upholding the meaning of authentic realization while refuting the claims of Lingzhi, I have been particularly thorough.
Nevertheless, as for the Master’s current and earnest efforts to propagate these writings—how [is it that he acts thus]?
"Does this not strike at its great principles? I said, "Alas! What you say is indeed so.

Nevertheless, as for the work titled *Tongzhen* (Penetrating Reality), in its inferences, verifications, explanations, and clarifications, it does not fail to point things out by raising the ear or demonstrate them by pointing to the palm and fingers.
However, if one merely observes a single coarse discourse and then casts aside the entire three-fascicle book..."
How is this different from detesting a single stalk of *jue-yao* (weed) while discarding ten thousand bundles of fertilized rice?
Moreover, to cite minor flaws as grounds for rejecting a great excellence is a warning against which the gentleman has cautioned us.

Have you not heard that the "Huang" jade of the Xia dynasty could not be entirely free of flaws, and the "Bright Moon" pearl could not be entirely free of specks; yet they remain treasures of the world?
Why is this so? It is because these minor flaws are insufficient to obstruct the great beauty. Those who examine this book hereafter should not fail to reflect upon it;
thus, I have composed this as a preface. At this time...
Compiled in the second year of the Genroku era, the Year of the Dragon (Ji-si), on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for the monastic community,
by the bhikṣu Emon Kōkun, a descendant of the Shien lineage,
at the Kegon chamber of Chōnichi. *Shakumon kikyōgi Tsūshinki*, Volume One (including preface).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Liao Ran of萧山 (Xiaoshan) during the Great Song Dynasty:
The Two Truths share a common root, and the Three Jewels possess a single nature; yet the multitude of beings are deluded regarding this and pursue the false.

It was for this reason that the Great Hero arose, opening the wondrous gate of the Eightfold Path with compassion and demonstrating the level Way of the Single Straight Path. There is nothing... [text continues]
Because the various views that fail to bring tranquility fundamentally reveal the source of one’s own mind, the sages of both past and present have all followed this path.
This "Ritual for Paying Homage within the Śramaṇa Tradition" was composed by my ancestor, Vinaya Master Chengzhao.
That Master exhausted the subtleties of the Three Studies, propagated the doctrine of the Single Nature, and scrutinized the proper way of taking refuge.
Reverence is the excellent ford to the Supreme Way, and the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional is the pivotal essence of contemplative practice.

Herein, the Tripiṭaka is synthesized and the Dharma of Reverence is extensively set forth; the two emptinesses are elucidated to perfectly reveal the purity of mind and affairs. Principle and phenomena are fully encompassed, and both letter and meaning are complete.

Having been graced by your compassionate moisture and having received your bequeathed words, I have examined them with careful reflection and exhausted my meager wisdom to offer this brief exposition.

The *Keshi Wencheng* (Exegesis on the Accomplishment of Text) consists of three fascicles, titled *Tongzhen* (Penetrating Reality). It is intended to provide access to the gateway of the two truths (*satyadvaya*) and to manifest the principle of the single reality (*ekasatya*).
May future authors not find fault with this modest composition. Thus it is said.

Regarding the five characters in the title of the *Śrāmaṇera-guìjìng-yí* (The Ritual for Taking Refuge and Paying Homage in the Śramaṇa School), there are two layers of distinction between the general and the specific. First, in contrast to the laity, the term "Ritual for Paying Homage" (*guìjìng-yí*) is general;

however, when applied specifically to the Śramaṇa school, it becomes distinct. Since the ritual procedures for paying homage are commonly practiced by the laity, the term "Śramaṇa School" (*shìmén*) is not included in their titles.
Thus, [the term "gate"] would be applied too broadly without a fixed standard; yet, if we restrict it to the single character "return" (gui), such a conventional usage is unheard of.

If we limit our analysis to Buddhist teachings while distinguishing them from other texts, then "Buddhist school" (shimén) serves as the general category and "returning with reverence" (guíjìng) as the specific designation.

Since titles such as the *Jìngchú* (Pure Kitchen) also designate the Buddhist school, we know from the current title "Returning with Reverence" that the following ten chapters do not pertain to other doctrines. As for the character "ritual" (yí): *The Essentials of the Ritual of Returning with Reverence* (Guíjìng yíyào) [End of excerpt]

"Comprehensively, it may be understood that 'Śākyamuni' is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; in full, it is Śākya, which means 'Able Benevolent One' (Nengren). 'Gate' (men) limits the internal and external;
by citing an object as a metaphor, it illustrates the fundamental principle (zong). 'Taking refuge' (gui) means to seek shelter;

'reverence' (jing) refers to the sense of veneration, turning toward [the Three Jewels], and so forth, as will be clarified below. 'Ritual' (yi) refers to the Dharma; it refers to the establishment of the teachings cited in the ten chapters below."

The ritual forms serve as models and possess fixed rules; however, this method of reverence applies to both phenomena and principle, and its meaning is explained in the following text, which should first be understood.
Written by the śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan at Ximing Monastery in the capital during the first year of the Longshuo era of the Great Tang.
Regarding the title within this commentary: according to the original manuscript, there was originally a separate preface title placed after the introductory remarks before the main title.
However, as the introductory section has been damaged and lost, I have set aside the original title and directly displayed the main title at the beginning;
I have then moved the commentary’s own title and placed it immediately following. Recorded by the śramaṇa Shi Ruchang, as he heard it from Daoxuan.

This is the posthumous name of the Great Master. His deeds and meritorious achievements are fully recorded in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*). Regarding "Dàtáng" (Great Tang): Héduōng Jìnyáng was the ancient fiefdom of Tángyú.
During the reign of the High Ancestor Shényáo of the Lí clan, he first received a fief from the Zhōu dynasty as the Duke of Táng.
Later, under the Sui, his rank was advanced to that of King of Táng. Upon succeeding to the abdicated throne from Emperor Gōng of the Sui, he first assumed the title [of Emperor].
The ministers and commoners of the Tang state revered him and thus added the title "Great" (Da) to his name; "Longshuo" was the reign era of the third emperor, Gaozong.
"Jingshi" refers to Chang'an, the capital where the Great Tang resided. The *Gongyang Zhuan* states: "What is 'Jingshi'?
It is the residence of the Son of Heaven. 'Jing' means great; 'shi' means multitude. The Son of Heaven..."

Regarding his residence, it must be described using the terminology of the great assembly: as for Ximing Monastery, among the eight monasteries on the two main streets of Chang’an, one was called Ximing.
In the first year of the Xianqing era, Emperor Gaozong established it while he was still the Crown Prince.

In the second year, by imperial decree, the Master was appointed as the Abbot (Upādhyāya) of Ximing Monastery; he respectfully declined and would not accept, whereupon the Emperor dispatched an official from the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si).
You, Liu Shengong, went to Zhongnan to pay homage and invite [the image] to be brought to this temple, which is the site where the record of its composition was written;
for this reason, it is marked here. "Temple" (si) means "succession" (si); it refers to those who manage affairs succeeding one another within it.
The state has nine temples (*si*), following from the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, when the Buddha-dharma first arrived.
The two venerable masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, arrived at Luoyang with the scriptures and images carried by a white horse.

By imperial decree, they were received with honor at the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù sì). In the eleventh year [of the reign], an edict was issued to construct a separate monastery outside the Yǒng Gate, named after the White Horse;
this was the beginning of Buddhist temples on Han soil, and from then on, monasteries became known by the name of this temple.
The commentator Liu Xie says: "The author is called a Sage; the expounder is called an Enlightened One. The Great Master [Buddha] manifests humility, and thus does not claim to be the author.

Respecting the origins of the Dharma’s emergence—meaning that at the very beginning of the Buddha's transformation, ritual propriety was unknown—the Sage's Dharma followed the times. As this practice of veneration was established, extensive citations of admonitions and teachings were made to serve as the primary source for faith. May it be so.
There are those who are not confused by these instructional expositions.

Regarding the discrepancies between the preceding and succeeding annotations within the table of contents: the former reveals the general purport of a section, while the latter explains the specific sub-headings of that section;
it may be that the meaning is identical, though the phrasing varies in its brevity or detail. This refers to the first part of the initial annotation.
The four phrases collectively clarify the origin of the veneration and the emergence of the teaching; the latter three phrases specifically reveal the intent behind the citation in this text.

"To mount" (*sheng*) means to ascend. Because the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teaching correspond, it is called "mounting the occasion. "To visit" (*ye*) refers to an audience request.

Second, regarding "Aiding the Age and Protecting the Dharma": (This means that because the faculties of people in the degenerate age are dull, the Dharma will not be propagated unless they show respect; therefore, to aid the timing of the era, one must synthesize and practice [the teachings] with a long-term perspective. Consequently, as people follow one another in emulation and the superior and inferior alike comply with this, social order is not disrupted, and the Two Jewels thereby flourish.)
In the first of the two subsequent commentaries, the initial four lines clarify how [the teaching] aids the times, while the following four lines manifest the protection of the Dharma.
This indicates that those who have mastered the practice and possess far-reaching insight have transmitted it in succession without interruption.

Based on the capacities of sentient beings, ritual protocols were established—meaning that as the times shifted between decadence and purity, and as dispositions varied between sharp and dull, the founders of the teachings opened diverse paths of encouragement and restraint; whether it be that the Buddha’s virtue is so sublime that he is said to erase transgressions, or that this [present] region fundamentally...
[The phrase] "purifying the two karmas can clarify [the path]" (淨二業能明等) follows.
Within the next three commentaries, the first two lines clarify the capacity of the recipient (*adhikāra*), while the latter two lines establish the teaching;

alternatively, the final four lines collectively reveal the reason for establishing the teaching in accordance with that capacity. Thus, the "corrupt" and "pure" represent the transformations of the times, while "sharp" and "dull" represent the capacities of the recipients.

For those whose faculties are particularly dull, one teaches through skillful means and the cultivation of worldly activities, saying: "Restrain your pursuit of profit so that you may practice rational contemplation and proceed directly toward the Supreme Vehicle.
This is called "opening up what is obstructed. These two practices correspond to the conventional and the ultimate truths.

Chapter Four: Conduct According to the Mind (This refers to the fact that while the object has not yet perished, one acts according to the mind; regarding the application of conditions and the flow of karmic tasks, one must recognize that they arise from the mind and pervade the three natures. When the objects are defiled, the six sense-fields become causes for merit or give rise to offenses;
do not think these are the path of karma.)
In the first four lines of the initial of these four commentaries, the general nature of the mind’s engagement with phenomena is revealed;
in the subsequent four lines, the specific characteristics of transgression and merit are demonstrated. To say that "phenomena exist" means that afflictions are actively manifesting.

To say "due to the operation of the mind" means that ordinary beings bound by fetters, having not yet opened their wisdom and understanding, must necessarily rely on the completion of actions (*saṃskāra*) in accordance with the karma they create.

The fifth [category] concerning the provisional and the ultimate based on conditions (*ālambana*) consists of five [aspects]: (1) the Dharma being adapted to expedient means; (2) the mind responding to the circumstances; (3) the principle of karma; (4) the two stages of mind and form; and (5) the finger pointing at the moon and the double reed-fence. Alternatively, it refers to those of vulgar and shallow capacity who, failing to recognize their own limits, recklessly presume upon the reality of others, thereby sinking into the mundane.
In the next five commentaries, the first two lines generally clarify the capacity [of the practitioner] and the teaching [of the Buddha] to reveal the phenomena and principles of the Dharma;

"phenomena" refers to the teaching that can enable, while "capacity" refers to the practitioner who is enabled. Since capacities are divided into sharp and dull, the teaching opens up provisional paths;

the provisional uses phenomena to encompass, while the path uses principle to provide succor. The latter two lines follow this to manifest correct practice: the body and mind belong to that which performs the practice.
Phenomena and principle constitute the body of practice; the physical acts of practice are like the finger, while the mind’s penetration of principle through contemplation is like the moon.

Since the body and mind, phenomena and principle, and the conventional and the ultimate proceed together, they are called the "double fish-trap" (*shuangquan*). Alternatively, the following section serves as a warning to repudiate deluded attachments;
it consists of three parts: first, to be attached solely to physical matters rather than understanding the principle is an error of narrow-minded fixation.
Second, if one is attached solely to the principle while neglecting physical affairs, the error lies in being deluded and reckless;
third, if one divides principle and affairs into two parts and the true and conventional into two paths, the error lies in creating separation—both points are fully detailed in the main text.

Section Six: Citing Teachings to Examine Traces (This refers to the fact that during the Dharma-Ending Age, faculties are dull and most are bound by their habitual natures; thus, one must cite the sacred words as authoritative teaching. Now, by examining conduct through the Four Reliances and verifying it with the Four Seals, all involvement with frivolous talk and deceptive pretension is severed).

In the first four lines of the initial six annotations, it is clarified that those of dull faculties find it difficult to believe and thus require the citation of authoritative teachings to demonstrate that [the doctrine] is not false;
the following four lines correctly reveal the principle of citing teachings and verifying facts within this chapter.

Section Seven: Regulating Time and Divisions (This refers to the fact that mental activities fluctuate in their intensity and diligence; therefore, one establishes methods to examine the mind, divides time, and exerts effort. Thus, one knows that diligent mindfulness in practicing the holy path has a destination;
otherwise, one will drift and sink, remaining the same as from time immemorial).

Next, within the seven introductory notes, the first four lines indicate the intent of the section, specifically clarifying the temporal context; the latter four lines cite secular precedents to encourage practice, with the underlying meaning residing in uninterrupted application.

(8) Ritual decorum is orderly: this refers to manifesting a reverent countenance and a heart of sincere devotion. One must now cite the authentic scriptures to fully enumerate the proper deportment; thus, one’s movements and pauses are as if in meditation, and one’s speech is composed and stable, not [neglecting] the Dharma...
If one uses a cord [to bind them], then hands and feet will have nowhere to rest).
Next, among the eight annotations, the first four lines demonstrate dignified demeanor; the next two lines clarify that there is a proper order;
the final two lines conclude by manifesting the deportment. The *Xiaojing* states, "Deportment is worthy of observation," while the last six characters are from the *Qu li*.
It is said: "The countenance appears solemn as if in deep thought, and his speech is steady and composed.

This refers to the power of spiritual resonance through practice. (That is to say: karma is provisional while its fruition is accomplished; it arises from the mind. When the mind harbors both defilement and purity, karma likewise becomes both real and illusory. Because conceptions and views have not yet been clarified, good and evil intermingle; thus, one does not manifest the conditions of retribution, and because of this deluded stagnation, clarity is difficult to attain.)

In the first of the nine commentaries that follow, the initial portion describes the functional application, while the final two lines demonstrate the capacity for spiritual resonance and penetration.

Regarding the "traces of established vessels" (the ten categories): this refers to the time when people rarely relied upon listening to words or observing conduct; therefore, formal rules were established to clarify the path of the mind.
In the tenth commentary, the passage "listen to their words and observe their conduct" is drawn from the *Analects* to clarify the intended meaning.

This implies that when one listens to their words and observes their conduct, there are few who act as they speak; therefore, having no other choice, he relies on this matter to give rise to his discourse.
It is not merely to provide for himself, but to aid those who come to study.

Chapter One: On the Arising of the Basis of Reverence (This means that establishing the basis of reverence does not arise from correct faith; yet without faith, reverence will certainly not arise. Since reverence must first be present, one must first harbor [the intent] as stated in the chapter on "Words," for it is because the basis of faith arises first and reverence follows thereafter).
In the title of the chapter "The Source of Reverence for the Rise of the Teachings" (*Jingben Jiaoxing pian*), "reverence" (*jing*) refers to ritual propriety, which necessarily arises from the mind;

the character "source" (*ben*) precisely explains "faith" (*xin*). Faith is itself the mind, and because faith is that to which one returns as the source of reverence, it is called the "Source of Reverence.

Regarding "teachings" (*jiao*), this refers to the words bestowed by the worthy and sages upon those below; regarding "rise" (*xing*), this is a term for the emergence and causal origins. Thus, it is "the rise of the teachings through the source of reverence."

The distinctions between the general and specific meanings of "pian" (chapter/section) are fully recorded in the main text and are not detailed here. Regarding the term "pian," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"It is an elegant name for a chapter or section and a distinct title for a division; it signifies that the categories are uniform and their meanings are identical.

As for "di" (number), it means "position"; as for "yi" (one), it means "beginning. Since this occupies the first position, it is called "the first. (The characters following "pian" may be explained by analogy. [Note]
The first two lines of the middle section generally clarify that reverence is the root from which the teaching arises; the next two lines provide a reciprocal explanation;

and the final two lines conclude by indicating the intent of this chapter. Since reverence is not established without faith, and faith does not stand without the teaching—if this is so, then faith must arise because of the teaching, and the teaching truly exists for the sake of faith. The commentary states: "Arising" means establishing reverence.
Thus, the intent behind the emergence of this teaching can be discerned.
The preface states: "Since the manifestation of the Dharma King, he has invariably prioritized the vision of stillness. Therefore, the treatise asks:
"In what place, at what time, and by whom is this vision aroused? It concludes that all views are thereby severed; this text is indeed a fine testimony.
In the first section of this text, "xu" (序) means "preface"; it describes the essential tenets of the root of reverence and the causes for the arising of the teaching.
The word "yuē" (曰) is a particle used to indicate that one must rely on words to clarify the fundamental teaching (the same interpretation applies to subsequent instances).

The first two phrases constitute the formal preface: the upper phrase refers to the person, while the lower phrase indicates the principle. "Dharmarāja" (法王) refers to the Buddha, distinguishing him from others.
Because he is the Lord of the World, he is called the Dharma King. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas.

Because he appears in the world according to the capacities of sentient beings, it is said that his appearance is beneficial (*li jian*). In the *Zhou Yi*, the second and fifth lines of the *Qian* hexagram both state: "It is advantageous to see the Great Man" (*li jian da ren*).

In those cases, it refers to a sage ruler ascending the throne who surely accords with the hearts of the times; here, it refers to the Descent of the Spirit of the Benevolent One, which is likewise appropriate.

Because they respond to the stimuli of sentient beings, they arise in accordance with the timing and accord with their capacities; is it not fitting that they appear for the benefit of all living beings?

Thus, he borrows from the Confucian classics to clarify the manifestation of his response. He speaks of "quiescence" and "vision": quiescence belongs to the mind of the Master, while vision is the affliction of sentient beings.
Although the afflictions of vision are many, the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) is their root, arising because ordinary people lack...
Initially, delusion (ignorance) arises based on the Truth; from delusion, one falsely discriminates a self (the self of persons and the self of dharmas);

from this self, views arise (namely, the five sharp afflictions such as the view of self, along with the sixty-two views such as eternalism and nihilism); from these views, poisons are unleashed (namely, the five dull afflictions such as greed and pride);

and from these poisons, karma is created. Following this karma, one undergoes retribution, revolving without rest. Therefore, for the sake of quelling these views, the World-Honored One, within the most pure [state]...
The Dharma-realm flows forth as the Wisdom of Essential Nature (*svābhāvika-jñāna*); from the Wisdom of Essential Nature arises the Subsequently Attained Wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
from the Subsequently Attained Wisdom arises Great Compassion; from Great Compassion manifest the Response and Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*);

and from these Response and Transformation Bodies flow forth all teachings—namely, the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, the Truths, the Bases of Mindfulness, the Perfections, and various other Dharma-gates—though they may differ in their emphasis on phenomena or principle, and in their partiality or completeness.
Established according to the capacities of beings, their original intent was entirely for the purpose of enabling those with quietistic views to equally attain the Buddha-way.

From before his appearance in the world when he first established this resolve, until after his appearance when he later set forth his teachings, he has consistently fulfilled his original vow to uproot the source of others' afflictions and to give full expression to his own inner aspirations;
therefore, it is said that one must take quietistic views as the priority. Thus, the following passage is cited from the *Zhongjing* (Sutra of the Middle) as scriptural evidence.
The full verse of that treatise states: "Because all phenomena are empty, how, where, when, and who could give rise to views such as the permanence of the world?
This verse reveals that all views are fundamentally empty. It further states:
"I now pay homage with my head bowed to Gautama, the Great Holy Lord, who out of compassion taught this Dharma that completely severs all views. This verse...
The World-Honored One established the teachings to lead people toward quiet contemplation.

Nevertheless, because the habits of long-standing conditioning make it difficult to achieve direct realization, it is necessary to establish reverence and ritual forms to open the way for the primary method of faith;
by conforming to human sentiments and codifying external appearances, the merit of perfected transformation is manifested.

In the first section of the initial chapter of this teaching, the first two phrases describe the delusion of sentient beings' habitual tendencies; the single character "one" (yi) refers precisely to ignorance (*avidyā*).
By the power of ignorance, thoughts arise and perfuse the fundamental storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), forming the seeds of views and pride.

Because this has continued from beginningless time through the long succession of kalpas, it is said that "days have passed. Having not yet encountered a true teacher, they have failed to return to the nature-awakening.

It is said that there is no way to grasp the ultimate convergence; thus, the following four lines clarify the establishment of the teachings. This refers to the "Dharma established" in the subsequent text.

"Establishing reverence" means, as in the *Benqi jing* (Sutra of the Original Beginnings), establishing the foundation for taking refuge and paying homage through such practices as the Three Refuges at the moment of birth.
"Establishing rituals" means, as in the *Buddha Sees King Bimbisāra Sūtra*, demonstrating the correct ritual forms for paying homage.
It is from this reverent ritual that the opening of sentient beings' faith begins; therefore, it is called the "Preamble to Faith.

As for "attaching to circumstances and summarizing characteristics," as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the categories of reverence are established by attaching to the sentiments of ordinary and sagely, monastic and lay persons, so that those practicing at the beginning of the Path may establish formal rules to accomplish the merit of transformation and guidance. Thus, one knows that the Buddha’s compassion is vast.
Deeply moved by the profound kindness of the Dharma-milk, I have compassion for those followers who are attached to the self; thus I have opened this method of "Quiescent Vision.

When first descending from the Mother’s womb, the transformative ritual was manifested; when the Way and its fruit were first perfected, the return to the Dharma was established. Now, I turn back those with deviant views so that they may abide in the orthodox current:
at the beginning, one seeks the secret empowerment of other Buddhas; in the end, one returns to the fundamental purity of one's own mind.

Since it is through this guidance that one ultimately reaches the Buddha-vehicle, we know that taking refuge in and revering the One Dharma is the root for entering the Way and the ultimate goal for attaining Nirvana.
Such is the general outline of the intention behind taking refuge and paying homage.
Thereafter, with liver and gall smeared upon the earth and physical frame shattered, one comes to know the ultimate sublimity of the universe;

thus, reverence exceeds that for natural kin (for while parents give birth to the body, the Buddha gives rise to the Dharma-body). Retribution and bestowal pertain to a single lifetime, whereas the repayment of the distant reaches its conclusion over successive kalpas. When merit is so great it is difficult to reward, and virtue so profound it cannot be thanked;

when wisdom is so deep it becomes ever more abundant, it is beyond the reach of recompense.
