Next, the "beast" illustrates that animals have no path to liberation. Because they receive forms that are base and defiled, it is said their retribution is heavy.

Because their afflictions are turbid and dull, it is said they are stubborn and thick; "stubborn" (*wán*) is synonymous with ignorance (*moha*). When the cause of ignorance is particularly predominant, one frequently falls among animals.

Now that our physical forms possess lightness and clarity, and our cognitive minds are stirred by their faculties, we should surely grow weary of the toil of past kalpas and rejoice in the liberation from the net in the future.

We must establish images as outward manifestations and prostrate ourselves with heads bowed toward the gathered dust; relying on these conditions to lead us forward, we shall wash away the burdens of affliction within our new minds.
Thus, though our emotions differ from those of oxen or sheep, we shall ride upon clear wisdom to propagate the Way, our bodies remaining as still as wood or stone.
Is it not so that one must undergo carving and polishing to become a vessel? Is it not so? When a mouse enters a horn, it meets its end;
what further destination could there be? When names and words are employed to reveal actual principles, they reach their ultimate limit here.

Furthermore, when the five impurities swirl together and the four mountains constantly press in, to still be able to endure the events of the time—is this not merely the delusion of those who are mired in ignorance?

Next, regarding the first part of the middle section: practicing by means of retribution refers to the body being light and pure because it differs from heavy karmic retribution; the mental faculty being uplifted refers to its difference from dullness and rigidity.
"Faculty" (jī) signifies circular movement, while "uplifted" (jǔ) signifies transcendence. One laments the cycle of saṃsāra in the past, thus there must be weariness with it;

one looks forward to the joyful retribution of the future, thus there must be cultivation for what is to come. To solidify this, the lower section demonstrates the method of cultivation: establishing an image means setting it forth.
That which is entrusted to his veneration refers to relying upon his cultivation of the Dharma; "dispelling the dust" refers to subduing the retribution-body;

"washing away the burdens" refers to clarifying the delusions of the mind. This concludes the section on the benefits for those below. Regarding the extension of admonitions and exhortations for those below, there are three parts:

first, an exhortation by means of a metaphor, citing a common proverb where the matter is superficial but the meaning is profound, hence it is cited as an admonition; second, an exhortation by citing the text; third, an exhortation by citing [the example].

The phrasing employs the will to abide by the name; "to lead" (yin) and "to transcribe" (xie) are inverted and combined to form "to lead" (yin). The name is used as a comparison; when the following example is raised, it exhorts [the practitioner].
The "five dregs" (wuzhi) are the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). The "four mountains" are as cited above. The final two lines are a reprimand regarding the time of practicing patience (*kṣānti*);
since the circumstances are favorable, it refers to past karma. "Dusk" (*hun*) means the time of delusion; "flattery" (*mei*) is synonymous with confusion.

Therefore, the Great Sage, knowing the proper time, employed universal transformation to mold and guide beings, establishing the Three Treasures of the Right Dharma to lead those with turbid consciousness toward their ultimate refuge;

he opened up the Four Seals to reveal that sentient beings are not inherently deluded. Thus, the Dharma has been firmly preserved for ten thousand years—a feat resulting from the merit of reverent devotion—and the spirits have ascended to the four heavens, truly relying on the power of its propagation. As extensively set forth in the *Maitreya Sūtra*, how could this be anything other than true?

How profound! Regarding the first section of the initial chapter, "Establishing the Jewels to Manifest Benefits," the first six lines demonstrate the Buddha’s establishment of the Dharma. "Great Sage" refers to the Buddha in general;

"to suit" (*shì*) means to accord with the capacities of sentient beings; "to mold" (*táo*) means to refine and shape; and "to entice" (*yòu*) means to guide and attract. This constitutes the Three Jewels in their true sense.
The term "those" is used to distinguish them from false teachers; "guiding those with turbid consciousness" refers to leading beginners.

Regarding the four seals (*catur-mudrā*), they correspond to the four ink-seals (*catur-maṣī-mudrā*) mentioned in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-eight, which asks: "For what reason did the Buddha teach the four ink-seals? It answers:
"Because he wished to speak the Dharma of ultimate reality. In future ages, bhikṣus shall clearly know what is the word of the Buddha and what is not the word of the Buddha," and so forth.

The "pattern" (wen) is like that ink; it refers to the seal of the phrases and sentences (*vyañjana-pada-mudrā*), meaning that one realizes through the seal of the teaching that the mind does not give rise to erroneous understanding.
Thus it is said, "not obscured" (*bu mei*). Next, the benefits of its merit are shown: first, the benefit of abiding in the Dharma; subsequently, the benefit of attaining retribution.

Regarding the text on revering and propagating [the teaching], although the phrasing mentions only one aspect, the meaning actually encompasses both. The *Maitreya Sūtra* is, in fact, the *Maitreya-uttara-sūtra*.
The scriptural passages concerning birth are cited below.

This current exposition is intended primarily for those of later generations who have recently begun their practice; it is a detailed instruction on the nature of merit and substance, rather than the profound foresight of former virtuous ones.

It is therefore necessary to provide earnest, finger-pointing guidance to fully unravel the characteristics [of reality], so that one may recognize that there are various provisional manifestations of the Three Jewels.

I intend to resolve the doubts of the seven assemblies regarding the rare aspiration for the Teacher, speaking with only plain and direct intent so that those who possess discernment may understand the purpose of practice without being burdened by excessive writing.
Thus, the Buddha said: "My words do not rely on ornate embellishment; it is essential that they enable people to receive understanding.
Daring to follow this path, I have recorded these notes in the preface.

In the first section of this work, I intend to establish four types of the Triple Gem; fearing that this might be considered overly prolix, I first present them here. Since they are intended for beginners, I must explain them in detail.
The teachings established by former worthies were mostly directed toward those of sharp faculties, and their literary style was concise and terse;

therefore, they cannot be compared to the present case. "Early" (zǎo) means "first. "Lù" (pronounced luògē) refers to "to enumerate" or "to detail" various kinds. It is a concern—that is, a matter of the mind—to ensure these are not overlooked.

The four aspects of expedient means (*upāya*) as shown below refer to skillful stratagems. Regarding the "seven assemblies," this term encompasses both monastics and laypeople alike, as they all equally revere the True Treasure;
thus, there is no difference in their ultimate orientation. "Explanation" (*jie*) refers to the act of guiding and instructing.
"Below" indicates the textual body of the work. "Below" introduces the cited texts as evidence. "Dare" signifies expressing one's sentiments in accordance with the Dharma to seek the reader's trust.

Subsequently, in this present chapter, the characteristics of the Three Jewels are revealed according to four sequential stages of perception that arise in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings: first, the single essence;
second, the principle of conditions; third, the manifested aspect; and fourth, the sustaining aspect. Each of these possesses its own specific name and characteristics.
Regarding the characteristics of the Triple Gem, the first section consists of four lines that provide a general summary, followed by a detailed enumeration.

"According to what is seen" means that seeing is the perception of the capacity (the *kīn*); this capacity is distinguished by the differences between the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as between delusion and awakening. Furthermore, such seeing varies according to whether it is hidden or manifest, existent or non-existent.
Thus, these Three Jewels arise in accordance with what is seen; this is because, in terms of their inherent nature (*prakṛti*), both delusion and awakening are fundamentally present.
To speak of the "one essence" (t'i-yi) is to eliminate delusion and preserve awakening, manifesting exclusively the Dharma-body (dharmakāya);

because there exists the rational essence (li-t'i), sentient beings possess the cause for seeing the Buddha, and as the Buddha appears in accordance with conditions, there exist the manifested forms (nirmāṇakāya).

Because those with turbid faculties have heavy obstructions and cannot reach the source of manifestation, while those with meager remaining resources are capable of receiving the legacy of the image, the "abiding and maintaining" [body] is established; these are spoken of in terms of time, while the "one essence" refers to the principle.

The essence of principle (*tattva*) exists identically throughout the three periods; the aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is restricted solely to the Buddha’s world; and the meaning of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) applies to both the beginning and the end.
Speaking from the perspective of persons: the single essence is possessed equally by ordinary beings and sages; the essence of principle resides only in sages;

the aspect of transformation and sustaining power are seen by both ordinary beings and sages. Speaking according to the teachings: the single essence is restricted solely to the Mahāyāna, while the other three meanings apply to both the Mahāyāna and [the Hīnayāna].
Because the explanations in the various sutras and teachings differ, the meaning of "according to capacity" (*yīqī*) is thereby made manifest.
Regarding the initial mention of the "Three Jewels as One Essence":
"One" means they are not two; "essence" refers to what is called the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Regarding the explanation of the term "one essence" (*eka-tattva*) within the section on explaining names: although the text itself provides an explanation, ancient interpretations have largely erred in understanding that there is no duality.
My present explanation of this passage briefly preserves three meanings. First, it distinguishes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) from the essence (*tattva*).

Although the essence is one, it is divided into three according to its characteristics; fearing that one might think there are consequently three essences according to those characteristics, this passage distinguishes them by stating they are "not two."
The *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Precepts Manual) states: "Now, having realized the fundamental principle of dharmas, there are in reality no three [categories], and so forth.
Second, the explanation that dispels numerical designations: according to conventional discourse, numbers begin with one, proceed to two, and extend to hundreds and thousands.

Herein, this single essence stands alone and independent; it originally lacks any counterpart. Yet, for the sake of provisional expression, we borrow the name "one" to designate its own nature. Fearing that if this were heard...
First, "one" refers to the fact that within a single entity there are two opposites corresponding to various numerical categories; therefore, this is negated by saying it is "not two.
Thus, the ancient masters said: "Borrowing 'one' to negate 'two'"—this is precisely its meaning.
Third, the explanation of reality clarifies that "one" is the true mind, the reality among all phenomena. Since nothing other than this one reality is true, it is called "not two."
Since these two are neither identical nor different, they manifest the single reality; thus the Great Master said: "All phenomena are fundamentally without reality;
there is only consciousness" (and so forth). What is called "fundamental consciousness" is *ālaya* in Sanskrit, also known as *ālayavijñāna*.
This is translated as "storehouse" (*zàng*) or "that which is not lost" (*wúmò*). It is called "fundamental" because it can store seeds and maintain them without loss.

Question: What is the meaning of "essence" (*tǐ*) as it relates to the fundamental nature? Since the causes and effects of defilement and purity arise based upon it, how do the essence of mind (*xīntǐ*) and the fundamental consciousness (*běnshí*) differ? Answer:

The essence of mind is manifested from the perspective of its intrinsic nature (*xìng*), whereas the fundamental consciousness is designated from the perspective of its phenomenal characteristics (*xiàng*). Although they share the same principle (*lǐ*) and refer to the same reality (*shì*), their distinctions can be understood through this difference.

If that is so, [one might ask: in the *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts), it says "the essence is the essence of mind," while in this text it says "this essence is... [how are these two "essences" to be reconciled?]

If it is asked why the text exclusively cites "delusion" and "truth" when the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is said to be both delusive and true, the answer is that names are provisional linguistic designations;

words do not stand independently, and names designate intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) while expressions manifest different aspects. Since the consciousness is designated according to its phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), its meaning must be understood according to those characteristics.

When discussing the correct principle in its entirety, both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are fully encompassed; yet when speaking of the fundamental consciousness, delusion penetrates all the way to truth.
When one raises the mind to examine its essence, it is found that the True encompasses the deluded derivative; because it is thus perfectly complete, they may be designated interchangeably.
Furthermore, the explanatory text below explicitly states that the essence of the mind is what is intended; reflect carefully on this correct principle and do not become confused by mere terminology.
It is only because the fundamental nature of the mind from time immemorial is pure like space, yet it has been obscured by adventitious delusions and defilements that follow along with attachments,
leading us from birth to death until this day, with no way to grow weary of or awaken to [the truth].

In the first section of the "Demonstration of the Essence," the first two phrases demonstrate the essence of the mind. Mind refers to the essence of the eight consciousnesses; this essence is True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the essence of phenomena.
Because its self-nature is pure, it is called "pure by nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*). This differs from other types of emptiness, which must be purified through cultivation.

The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states that there are two kinds of purity: first, the purity of being unstained while in the causal stage; second, [the purity of being unstained while in the resultant stage].
The stainless purity of the fruition is of one essence with that which exists in the cause as undefiled purity;

space is used as the metaphor because it possesses qualities such as omnipresence and immobility, and thus serves as this analogy. However, while space is merely a state of inert vacuity, it lacks spiritual intelligence (*vijñāna*);
therefore, it does not reach the scope of the metaphor. As the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Originally undefiled," and the *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "It is essential..."
The consciousness-mind is fundamentally the principle of the Mahāyāna; its essence is pure, and its wondrous function is empty and pervasive. As the *Zhengguan* (Correct Contemplation) states:

"Observe that the self-nature of one's own mind is inherently pure—neither empty nor existent, neither defiled nor pure. Thus, one knows that the substance and characteristics of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) are perfectly interfused.
Yet, many people, upon merely hearing the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), immediately speak of it as a mere phenomenon.

Upon reading this, one who follows their own biased views might reject the ancestral vehicle and lead later generations astray, while disparaging the former sages and failing to consult the wise of the future.
Yet, by carefully examining this text, one will know that it designates the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as the name and explains the pure mind as its essence;

thus, its nature and characteristics are perfectly complete, and the ultimate and conventional truths do not conflict. This is truly because its magnificent prose and profound meanings require the utmost reflection.

Refining the essence of the wondrous contemplation, the aim of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanmen) lies in deep immersion; how can those with shallow understanding, who rely on hearsay and lack learning, be deemed fit to speak of it?
The first six lines clarify that delusive consciousness is identical to True Suchness (Tathatā) as it follows conditions.
The first two lines address the primary cause of the arising of delusion: delusive thought (*vikalpa*) is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), whose nature is unstable, likened to a guest that defiles.
The true nature is called "dust-enclosed"; delusion is said to arise falsely, obscuring the true.

To follow defilement means the true follows the false in movement, leading to the two subsequent lines on flowing and transforming according to conditions—this is the aspect of the nature (xing-xiang), for it undergoes birth and extinction; thus it is said that the aspect follows [the nature].
Regarding the two subsequent lines of the sutra, "clinging to the false and not returning," one asks: since the substance of the mind is already pure, how could it admit of false defilement?

Answer: The essence of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) is that truth and falsehood share a common source; because defilement and purity have not yet been distinguished, there is room for falsehood to arise.
Thus, when ignorance (*avidyā*) arises, the entirety of the True becomes false. This does not mean that there is a separate false dharma outside of the True that comes to defile the pure mind.

The water and waves, or gold and its images, can serve as metaphors for this. As the *Jingxin jieguan* (Admonition on Contemplating the Pure Mind) says: "Birth-and-death and afflictions arise from the True."
The analogy for the nature-arising (*xingqi*) is like a great body of water that is fundamentally pure and still;
due to the wind, waves are subsequently produced, and later, because of intense cold, it freezes into ice. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is fundamentally pure like water;

through the winds of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, the waves of birth-and-death arise, and as craving and attachment solidify, they form the ice of afflictions. The *Awakening of Faith Treatise* states: "In reliance upon the Tathāgata..."

Because it stores [seeds], there is arising and ceasing; that which is called "neither-arising-nor-ceasing" is in conjunction with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different, and is named the *ālayavijñāna*, and so forth.
Question: If delusion arises falsely and dispels the True, and if the source of reality (*tattva*) arises and ceases of its own accord while remaining immutable, why do you say it "follows delusion"?
Answer: It is because of the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*). The True follows the False and flows along with it. Question: Since the True has already become deluded...

Question: What is meant by "originally pure"? Answer: It refers to the meaning of being unchanging; its nature is inherently and spontaneously true. Question: True Suchness is immovable, while the Dharma-body involves arising and ceasing;
the teachings and schools differ, as do the distinctions between nature and characteristics (*dharmatā* and *lakṣaṇa*). To which of these meanings does this ritual text correspond? Answer:

The principles of the Nature School (*Xingzong*) and the Teaching School (*Jiaozong*), as well as the intent of the text, are clearly elucidated here. Question: According to the Characteristics School (*xiangzong*), the seeds of the eight consciousnesses give rise to phenomena. How is this understood here? [End of excerpt]
In the School of Nature (Xingzong), when delusion arises, the true nature follows conditions; now, to designate this single essence, we speak only of the "fundamental consciousness" (ben shi).
How could this be the same as the "dharma-nature" (faxing) arising falsely from the True? This has already been explained at length previously, so you may reflect upon it and take it for yourself.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The nature and characteristics of all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent;

sentient beings delusively calculate self and other, gain and loss, and transmigrate through birth and death, failing to attain liberation. Another sutra says: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;

this is the exalted name of my own fundamental consciousness emerging from its obstructions. Due to delusion, one is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); upon awakening, one is named a sage (*ārya*). This is why a poor woman possesses a treasure-store within her."
The jewel on the crown of a noble person is by nature eternally pure; yet, though it exists, it serves no purpose as it is shrouded by delusions and has no means to manifest its radiance.
As the sutra says: "It is like a treasure covered by deep thickets, or a stream of diverse flavors [hidden] away. Nevertheless, its fundamental nature is luminous, profound, and without blemish.
Next, the first passage of the cited evidence is from the *Dancha jing* (Sūtra on Examining the Gallbladder), which first proves that the nature is pure like space;

the subsequent section proves that delusion arises from the truth. Furthermore, the first two lines of the "Tathāgata-nature" chapter (*Rulai xing pin*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* directly cite the scriptural text, while the following portion explains and demonstrates the meaning of that scripture.
The "Buddha-nature" mentioned in the sūtra is my own fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); the Buddha translated this as "awakening" (*jue*).

The "excellent name" (*kalyāṇa-nāman*) refers to the fruition-virtue (*phala-guṇa*), whereas "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) belongs to the deluded mind and is thus the causal designation for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Now, while abiding in the stage of an ordinary being, to manifest the name of "Awakening" (*bodhi*) means that one knows the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) within the mind of afflictions has never failed to be awakened;

it is merely that when deluded one is an ordinary being and when awakened one is a Sage—the names have simply shifted. Both the "precious storehouse" and the "forehead jewel" are used as metaphors for this reality, as recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet it is constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions;

therefore, sentient beings are unable to perceive it. It is like a poor woman’s house where there is a vast treasury of genuine gold, yet none of her family members, whether young or old, know of its existence.
However, a stranger who is skilled in expedient means discovers it and digs it up from within that very house.
"Good son Kancana, I now universally show all sentient beings that their Buddha-nature is covered and obscured by various afflictions,
just as that poor woman possessed a treasury of true gold yet could not see it,
or like the jewel on the forehead of a strong man. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, for example, there was a great strongman in a royal household whose eyebrows...
Once, while he was wrestling and contending his strength with other wrestlers, one of them struck him on the forehead with his head;
the jewel immediately sank into his flesh, and he was entirely unaware of its location.
A sore formed at that spot, so he summoned a skilled physician to treat it himself. When the time came for the application of ointment, he took up a mirror to look at it.
The two lines beginning with "the jewel appears clearly and manifestly within the mirror" explain the nature of the two preceding metaphors.

Because the nature of the treasure in the house and the crest-jewel is eternally unchanging, yet they are useless because they are obstructed by earth and flesh; these two lines serve as the synthesis for the two preceding metaphors.
Regarding the delusions: "earth and flesh" applies to both together, while "light being obscured" and "the jewel hidden deep in thick undergrowth" apply separately.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Jewels and so forth," it also appears in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Upon examining the scriptures, there is only the analogy of the medicinal herb. It says:
"Good son, for example, on Mount Himavat there is a medicinal herb of a single flavor.
In ages past, there was a Cakravartin King who, for the sake of this medicine, constructed wooden tubes here and there across the mountain to receive the medicine. This medicine ripened..."
At that time, the substance flowed from the earth and collected within wooden tubes; its flavor was truly authentic.

After the king had passed away, this medicine later became sometimes sour, sometimes salty, sometimes bitter, sometimes pungent, sometimes sweet, or sometimes bland—thus, while it was a single flavor, it took on various flavors according to where it flowed.
The true flavor of this medicine remained fixed in the mountain, like the full moon.
Ordinary people of meager merit, though they apply effort with hoes and mattocks to labor over the granaries, are unable to obtain it.
Yet, when a Sage-King appears in the world, by virtue of his meritorious causes and conditions, one immediately obtains the true flavor of this medicine.
Son of good family, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is likewise; it is obscured by the thickets of various afflictions.
Sentient beings shrouded by ignorance are unable to perceive the single-flavored medicine;
this is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature, which, due to afflictions, manifests various flavors, namely those of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals (and so forth).
Therefore, because the former sages heard this and exerted themselves in diligent contemplation day after day, they eventually realized these virtues and attained wondrous enlightenment;
thus they turned to rely upon the Dharma-body, which is not something newly born, but is manifested by relying on conditions through cultivation.

Section One: Refuting Delusion and Encouraging Cultivation. Subsection One: Revealing Realization through Cultivation Based on the Cause. The first phrase indicates hearing the Dharma; the second phrase indicates initiating practice;

the third phrase indicates the duration of time; the fourth phrase reveals the realization of this merit—which is the virtue of the pure radiance of the original nature—and below this, it serves as a counter-illustration.
First, it shows that cultivation must necessarily rely upon the nature. "Sublime Awakening" refers to the Sage of the Ultimate Fruit. "Three Kalpas" [refers to the three great asamkhyeya kalpas].

It is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) because practice is perfected, obscurations are exhausted, and awakening is fulfilled; it is the intrinsic nature of the *dharmakāya* that is inherently present.
As for "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it refers to the transformation from the defiled portion to the pure portion. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"When the antidote arises, one becomes separated from the defiled and impure categories of the fundamental consciousness (the eight consciousnesses) and becomes associated with the pure category (the true consciousness). Therefore, it is called "transformation."

Following the phrase "relying on the body," the next section reveals that while the nature [of the mind] is provisionally established through conditions to form the body, although it is inherently present, it is not manifested without conditions;
therefore, one relies upon the Three Studies to manifest the wondrous mind.
Subsequently, having heard this, the practitioner arouses a great resolve; once they have departed for that [state], how can I remain? Thus, following the path, one advances in virtue.
He returns to ascend to the ultimate position.
Next, the first two lines of the middle section follow upon that previous cultivation to demonstrate the great resolve of subsequent progress, which is precisely the bodhicitta.

The following passage from the sutra provides a general illustration of the reason for generating this resolve through both prior and subsequent cultivation. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like..."
Suppose two people hear that in another region there is a mountain of seven precious gems, upon which there is a clear spring whose water is sweet and delicious;
those who can reach it will forever sever poverty, and those who drink its water will increase their lifespan by ten thousand years.
However, the road is remote, steep, and fraught with many hardships. At that time, both men desire to go together, and one of them prepares various kinds of [provisions].

As they traveled, one of them was empty-handed and carried nothing at all as they proceeded together. On the road, they encountered a man who was carrying many precious goods and possessed all seven treasures.
The two men went forward and asked him, "Virtuous one, is it true that there is a mountain of the seven treasures in that land?
The man replied, "It is indeed true and not false; I have already obtained the treasures and drunk from their sweet waters."
The spring was situated only on a perilous path, abounding in bandits, saline soil, and thorns, and lacking water and grass;
of those who went there, though they numbered in the thousands, those who returned were very few. Having heard these words, one person immediately felt regret and spoke thus:
"Since the road is so remote and the hardships are manifold, of those who have gone there, countless in number, those who have returned are but few. How then can I [go]?"
When they were able to reach that place, one person spoke again, saying: "There is someone who can surpass me; I too can surpass him.
If we attain the goal and reach our destination, we shall obtain our wishes, gather precious jewels, and drink that water. If we do not reach it, let death be our limit.
At that time, of the two people, one regretted and turned back, while the other pressed forward until he reached that mountainous region. Much...
Having obtained rare treasures as desired, he drank water, took along all his possessions, and returned to his dwelling to support his parents and provide for his kinsmen.
When those who had repented saw this, their hearts grew hot with regret; thinking, "He has already left and returned, so why do I remain?
they immediately adorned themselves and set out upon the road. This follows and combines the meaning of the two lower lines.

In the first phrase, both the dharma and the simile are revealed; in the second phrase, it is explained solely from the perspective of the dharma. Within the text, the scripture is not cited in its entirety, but rather its underlying intent is employed implicitly.

Since ancient times, those of this vehicle—who possess no provisional means—have all attained perfect enlightenment, transcending the cage of worldly existence while looking down to respond to the minds of the multitudes.
Arousing compassion for those who respond to my call, I realize that I and the Buddha have been truly one and the same since beginningless time. Because he was first awakened, he emerged before me;

yet I alone have failed to realize this, lingering among the common folk. If I contemplate this matter even once, what use is there for regret and burning remorse? If I do not cultivate myself now, upon what can I rely in future lives?

Among the three [sections], the first six lines show that the Buddhas of the past, having completed their causal cultivation, have realized this; the first four lines clarify the Dharmakāya from of old.
The two characters "past" (wǎngfó) refer universally to the Buddhas of the past. This vehicle is precisely the single essence;

like a great white ox carrying an endless load, it is metaphorically called the "Single Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) because it is pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous, transcending all numerical categories. One.
Because the nature of the vehicle (*yāna-svabhāva*) is the true path, it is said to be "without expedient means" (*anupāya*); this is the self-nature *dharmakāya*.
Since its nature is fundamentally true, all who practice will necessarily realize it; thus, it is said that "all become perfectly awakened" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). This is the *svasaṃbhogakāya*.

The previously mentioned realization of merit consists in the permanent transcendence of the two deaths and the permanent severance of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*); once these are severed, one is no longer bound by the three realms.
Because there is no binding or confinement, it is said to be "far beyond the cage. A "cage" (*fánlóng*) is an instrument for imprisoning sentient beings;
that made of wood is called a "pen" (*fán*), and that made of bamboo is called a "cage" (*lóng*). The two following lines clarify the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*):

because the Buddha’s body and mind respond when there is a resonance within the minds of the multitude, it is said he "bends down to respond. This generally refers to the [response-]body and the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Below this are ten [points].

The verses primarily address the present capacity [of the practitioner] to stimulate progress. The first two lines reveal that the nature is identical; the subsequent four lines clarify the distinctions between stages.
"Lingering" refers to being indolent and failing to advance. The final four lines describe awakening through realization and initiating cultivation.
"One" refers to negligence. I am ordinary while the Buddha is holy; the Buddha is awakened while I am deluded. When phenomena manifest and stir the mind, how could one not be moved to indignation?

Thus, I uphold and follow the Brahma Net Sūtra to ensnare the fish and dragons (the sūtra’s metaphors likening internal poison to the dragon that is difficult to touch, and desire-attachment to the whale that swallows the sea);
I bow in reverence to the Three Bodies and rely upon the Three Studies.

In the first section of the initial part on demonstrating the cultivation of the Dharma, the first point is to instruct one to rely upon and follow the teachings, which means to receive and uphold them.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Fanwang) is the sacred teaching; it is like a net capable of catching fish and dragons, for the teaching can ensnare delusions and karma—hence the metaphor.

In the commentary, the dragon is used as a metaphor for anger (*dveṣa*), and the whale for greed and ignorance (*lobha* and *moha*). Although the poison is not explicitly manifested [in the text], it must also be understood to be fully present within.
One should perform the "Angry Whale" gesture; this belongs to the oceanic lineage. Cui Bao’s *Gujin zhu* states: "The large whales are a thousand li long, while the small ones are several zhang;

they drum the waves into thunder and spray foam into rain, drinking water as if it were being poured from a vessel. Regarding the sequence of gestures: first, the "Greeting" (equivalent to the next instruction for rising and walking);

"greeting" refers to respectful yielding, and "wearing" (the belt) refers to being moved to sincere devotion. As for the "Three Bodies," they are— [Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary liturgical or commentary-style passage. The final sentence is incomplete, and the translation reflects the available text.]
The Dharma is that which should transform beings; the three trainings are precept, concentration, and wisdom; the three bodies are the fruit, while the three trainings are the cause.
Inferring the cause from the fruit, and realizing the fruit through the cause, this work provides a summary of the essential principles to demonstrate the core of practice.

Now, at the very beginning of setting foot [upon the path], one first honors the school of the precepts (*śīla*). There are three types of precepts, which are the foundation of the Three Bodies (*trikāya*):

First is the *pratimokṣa-śīla* (the precept of restraint), which means severing all evils; this is the cause of the *dharmakāya*. (Because the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally pure, it is not manifest when obscured by evil; now, through the cultivation of abandoning evil, when the merit is perfected, the virtue becomes manifest.

Second is the *kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas), which means cultivating all forms of goodness; this is the cause of the *saṃbhogakāya*. (The *saṃbhogakāya* is formed by a multitude of virtues; the perfection of these virtues is achieved through the practice of non-ceasing and non-doing.)
Now, by cultivating the two wholesome practices of cessation and activity, one establishes the conditions for the Reward Buddha;

third, the precept of gathering in sentient beings is the compassionate salvation of those with mind, which accomplishes the cause of the Transformation Buddha (for the Transformation Buddha is mindless and responds immediately to stimuli; now, when the intention of great compassion and universal salvation is applied, they are equal).
In the first section of the "Exposition of the Causes of the Precepts," the first part clarifies that the seven groups of practitioners take the precepts as their cause;
next, it clarifies that the three bodies take the precepts as their cause. First, there is a general indication; second, there is a detailed correlation. Regarding "restraint" (*saṃvara*):

it refers to the orderly arrangement of the categories and clusters of offenses, their gravity or lightness, what is permitted or prohibited, and what is maintained or transgressed, so that the models do not fall into confusion. As for "precepts" (*śīla*), they serve as a warning and instruction, as clearly explained in the *Śīla-vyākhyā*.

Regarding the severance of evil: as for the precepts against sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth, which are established in the *Śīla-sūtra*, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, and the various sections on the Vinaya rules, one gives rise to remedial practices and mental attention to guard against them;
this is the practice of "stopping and upholding" (*śamatha-vidharaṇa*), which is the cause of the virtue of severance.

Because the commentary first clarifies the "intrinsic virtue" (*prakṛti-guṇa*) when stating that the Dharma-body is fundamentally pure, the following section now demonstrates the cultivation and manifestation [of that purity].
Therefore, it is said that "leaving behind evil and gathering wholesome dharmas" refers to the practice of the six perfections and myriad deeds;

there is no virtuous principle that is not cultivated. This constitutes the practice of upholding through action. By means of these various virtues, one accomplishes great wisdom; this wisdom-virtue is the cause for the eventual realization of the Buddha of Retribution (*vipākaphala-buddha*).

In the commentary, the phrase "accomplished by virtue" (*śubhena siddham*) reveals the Buddha-virtue of the fruit. Now, the cultivation of cessation (*śamatha*) and activity (*pragraha*) demonstrates the cause.
Regarding "practice": if one relies on "stopping" (śīla) to belong to the superior discipline, then through stopping one achieves goodness and returns to the subsequent aggregate;

this does not obstruct the preceding aggregate, which naturally possesses the three aggregates of action, maintenance, and cultivation, practiced in harmony without contradiction between the preceding and succeeding stages—reflect upon this.

Since the text indicates the fundamental basis, it says "body is the cause"; the commentary indicates that which enables accomplishment, thus calling them "conditions. As for "gathering sentient beings," the preceding...

Second is self-benefit; now, this benefit for others utilizes these two virtues to universally encompass all sentient beings. By universally applying compassion to extract suffering and bestow happiness, this is the practice of benefiting others.
This is the cause of the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), which will result in the attainment of a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha.

In the commentary, the first two phrases clarify the virtue of the fruit: that the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha is "without mind" means being devoid of a mind of attachment or aversion toward self and others.

Because one does not perceive anything to be grasped within attachment, one responds spontaneously according to what is encountered; because of great compassion for all things, one does not abandon sentient beings.

Now, the following clarifies that because the causal practice and the cultivation of compassionate conduct are identical to the function of the fruit, it is said that "the intention and the function are equal."

Regarding the Buddha, there are three [bodies] according to the meaning; these are distinct from the three [other] objects of cognition. All considerations outside of the mind converge upon this principle;
in reality, it is thus and cannot be seen otherwise.

Next, in the first section of the middle part, because the three preceding aggregates are individually assigned to the three bodies, there is a premonition that later generations might actually give rise to three [distinct entities].

Because they are distinct, the first two phrases refer to the aforementioned separate divisions; the subsequent two phrases integrate the objects with the mind, indicating that objects are not external to the mind—this is the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
That is to say, the myriad objects of dust and sand prevented by the precepts are all transformations of consciousness and are therefore not external to the mind.
As the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "One does not falsely take objects as conditions; they are merely..."
"A single consciousness gives rise to a hundred deliberations. The *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* says: "The world returns to the same destination yet takes different paths;
it unifies in a single principle yet involves a hundred deliberations. I have borrowed these latter two lines here to exhort and resolve [the reader] toward the correct principle.

Some may be confused by this and attempt to expand upon it further; however, the root of merit is not propagated without precepts. At the beginning of the Path, when the laity take refuge, they must first reverently receive them.

As the mind arises in response to various objects, there is nothing that does not fall within the three types of precepts: to refrain from harboring evil in one's thoughts throughout one's life is the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint);

to give rise to compassion and perform wholesome deeds is the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas); and to bring about liberation from suffering is the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings).
Since this is so regarding the internal conditions for birth, it is likewise for all three types of Buddhahood.

Within the first two phrases of the section on the perfect observance of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), the intention of their gravity and extensiveness is indicated. Below that, the actual explanation begins. First, the single precept is shown as the three clusters (*tri-skandha*).

This further divides into two parts: first, the essence of the undertaking is indicated; following that, the subsequent practice is indicated. First, the objects of the practice are explained in general.
Since the myriad objects encompass both the animate and the inanimate, the Great Master said: "When a thought moves, there is an object; that object must be guarded by the precepts.

This is explained in detail below according to their respective assignments. Regarding a single lifetime, citing the objects of the precepts, "not harboring evil" demonstrates the characteristic of the precepts.

Thus, the *Yejieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "For example, a single precept against killing encompasses all three positions; it eliminates the conditions for killing and subsumes the Vinaya."
The ritual conduct carries out the mandate of bestowing grace, which is the gathering of wholesome dharmas; because it protects the preceding mandate, it gathers sentient beings.
Since this one case is thus, the others follow the same principle; they are largely identical to this. Next, below, the single essence and the three bodies are shown:

"internal" refers to the mind, and "conditioning" refers to the function of the mind. Since the precepts consist of the three clusters within a single mind, the Buddha likewise consists of the three bodies within a single [essence].
In essence, all things are subsumed within and return to the mind;

there is nothing that is not *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Whether they are separated or unified depends on the occasion, as the relationship between the one and the three is indeterminate. Thus, a sutra states:

"This body of mine is itself the Dharma-body"—this is the fundamental [principle] derived from its traces. It also states: "To perceive me through form and sound is called practicing a deviant path"—this is the trace that differs from the fundamental.

Regarding the first section of the "Meaning of the Teachings on Separation and Union," the first two phrases provide a general enumeration, which is why the following citations and indications are presented.

First, the sutra clarifies the text on "union" from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where "I am Śākyamuni" is a self-reference by Śākyamuni; since his very substance is the Dharmakāya, it is said that "he is [the Dharma-body].

Below this, the intent is indicated: if one distinguishes them by way of phenomena, the fundamental belongs to the True Body (*dharmakāya*), while the trace belongs to the Transformation [Body] (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The body now seeks the true transformation through principle because they are non-dual; thus it is said that the fundamental [nature] arises from the traces.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage clarifies that by departing from the words one sees the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*. Below this, it indicates that the true essence is signless (*animitta*);

therefore, while it is not form or sound, this reveals that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possesses signs, yet these are not real. Thus, the true and the transformed are separated, and the fundamental and the traces are divided.
Therefore it is said that the traces differ from the source.

Thus, the path of Māgha was realized at Mount Vulture Peak as the first illumination; at Jetavana, he opened the governance of the Lesser Vehicle, with the subsequent discourses fully prepared therein, which may be used as a universal mirror.
In the first section of the following division, the initial four lines correctly clarify the first demonstration: the Sudden Teaching.

"Makuta" (摩竭), here translated as "Excellent Victory," refers to the place where the Buddha first attained enlightenment; it was there that he first proclaimed the *Avataṃsaka*—the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle—just as the sun first shines.
Those of superior capacity who were reached by this teaching and awakened upon hearing the Dharma are like high mountains. Next, the Gradual Teaching is demonstrated.
This was because the followers of the Two Vehicles were incapable of receiving the Great Dharma;
therefore, [the Buddha] set aside the Great and bestowed the Small, manifesting birth on the Snowy Peaks to complete his practice and fulfill the fruit upon the Golden Terrace.

From the Deer Park until the Crane Grove, over forty-nine years and more than three hundred assemblies, he guided beings according to their capacities, extensively expounding the various vehicles. Only then did he establish the One Vehicle alone as the ultimate.
Regarding what was taught during the intermediate period of deliverance, it is not that there is no comprehensive integration; rather, its essence is a single Dharma.

Because [the Buddha] opened [the teaching] according to the capacities of sentient beings, those with dull faculties were taught shallow doctrines; thus, emptiness and existence were not balanced, sometimes the single essence was not discussed, sometimes the three trainings followed separate tracks, sometimes the three aggregates were incomplete, or sometimes the three bodies were established separately. Because the faculties were superior, the teaching was complete; therefore, it is the Truth.

In the mundane world, non-duality is not explicitly taught; here, the single essence is revealed, the three trainings are perfectly cultivated, the three aggregates are perfectly fulfilled, and the three bodies are perfectly manifested.

Their separation and union depend upon the timing [of the teaching], which can be seen herein. By comparison with the current text, the meaning of the "perfect" and "distinctive" can be understood as differing from the previous account of Magadha;
thus, it is designated as Jetavana. In full, it is called Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma. "Jetavana" (祇陀) is translated as follows:

The matter of "victory in battle" is cited as usual; it refers to the place where Śākyamuni first established the gradual teaching (*śanadao*) and manifested his transformation according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Thus, it is called the "opening of the governance. Because this is contrasted with those of superior capacity, it is designated as the "Lower Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*).

Because it is contrasted with the *Avataṃsaka*, it is called the "later session" (*houxi*); "session" (*xi*) here means an assembly. The final two lines conclude by clarifying that the general citation of all teachings is nothing other than waiting for the appropriate time.
Thus, the various explanations provided by Bei and others have already been addressed.

Therefore, I first manifest that which arises from conditions (*pratyaya*), and subsequently clarify its nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). I wish to clarify that the essence of nature (*svabhāva-tattva*) is reached through words;

it is not a mere ornamentation, for all things ultimately return to the manifestation of reality (*bhūta-artha*). This is intended to provide a comprehensive understanding of the essence of nature, so that the mind may later be illuminated by the lamp of wisdom, using the textual raft as a means.
It is appropriate to disembark and leave the raft.
The first two lines of the manifest meaning follow from what preceded to introduce the main intent of the text.

First, it describes the state of being lost in delusion, wherein the principle must be made explicit as previously described; the underlying purpose is to clarify the mind, for fear that [the reader] might consider this to be mere rhetorical ornamentation.

This serves to prevent slander; what follows below clarifies that words can only be dispelled after awakening has occurred, which is why it says, "later caught by the trap of the text," etc., thereby universally clarifying that this is awakened understanding. The "lamp of the mind" (*cittadīpa*) is a metaphor; the doubt is that it refers to the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (*akṣayadīpa*) traditionally passed down in the world. It is surrounded by mirrors, with the ten realms encircling it, and a single lamp is placed in the center to symbolize the One Mind. Thus, it is said: "The mirror reflects the ten realms, The lamp illuminates the three worlds. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The lamp of the mind is like a great ocean; within it, the waves of consciousness arise and subside. This means that the mind-lamp is like a vast ocean, and the various waves of the eight consciousnesses arise and cease within it. Therefore, it is said: "The ocean of the mind is tranquil and still; The waves of consciousness arise and subside. Moreover, the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* states: "The mind-lamp shines throughout the ten directions; its light is pure and unobstructed. This means that the mind-lamp radiates throughout the ten directions, its light being pure and free from hindrance. Therefore, it is said: "The mind-lamp shines throughout the ten directions; Its light is pure and unobstructed. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s mind-lamp is eternally abiding and never extinguished. This means that the Tathāgata’s mind-lamp is eternally present and never ceases. Therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata’s mind-lamp is eternal; It is never extinguished. Thus, these passages all clarify that the mind-lamp is the essence of the Tathāgata-garbha. It is not the same as the "Inexhaustible Lamp" mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which refers to the merit of giving lamps to the Buddha. That lamp is merely a physical object used for offerings, whereas the mind-lamp is the luminous nature of the true mind. Therefore, it is said: "The mind-lamp is the essence of the Tathāgata-garbha; It is not the same as the Inexhaustible Lamp of the Lotus Sutra. Thus, one should know that the mind-lamp is the fundamental source of all dharmas, the very substance of the Tathāgata-garbha, and the gate to the path of Buddhahood. It is not something produced by causes and conditions, nor is it a dharma that arises and perishes. It is the true nature of the mind, eternally abiding and unchanging. Therefore, it is said: "The mind-lamp is the source of all dharmas; It is the substance of the Tathāgata-garbha. It is the gate to the path of Buddhahood; It is not produced by causes and conditions. It is the true nature of the mind; Eternally abiding and unchanging. Thus, one should diligently cultivate and maintain this mind-lamp, so that it may shine brightly and illuminate the darkness of ignorance, leading one to attain the fruit of supreme enlightenment. Therefore, it is said: "One should diligently cultivate the mind-lamp; Let it shine brightly to dispel the darkness. By this, one attains supreme enlightenment; This is called the gate of the Tathāgata. Thus ends the explanation. May all beings awaken to this truth. Amity. May there be peace.
