The True and Semblance Dharmas each last one thousand years, while the Final Dharma lasts ten thousand years.
This is merely citing the general figures. Below, this traces back to reveal the decline and flourishing [of the teaching] in order to demonstrate the fixed number. Furthermore...
Regarding the first of the three sections, the initial eight lines state that although the chronological succession of the teachings has been suspended, they have not perished.

The next four lines state that the mandate of Heaven has come to an end and the compassionate light has been eclipsed. The final five lines cite a future Buddha to demonstrate that the teachings have indeed not perished.

Within the first of these [three], the opening line concerns the concealment of the teaching in Central India at the Golden River (*Hiraṇyavatī*); "Bhadra" is the Sanskrit term for the World-Honored One’s *nirvāṇa*.
Because [the Buddha] dwelt on the bank of this river, it is called "West Exhausted" (Xijie). The second phrase refers to the "Flow of the Dharma" (Faliu) in the Eastern Xia (China).

"Jade Pass" (Yuguan) is the name of the pass where the lands of the Yi (barbarians) and Xia (civilized Chinese) meet; it is what is known as the Yumen Pass. As the Buddha-dharma gradually flowed eastward, its traces entered through this very place.

"Dashing forward" (mùchí)—the pronunciation of "mù" is wù—means to gallop. The four phrases following this describe successive generations encountering hardships, yet the Great Dharma remained ever more steadfast; thus, successive generations emerged.

The eighth and ninth [points]: From the *dingmao* year of the Han Emperor Ming’s reign when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived, until the nine successive dynastic changes up to the Tang era, the total span of the sexagenary cycle (*jiǎzǐ*) is over six hundred years.
Regarding the three occasions when the Dharma was eradicated, the *Zhùfǎ túzàn* (Praise of the Illustrations of the Abiding Dharma) states:
"In the early summer, Helian Bobo seized the lands of the Three Qin; he utterly did not believe in the Buddha and used painted images as clothing to wear."
This man had people prostrate before the Buddha as a way of paying homage to me; subsequently, he was struck by lightning and died. When he was buried, lightning struck again and dug him up.
His son, named Mao, succeeded to the throne, destroyed Chang’an, and suppressed the Buddha-dharma; whenever he encountered monks, he would have them executed.
A śramaṇa named Tanshi was wounded by his blade but remained unhurt; because of this, Mao changed his heart. Later, under Emperor Daowu of the Northern Wei, the Way was once again honored.
The scholar Kou Qianzhi established the Daoist Altar for the Way; meanwhile, the Minister of Education Cui Hao slandered the Buddha-dharma, and the Emperor agreed with him.
In the seventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era, he consequently suppressed the Buddha-dharma, ordering the execution of monks by beheading, up to ten thousand.

In the eleventh year, Tanji again remonstrated with the Emperor, who was then afflicted by a malignant illness; he subsequently executed the Cui clan, and his son, Wencheng, re-established the Buddha-dharma.
Guangxian Shaoxu also followed this. Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, he accepted the Daoist Zhang Bin and the former monk Wei Yuansong;

through their slander, he subsequently destroyed the two teachings. Dharma Master An composed the *Lun on the Two Teachings* (*Erjiao lun*) to resist them. When the Emperor heard of this, he realized that the principles for preserving or abolishing [the teachings] were contradictory, and thus he abolished both.
In the third year of Jiande, he swept away [Buddhism] within the Guannei region; in the sixth year, he abolished it throughout the realm.

Tang Guandong claimed for himself that he had achieved his ambitions throughout the world; yet before even a year had passed, his life was lost and his state destroyed—there is no principle by which one can avoid being subverted from below.
Once the conditions for Śākyamuni have ended, the era of Maitreya shall open. When the era opens, it is fitting to manifest; when conditions end, it is fitting to remain hidden.
One hides and one manifests, never failing to accord with the opportune moment; this is to seek the source according to its fundamental basis.
Since the source is truly the one Buddha alone, the Lotus Sūtra states that Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others are all my own body, appearing and disappearing according to the times;

in reality, there is no arising or ceasing. "Conditioned arising" refers to the ripening of the capacity [of sentient beings]. When the Way meets and accords with this capacity, the preaching of the Dharma is easily effective for transformation.
This clarifies that the Jewel of Principle is the foundation of our refuge; therefore, it is examined in detail so that the mind may have a place of reliance.
It is said: "The Way resides in the heart; regardless of whether one is old or young, it is only through resolute vigor that it is called the Way.
With faith thus maintained, what can one not achieve? This is a fine textual proof—how could one fail to reflect upon it?

Within the section on "Bonding" (*bandhana*), one should first ask: "Since this clarifies the essential nature of reality (*tattva*), why is there such extensive discussion of the manifested marks (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*)? This is answered by the text:

it is because one wishes to reveal that the essential nature of reality is the primary principle (*mūla*) of these three types [of bonds], thereby manifesting the fundamental through the derivative so that the mind may have a point of reliance.
Thus, the subsequent citation of scripture to provide exhortation contains two intentions: the first is that its fierce intensity is intended to encourage cultivation; the second...
It is said that the intent of "faith" (śraddhā) is to encourage belief.
Regarding the "three transformed manifestations of the Triple Gem" (triratna):

the term "transformed manifestation" (nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa) is used because they appear with physical forms in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; thus, both the Buddha and the Saṃgha are [included].
The mind that realizes the principle of cessation abides in the signless (*animitta*), yet it manifests these signs;

therefore, they are called "transformed signs" (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). That is to say, Śākyamuni Tathāgata is the Buddha Jewel; the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) he has taught is the Dharma Jewel;
and the prior wisdom that brings an end to suffering is the Saṃgha Jewel. These three transformed jewels may also be termed "distinct characteristics."
In the initial section of the explanation of names and essence within the commentary: "Śākyamuni" is the specific epithet of a single Buddha, whereas "Tathāgata" is the general name for all Buddhas.
Now, the designation "Śākyamuni" is used to manifest the distinction between the particular and the universal; the meaning of these particular and universal names is as commonly heard.
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the same as before; however, while previously it was discussed in terms of the principle realized, here it is based on the teaching proclaimed. First...

Those who possess the wisdom that exhausts suffering encompass the five stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) of the Hīnayāna. First, "wisdom" refers to the persons of the seven preparatory stages (*saptavidha-prayoga*);

as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "first comes dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), followed by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)," referring to those liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*). [As explained therein... "Exhaustion of suffering" refers to those who have realized the four fruits (*catur-phala*).
Having realized the truth and severed suffering, they do not enter the evil destinies (*apāya*). Although the noble ones differ in their specific attainments, they all [possess these qualities].

Regarding the "attained" (sākṣātkṛta), it refers to the suffering attained; this belongs to the preceding principle of the essence (*dharmatā*). Now, because we take the "attainer" (*sākṣātkartṛ*), it is called the "transformed appearance" (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Question:

If one takes the formal appearance (*ākāra*), there is a confusion with the "maintaining" (*sthiti-dhāraṇa*) [aspect]. Answer: One distinguishes them by dividing between ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*). Question:

Does "ordinary" refer to those during the Buddha's lifetime, while "sage" refers to those in the future? Answer: Sages after the Buddha’s passing are not of the transformed appearance; ordinary beings during the Buddha’s lifetime are of the maintaining aspect.
The lower section explains the different names. Question: External schools also discuss the distinctions between specific characteristics and general similarities; how do you respond to this? Answer:

They [the external schools] hold that the Buddha has the three distinct bodies of Dharma, Reward, and Transformation; that the Dharma has the fourfold distinctions of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit;

and that the Sangha has the differences of the Great and Small Vehicles, the eight ranks, and the five stages. This, however, is a general summary based on the three bodies and their phenomena and principles.

Regarding the discussion of distinct characteristics (*biphasa*): if the Huayan school separately emphasizes Vairocana, speaks of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) as distinct, and posits it for those of superior faculties—just as a king differs from the common masses—the term "distinct" used here refers specifically to the aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Thus, the bodies of the various Buddhas differ; for instance, the physical dimensions and lifespans of the bodies of Śākyamuni, Amitābha, and others vary in size and duration.

Question: Since the True Dharma is taught according to the various differences among sentient beings, it is called "distinct characteristics" (*betsusō*); thus, while the names are the same, the meanings differ as can be distinguished above.

If one were to correlate the three bodies (*trisambhoga*) with the present four jewels, what would the principle be? Answer: Regarding the three bodies, if distinguished according to the teachings, they are not the same;
however, if investigated according to the ultimate principle, they are in reality only a single Buddha. Because he descends from his original state to manifest traces, there [are these distinctions].
Regarding the two bodies (the True and the Responsive), there are three bodies (Dharma, Enjoyment, and Transformation) according to the capacities of beings, whether great or small.

When wisdom and principle are distinguished, there are four bodies in total: (1) The Self-Nature Dharma Body (*svabhāva-dharmakāya*), which is the principle shared by both ordinary beings and sages; (2) the Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*), which is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifested through cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas; (3) the Other-Enjoyment Body (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*), which arises from the essence as function to respond specifically to superior capacities and is the Equality Wisdom;

and (4) the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which responds to the capacities of the Three Vehicles by preaching the Half and Full Teachings and is the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks. Now, regarding the Dharma [Body] at the causal stage of the Self-Nature...

The body is assigned to the single essence; the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) is assigned to the fruit as its own nature (*svabhāva*), while the enjoyment body for others (*parasambhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) both belong to the manifested marks (*nimitta*), as each is taught according to the specific capacities of sentient beings. Their provisional establishment through maintenance cannot be so assigned here;
furthermore, although they are distinguished according to phenomena, they ultimately converge in the single principle.

The substance [of the Buddha] is impermanent and subject to the transformation of the four marks; though it has passed away more than a thousand years ago, one may only honor its distant legacy to increase one’s reverent devotion.
Regarding the initial section on the "substance and form," this is a formal demonstration based on the Jewel of the Buddha;

the four marks are birth, aging, sickness, and death, such as the Buddha manifesting the appearance of birth and the appearance of passing away for humans. Other schools refer to these as conditioned, untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*). Below, [the text discusses] cessation.

The "Exhortation to Reverently Honor the Ancestors" is excerpted from the *Analects*, which states that since the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, one no longer beholds his compassionate countenance;
one can only look back with longing and contemplate the Sage’s grace, thereby giving rise to a heart of reverence.
Since the three Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have already passed away, and the fourth Buddha, Amitābha, has not yet appeared, upon whom can sentient beings rely?
Left to sink long in the ocean of suffering with no path to liberation, the Muni (Śākyamuni) has appeared in this world at the appointed time to preach the Dharma and deliver humanity.
In the first section of the initial division on "Manifesting Meritorious Benefits," it first points back to the Buddhas of the past to clarify the purpose for appearing in this world.
Regarding the "Auspicious Eon" (*bhadrakalpa*): it is so named because one thousand sages appear within this eon. As for the "three Buddhas who have already passed":
the first was Krakucchanda, the second Kanakamuni, and the third Kāśyapa. Once these three Sages had entered extinction, their orthodox teaching became latent.

If the four Buddhas did not appear, sentient beings would have no one to rely upon; this passage below reveals that [the Buddha] has now manifested his activity to illuminate and succeed to the holy legacy,
opening the wondrous gate of the Eightfold Path and demonstrating the level way of the Single Vehicle, leading others out from the mire of desire of humans and devas, and far—

Ascending the ferry and raft of the worthy and sages to approach this Way, there is a gradual progression through which one may attain it. By expounding the principles of the Three Jewels, one causes sentient beings to turn toward them;

is this not because the True Dharma abides eternally? Riding upon the provisional to govern the ultimate, one loosens the bonds of body and mind and is called a Son of the Buddha—a guest who receives the Way.
Realizing the fundamental purity of the essence of clarity, the metaphors of the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare reveal the profound principle of the emptiness of nature.
The meaning of the phenomena is radiant, the divine function is luminous, and the cycle of birth and death upon which all living beings depend is brought to an end.

Regarding the first section of the middle part [of the text], there is first the formal demonstration and then the conclusion on receiving the Way. Within the first of these, the first two phrases provide a general demonstration of the Dharma-gate being taught;
the Eightfold Right Path consists of right view, thought, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration—these eight, taken collectively, are as follows:
Regarding these three trainings: the first two belong to wisdom (*prajñā*), the middle three belong to ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the final three belong to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is precisely by means of distinguishing the right from the wrong gate that one enters the Path; since the noble ones of the Three Vehicles enter by way of this, it is the direct and level path, which is itself the One Vehicle.

The following two lines, "near and low," indicate the intent behind establishing the teachings: if categorized according to the Five Vehicles, they serve to extract beings from the suffering of the three miserable realms and—

The bliss of humans and devas refers to these very beings as the point of departure; now, according to the fundamental intent, although humans and devas are superior, they still remain mired in the mud of desire.
Therefore, the three vehicles are established to enable them to transcend the triple world. Thus it is said: "near departure" and "distant ascent.
Furthermore, what was previously termed the Eightfold Path is the raft upon which one rides; what is now called the noble ones (*ārya*) refers to the persons who ride that vehicle. (8)

The correct principle is that the Three Vehicles are cultivated together by sages and saints; yet, as for the distinct stages of the Great and Small [Vehicles], there is a single, level path upon which the Bodhisattva travels alone to reach the ultimate destination.
This is the Buddha’s fundamental intent. The following four lines are set forth to demonstrate the sequence of his transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*).

This Path is the very essence of the Three Jewels (*triratna*); when one sets aside conventional names and accords with the principle, this is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and this Vehicle is profound.

Because wondrous entry must proceed through gradual stages, the Eightfold Path and the Three Vehicles are established as steps and gradations; subsequently, the One Vehicle is taught to reveal the principle.
When sentient beings hear and understand this, they attain realization of the One Vehicle—all of which is due to the True Suchness (tathatā) that is the principle taught.

How could the following four lines fail to praise the Sage’s intention? His methods of transformation are formal and systematic, yet the essence of the principle is real, while the manifestations of the transformation are provisional.

This is the provisional principle; its essence is formless, yet without the provisional there would be no manifestation. Therefore, one employs the provisional of the phenomenal marks of transformation to govern the reality of the essential principle;
thus it is said: "Riding on the provisional to govern the real. Sentient beings have their forms and minds bound by worldly habits, like shackles and fetters.
The Buddha bestows the wondrous teaching to liberate them, like loosening those bonds. To speak of "sons of the Buddha" refers to the Dharma.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Truly, these sons of the Buddha are born from the mouth of the Buddha; they are born through transformation by the Dharma, and they obtain a portion of the Buddha-Dharma.

In this passage, the first two phrases clarify the attainment of benefit regarding the capacity [of the practitioner] that has realization: this refers to original purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). The latter two phrases clarify what is revealed through the teaching:
this refers to the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*). That deluded thoughts are fundamentally quiescent is called "clarity" (*prasāda*); it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

"Natural" (tianzhen) refers to the fundamental purity of the nature; because it is fundamentally pure, it is called "nature-emptiness" (xingkong). Regarding the "matter" (shi), this next section concludes with a praise of the first two lines:

the first praises the teaching, for it is through the teaching that the principle is revealed; the second praises the "mystical function" (shenyong), for it is through wisdom that the capacities [of beings] are discerned.

"Radiance" (guang) means luminous manifestation; "clarity" (ming) means there is nothing hidden. The final two lines praise the capacity [of the audience], which relies upon the "provision" (zi)—that is, the teacher.

Because they reverently received the Master’s teachings and reverently practiced them, all attained realization of the fundamental principle; thus it is said that "birth and death have been exhausted.

Now that his great work was fully accomplished, he announced the arrival of the end of his allotted years. By manifesting physical form through non-form, he demonstrated that the Dharma-body does not perish;
by leaving behind bone-relics through formlessness, he showed that the traces of his transformation do not vanish. Thus, he shattered his body to engender faith in sentient beings.
With his all-seeing eyes he guides through divine power; regarding this Way, one cannot conceive of its grace, nor can one repay it.
Within the section on "Arising, Abiding, and Sustaining," the first subsection clarifies the manifestation of the signs of transformation and the display of passing into extinction.

That "the matters of transformation were flourishing" refers to the profusion of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s transformative activities throughout his single lifetime. However, where there is flourishing, there must be decline; where there is birth, there must be extinction. Since that which was performed...
Because it was necessary to enter *nirvāṇa*, he spoke of the end of his allotted lifespan; this was not primarily to clarify the origin of birth.

First, by manifesting the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to reveal the true body (*dharmakāya*), he demonstrated that it does not perish. Having spoken of entering extinction, he then returned to the *dharmakāya*;

because the *dharmakāya* is perfect stillness, it is said to be "not form. Yet, emerging from the golden coffin, he again manifested his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); thus it is said that "form appears," even though [the transformation-body] has already ceased.
Furthermore, it is manifested as something verifiable, never lost, and without inferiority. Next, the presiding [monk] employs this to manifest the signs of transformation;
because the signs of transformation have already ceased, it is said that "there is no form," yet because the relics still remain, it is said that "the bones and fragments of the body are preserved.

Regarding "the shattered holy body of a Vajra becomes the relic-bones," Wang Bo stated this. Regarding "the complete eye," the *Śākyamuni Fāngzhì* (Record of Śākyamuni’s Regions) states: [The text continues with the description of the relics.]
The city of Nāgalāra is the ancient city of Pāṭaliputra. More than thirty *li* to the southeast of the city, there is the Buddha’s skull, shaped like a lotus leaf;
its color is yellowish-white. There is also the Buddha’s eye, as large as a crabapple, with a clear, translucent blue-and-white luster.
The following section concludes by manifesting the power of the transformative signs, thereby demonstrating that the true Buddha possesses these inherent capabilities himself.
Benefiting sentient beings and further sustaining this [Dharma]—this kindness and virtue are boundless and difficult to repay; hence it is said that they cannot be thanked.
Therefore, one should reverently support the stupas and images and give rise to the root of faith; only by first preparing this mind will one come to know the details.
Next, because one wishes to establish the maintenance [of the Dharma] within this [teaching], one first exhorts faith; this is precisely the mind of faith.
Regarding the "Fourfold Maintenance of the Triple Gem":

among these four, the term "maintenance" (zhuchi) is designated; "maintenance" means that "dwelling" (zhu) refers to abiding in the world, and "holding" (chi) refers to sustaining [the lineage] without interruption.

It is through human agency that the Way is magnified; for ten thousand years, compassion has flowed forth. The Way relies on humans to be propagated, and thus the Three Dharma-seals were opened and established in this world.

Consequently, from generation to generation, the teachings have flourished and been planted, and they have been transmitted and spread everywhere. Had it not been for the monks who proclaimed them, the Buddha-dharma would have remained submerged.

For instance, during the height of Emperor Wu of Han’s reign, the name of the Buddha was first heard; yet, as the transmission of the monks was severed, the opening of the lineage was exhausted. It was only when Emperor Ming of the Later Han opened [the path]...

It was through the diligent travels of Dharmakṣema to China that Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmarakṣa were able to come and grace the land with their presence. They propagated the teachings of the voice and transformed the customs of the people, establishing their affairs;

they inspired faith and led others to take refuge in the heart. This was truly due to the labor of their extensive preaching and relied upon the power of their exemplary conduct; such individuals are indeed the jewels among monks.
In the "Explanation of the Middle," the inference regarding the Sangha Jewel has three parts. First, the initial eight lines establish the principle and infer the merit;

next, the following ten lines use concrete matters to reveal the reality by way of contrast; finally, the last three lines provide a concluding judgment. Within the first part, the initial four lines clarify the correspondence between person and dharma:
the upper two lines concern the person propagating the dharma, while the lower two lines infer the person by means of the dharma. These are the three dharmas.
The Three Jewels: the final four lines specifically manifest the merit of transmitting the Dharma and maintaining the teachings through successive generations across time and in various locations;

the meaning of "establishing and propagating" is equivalent to "circulating and spreading. Regarding the first two lines of the middle section, it is said that without the Sangha, the Dharma cannot be propagated;
this refers to Emperor Wu of Han—specifically Emperor Wu of the Former Han—who, during the Yuanshou era, launched a northern expedition against the Xiongnu and captured their King.
The Jin people regarded him as a great deity and enshrined him in the Ganshui Palace to be worshipped. Later, while dredging the Kunming Pool, black ashes were discovered.
When they questioned Dongfang Shuo about them, he said, "This is not something I know; you may ask a foreign monk from the Western Regions.
By this, the "foreign monk" refers to the Buddha. The following six sentences were opened by a monk.
Dharmakṣema’s "Zong" refers to Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the second sovereign, whose posthumous title was Xianzong (Manifest Ancestor).
He was the fourth son of Emperor Guangwu. In the third year of the Yongping era, during the night, [the Emperor] dreamed of a golden man. Fu Yi memorialized, saying:
"Your servant has heard that there is a Sage in the West whose teachings will flow to this land a thousand years hence; what Your Majesty has dreamed must surely be him."
In the seventh year, the Jiazi year, Cai Yin and others were dispatched on an imperial mission to seek [the Dharma].
Upon reaching the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi, they encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who arrived from the West carrying scriptures upon white horses and painted images of the Sage.
In the tenth year, the Dingmao year, they returned together to the land of Han; this was the beginning of the Three Jewels in the Divine Land (Zhōushén) through these two venerable masters.

He first proclaimed the compassionate teachings, bringing joy and submission to those of heterodox views; he manifested rare spiritual powers and opened the faith of those whose potential was yet unawakened.
From then on, his virtuous transformation caused people to bow like grass before the wind, and even unto this day, all continue to receive his bounty.

That which is spoken—names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*)—takes the principle (*artha*) as its priority; since the principle cannot be apprehended through awakening without verbal expression, the conditions of speaking and listening based upon these names and teachings are called the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).

Next, within the section on the Dharma, the primary purpose is to correctly demonstrate that [the teaching] does not transcend sound, name, phrase, and syllable, taking the textual expressions of both the Great and Small Vehicles as its basis.

The "entity" (tǐ) refers to names and words (*nāma-pada*), which are the expressive phrases for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); the "phrases" (*jù*) refer to the syntactic units (*vākya*), which are the expressive [terms] for specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

These two are alike neither matter nor mind, as they necessarily depend on sound for their transmission; therefore, it is said they are "that which is spoken. The above concerns the principle of the expresser (*vācaka*);
since this is the principle that is expressed (*vācya*), it is said to "manifest the principle. The following provides the concluding demonstration.
This principle is profound and subtle; none but a Sage knows it. Although the Sage has passed away, his image remains established—this is called the Jewel of the Buddha.
Within the Jewel of the Buddha, the first two lines infer the person by means of the Dharma, while the final three lines explicitly manifest the Jewel of the Buddha itself.

It is simply because the merit of sentient beings is shallow that they do not reach the source of transformation; yet, possessing meager remaining resources, they still encounter the Dharma left behind.

The first two lines express joy at meeting [the teachings], while the second set of two lines reproaches oneself for failing to meet the manifest form of transformation—this being due to heavy obstructions—and rejoices in having encountered the surviving image, truly thanking one's past causes.
The essence of these Three Jewels is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and fully possessed of outflows and defilements; it is insufficient as an object of veneration.
Nevertheless, it is the support for the Jewel of Principle (*dharmaratna*), which possesses the capacity to be honored and respected, and from which [the Jewel of the Community] emerges accordingly.

Regarding the first section of the initial part on "Inferring Reverence Based on Substance," the first four lines demonstrate the substance [of the Buddha]: that the Buddha is made of wood and earth, while the Dharma consists of paper and silk—all of which are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Pointing upward, it refers to Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna as the Jewel of the Saṅgha; how could they be called free from outflows (*anāsrava*)?

Now, based on the fact that in this final age most are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their state of being with outflows and defilements means, in principle, they are not worthy of reverence. However, when inferring their merit below...
The first [of the three jewels] is able to manifest the principle, while the second is able to guide sentient beings.
Just as when a secular king’s messenger travels through various regions, they are not honored for their physical appearance but for their singular office; thus, the sutra says:

"In the world, silver and gold are considered the supreme treasures; yet where there is no silver, brass is also called priceless. Therefore, the respect accorded to the Three Jewels at the end [of the age] is likewise so.
To perfect one’s truthfulness:
if one does not now add reverence, there will be no further means to show respect; where can the mind be directed, and upon what can it rely for refuge?

Therefore, outwardly one pays respect to the sublime form, while inwardly the mind dwells on the ultimate truth. Guiding conditions and establishing transformation, the meaning reaches its pinnacle here.
In the section on "Reproving Faults and Exhorting Practice," the first four lines demonstrate the faults of disrespect; thus, the following two lines establish the method of reverence.
Here, the physical form belongs to that which can be revered, while the sublime countenance (*liṅyi*) belongs to that which is revered.

To revere the image with the body and to contemplate the principle with the mind—whether one contemplates the object of reverence as the very essence of reality (*tattva*), or understands it through *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)—the conventional and the ultimate are perfected within the pure mind.
The meaning of "cultivation" is as explained below. The final two lines conclude by describing the sublime ritual of making images.
The Sūtra states: "By fashioning an image [the size of] a grain of wheat, one obtains inexhaustible merit, for it is a vessel for the Dharmakāya.

The Śāstra states: "Gold, wood, stone, and earth are insentient in their substance; yet because they are used to fashion images, those who show respect or contempt toward them personally obtain merit or transgression."
The Dharma-body is not manifested, which causes its functional efficacy to be infinite.
Among the four [sections], the first cites the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (Unsurpassed Basis Sūtra) to use the extremely small as a metaphor for the great;
the second cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to infer its principle by means of non-sentient things. The scriptural passages are fully cited below; the offenses and merits are the same as above.
This is what is clarified.
Thus, when practitioners with a mind encounter these sacred vestiges, there are none who do not shed tears that flow profusely, nor fail to feel an increase in reverence.

Since the true form has already passed away and only the remaining traces remain, it is as if one were standing before a pure ancestral temple; naturally, a sense of sorrow and solemnity arises at every glance.
I feel as though he were still here, free from doubt; I am now just like that. Since the Compassionate Honored One has long since departed, only his image remains to topple the banner of my pride.
Therefore, I must bow down and prostrate at its feet, as if before his true form, so that he might preach the Dharma for me.
Yet, not seeing nor hearing him now, my mind lacks faith. How can this be known? It is simply because when the mind is directed toward it, even the three realms...

How could this single hall be so stubbornly dull and unmoving? The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "The Buddhas constantly emit light and preach the Dharma, yet because sentient beings have committed sins since beginningless time, they do not see them even when face-to-face."

In the first section of the initial matter within the demonstration of reverence for the Dharma, there are two parts. First, the demonstration of the sentiment of reverence as if facing [the Buddha] below;

second, the reprimand for failing to perceive the transgression. Within the first part, the first four lines directly demonstrate the sentiment of reverence, while the subsequent lines trace back and develop the reason for this reverence:

because one does not see the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation Buddha), but sees only the *dharmatā-kāya* (sustaining Buddha), one is moved by this to give rise to sorrowful yearning. The following four lines explain this further.

Citing common worldly examples to illustrate the *Qingmiao* (Pure Temple)—that is, the ancestral temple of the state—where the countenances and deportment of the ancestors are depicted so that descendants may perform sacrifices and show reverence, thereby strengthening the virtue of their progenitors; thus it is called the *Qingmiao*. The present case is comparable to this.
Now, the four lines below conform to the principle; specifically, the final two lines employ the facts to infer the underlying sentiment, which must be further augmented.

Respectfully following the middle section, there are again three parts. First, the initial four lines invoke the facts to offer a direct reprimand: since the Buddha is impartial, one should respond with sincere devotion;
yet, though the spirit is moved by such sincerity, the response is not yet attained because I lack faith. This failure arises from the mind; what follows next?

The subsequent five lines inquire into and reveal the distinction between reverence and arrogance. First, they cite a factual analogy to illustrate the function of the mind—that is, volition—and how the mind creates goodness.
The retribution for evil is divided into the six realms because karma consists of both determinate and indeterminate types; thus, the three worlds are distinguished.

How could one use the analogy of reverence to argue that a single moment of deluded mind can still form the three worlds, yet a sincere heart and firm faith cannot move the sacred images in a hall to emit light and manifest auspicious omens to demonstrate their spiritual efficacy? Regarding this stubborn ignorance, the aforementioned text states:

Statues are insentient objects whose nature is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). [The following three citations from the treatise] serve as a counter-proof for the faults of those who lack faith.

Since this must be so for one statue, it follows by analogy for all others; trees, stones, mountain forests, and so forth are established according to their characteristics to guide the path of our minds, never exceeding the sacred ritual forms.
The subsequent section has two parts: first, because it does not focus exclusively on a single image, it is said that "other images" follow this same principle;

second, because it does not focus exclusively on sacred images, it encompasses all phenomena, for since the mind manifests through objects and the mind pervades all objects, trees, stones, and so forth all represent the sacred countenance.

Furthermore, one forms this thought: "To see that although there is form, it is the mind that perceives form, and that there are no external objects apart from the mind, is called 'True Contemplation' (paramārtha-vipaśyanā).
To say that [objects] arise from the mind and that they are in reality 'mere consciousness' (vijñapti-mātra) is called 'Conventional Contemplation' (saṃvṛti-vipaśyanā)."

The first section of the *Lízhōng* (Meaning of the Middle) is precisely the wondrous contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*). Question: Since this passage elucidates the Three Jewels, why does it speak of "Consciousness-Only"?

Answer: It is logically appropriate to do so. The initial teaching of the "single essence" (*eka-rasa*) is precisely Consciousness-Only. The term "one" excludes duality; it negates the existence of external objects.

This essence is the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which expresses the reality of the principle (*tattva*). When one cultivates and realizes this essential principle, one transforms consciousness to achieve [enlightenment].
First, wisdom; next, based on the realization of the principle, the manifested aspect appears—this is the manifestation of function from essence.
Finally, based on the manifested aspect, the arising and maintenance [of the teachings] occur—this is the preservation of traces through function.

Although there are differences between the essence and function of delusion and awakening, all are without exception the outflow of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Nevertheless, the Three Jewels of the Buddha-Dharma currently maintained are insentient.

The Sangha, though possessed of outflows and defilements, is fundamentally one with the source where truth and falsehood arise together; yet, without the integration provided by contemplation, they lack the capacity for purification.
Therefore, by now employing principle to integrate phenomena, the body faces the sacred icons while the mind dwells upon ultimate truth.
Ultimate truth is precisely the fundamental nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*), which is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas; thus, one is enabled to perform acts of reverence.
When a person, through the ritual demeanor of paying homage to the abbot, attains the wondrous contemplation of Vijñaptimātratā (consciousness-only), realizes the true nature of the single essence,

and witnesses the Dharmakāya of the principle-body— it is known that our Patriarchs, by means of this single dharma of reverent salutation, extensively revealed the intent regarding the ultimate and conventional truths,
precisely to clarify the true contemplation of Vijñaptimātratā. Furthermore, this is discussed here specifically in terms of the supreme object of veneration.

Regarding the clarification of the ultimate and conventional truths: if one can respectfully attend to the principles of the actions performed by body and mind, these matters are all explained in detail in the "Section on the Ultimate and Conventional.

This section consists of two parts. The first three lines summarize the preceding events to reveal the general principle; the subsequent five lines specifically demonstrate the ultimate and conventional truths.

Within the first part, because the principle is elucidated through specific events, it says, "Furthermore, one forms this thought," which refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the cognitive faculty capable of contemplation.

Form (*rūpa*) is the object of veneration for spiritual images; because it is perceived as having substantial reality through the deluded views of the emotional mind, it is said that "seeing is form," which is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Now, entering into correct contemplation, the perfect understanding of wondrous wisdom realizes that these are merely objects manifested by one's own mind;
thus it is said that "understanding form, the mind arises," which is the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Question: Does the mind encompass both the true and the deluded?
Regarding the question of whether this arising of the mind is true or false: if one considers it from the perspective of the true giving rise to the false, there is only the single true mind.

However, in the present context of returning from the false through gradual cultivation, a sequence is necessary. According to the subsequent mundane contemplation (*sāṃvṛta-darśana*), two aspects of mind should be included here.
The first is that what arises from the mind is the six consciousnesses and mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*); thus, names and appearances (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) exist. The second is...

The reality that "only consciousness exists" means that the eight consciousnesses are the falsely manifested objects; because it encompasses both meanings of "having images," it is said that "the mind gives rise [to them].
Of these, the middle and upper two lines clarify true contemplation (*tathatā-vipaśyanā*), while the lower three lines manifest conventional contemplation (*saṃvṛti-vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the first point, "there are no external objects outside the mind": since one has previously realized that form arises from the mind, one is now able to analytically dispel [the notion of external objects].

The false attachment to external objects is overturned by the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature); because one realizes the *animitta-lakṣaṇa* (signless nature), it is called "True Contemplation.

The *Xingshichao* states: "All dharmas and external objects are fundamentally non-existent. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Knowing that objects do not exist, one penetrates the True [nature]... (and so forth).

Within "Conventional Contemplation," the aforementioned "True Contemplation" is applied: form is subsumed within the mind; once the characteristics of form are emptied, the characteristics of the mind must likewise be emptied.
To reveal that the mind has two aspects, it says that "arising from the mind" refers to mental discourse (*manojalpa*). If it were merely mental discourse, it would be confused and unreal;

although pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*) is empty, if one only dispels false objects while failing to understand the dependent nature (*paratantra*), one will ultimately remain bound by pervasive imagination.
Therefore, to dispel this confusion and specifically indicate the source of the mind, it says: "In reality, consciousness alone exists; both are aspects of the mind."

Therefore, it is called conventional observation (*saṃvṛti-darśana*). One must know that what was previously explained as true observation (*tattva-darśana*) is devoid of the conventional, and what is subsequently explained as conventional observation is devoid of the true;
one should understand them as being observed simultaneously and not doubt their sequence. Question: At what stage can a person abide in this observation? Answer:
Since the stages of practice differ, they cannot be treated as a single category. Speaking in terms of practice, even an ordinary person at the initial stage [can do so].
To cultivate this contemplation is itself to designate such a person as a great bodhisattva; for it is taught that these practices are the conduct for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood.
Thus the text says: "The four stages of Consciousness-Only are studied by both ordinary beings and sages. The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"At the very moment of generating the mind at the beginning of the ten stages of faith, one contemplates the essence of the causal and resultant aspects of the dependent origination of the fundamental consciousness's own nature, thereby achieving [realization]."

Based on the position of "Correct Faith" (*samyag-śraddhā*) and according to the texts and treatises, the practitioner who acts through aspiration and joy (*adhimukti-caryā-pratipanna*) is able to realize this principle (namely, the forty stages of mind and the four preparatory practices).
Question: Various schools include all four positions within this; why do you now specifically differ from them? Please explain the reason. Answer:

Because they do not recognize the characteristics of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-lakṣaṇa*), there is confusion and overlap. This contemplation only eliminates external objects; however, mental discourse (*manojalpa*) still remains.
How could one attain this false penetration of high stages? Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"If one has reached the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), then even the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that resembles *vijñapti-mātra* cannot be established. Now, observing this mental verbalization, how could it possibly penetrate high stages?

The text clearly judges it to belong to those who practice the path in the Stage of Joyful Aspiration (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Question: Since it is said to be the "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*), how can it be so described?
This statement does not refer exclusively to those who practice the path within the stage of "aspiration and joy" (pramuditā-bhūmi).
The text itself explains this regarding the stage of cultivation: "The path is for people to cultivate; people are able to cultivate the path. How could one fail to understand this?

Gradually increasing in clarity, there is no moment when it ceases; as merit accumulates, the power of cultivation increases further, and the path of contemplation becomes refined and clear, so that one is not deluded by the provisional names of conditions.

This refers to those who delight in the stage of practice, the practitioners of the Way. Because the Way is cultivated by persons, and because persons can cultivate the Way, such a practitioner is called a "person of the Way" (*dōjin*).

In the section on "Cultivation through Causes" (*yinxiu xianwei*), the first six lines describe the sequential observation that initiates cultivation; the following two lines clarify its practice and stage;

and the final four lines provide a reverse explanation of the path of observation, clarifying that one abides in true contemplation (*zhenguang*) while not being deluded by conditioned phenomena (*yuanjia*), and abides in conventional contemplation (*suguan*) while not obscuring the ritual protocols of phenomena (*shiyi*). Furthermore, the path of observation is itself the observing wisdom (*nengguanzhi*) regarding conditioned phenomena.

The "object of observation" refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) of all dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*). "Provisional" means provisionally existent, referring to consciousness which depends upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

That which is dependently originated is fundamentally non-existent; this is the realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). That which is provisionally existent as consciousness-only is the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Because the wisdom of observation is clear and the distinction between the ultimate and conventional truths is manifest, it is said that one is "not deluded," and so forth, regarding those who aspire to the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

The provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*) are as previously explained. Regarding the practitioner on the path, the text itself provides its own explanation, which differs from that of the ancients;
this refers to the stage of cultivating the path.

Now, as for "hearing the instruction and harboring resentment," this truly constitutes a record of actual fact, referring to what is called "daily decline. This is self-evident herein, so it need not be further questioned.
A word of caution!

Within the intent of this admonition, it is meant that if anyone hears what has been told here and gives rise to suspicion, they should simply take these true words and records as a means to awaken themselves;
thus, may their afflictions diminish day by day and their contemplative path be renewed daily.
*The Commentary on the Ritual for Taking Refuge and Paying Homage in the Śākyamuni School: Penetrating the Truth*, Scroll One.
*The Commentary on the Ritual for Taking Refuge and Paying Homage in the Śākyamuni School: Penetrating the Truth*, Scroll Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shì Lǎorán of Xiàoshān during the Great Song Dynasty.

Chapter Three: Establishing Teachings According to Capacities (*Suiji lizhiao pian*). (This means that wisdom has degrees of obscurity and clarity, and reverence is maintained between principle and phenomena.

Regarding the title of this chapter, "Establishing Teachings According to Capacities": "capacities" (*ji*) refers to those who are to be taught (*suobei*), while "teachings" (*jiao*) are that which perform the teaching (*nengbei*).

The two characters "accordingly establishing" (*sui li*) pertain to the Master of the Teaching. If one traces the treasury of teachings back to antiquity, they originate with the World-Honored One; however, according to the present text, they properly...
In my ancestor’s commentary, the first phrase of the verse reveals the differences in spiritual capacity (*mūka*), while the second phrase demonstrates the distinctions in the teachings (*śāsana*).
The preface states: "Ritual (*li*) means to tread upon; it is simply reverence (*jing*). This refers to what the Sūtra says: "To revere stūpas and temples, and to show humility toward bhikṣus."
In the first section of this text, the first part correctly explains the upper phrase by clarifying its definition, while the lower part indicates its underlying intent;

the text of the passage comes from the *Xiaojing*, and the subsequent citations come from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Although Confucianism and Buddhism differ, there is no distinction between their reverence and righteousness.

Thus, as their natures range from the obscure to the enlightened, their calculations and deductions are mostly limited; they largely follow conventional names and forms while rarely harboring far-reaching insights.
Consequently, they merely practice by following the literal text and transmit what they have heard on the road, never engaging in critical discussion. They recklessly compose chapters and sentences;

even in secular learning it is said that "to learn without thinking leads to delusion, and to think without learning leads to peril. How much more so in the Buddha-dharma, which is profound and mysterious, encompassing both principle and phenomena?
That which is heard immediately leads to various forms of sinking and delusion according to one's practice.

Next, the capacity for the teaching (*mārga*) is clarified; within the section on the "initial capacity," the first two lines provide a general explanation of the sharp and dull faculties, while the subsequent section specifically addresses those of dull roots.
Herein, "nature" refers to the spiritual vessel (*indriya*); since these vessels are either sharp or dull, they involve varying degrees of obscurity and clarity as one progresses through the stages.

"Universal versus limited" refers to the difference between those who study broadly and those who specialize. Because those of sharp nature and quick intelligence are comprehensive and vast in their learning, they are "universal";

because those of dull nature and obscured consciousness are narrow in their focus, they are "limited. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the formal critique; second, the citation of secular examples as an illustration.

In the first part, the first two lines show that biased and limited views of knowledge and insight mostly follow the vulgarities of studying mere names and appearances, while few harbor thoughts of the profound and far-reaching.

This is a narrow view. Regarding the four lines cited below, the explanations and transmissions are erroneous; they were heard from the roadside and passed down through hearsay. The text originates from the *Analects*, where it says: "To speak of the road.
In the middle section, the initial passage correctly cites the text from the *Analects*: "If one learns but does not reflect, the meaning will be obscure;

if one reflects but does not learn, one's achievements will not be distinguished. Furthermore, regarding the initial line of the subsequent admonition, it states: "Its... [The text here appears to be truncated].
The second phrase refers to the profundity of principle; the following two phrases reveal the narrowness of their understanding.

To seek a profound and vast gateway with such shallow and narrow views results in a lack of great perspective and instead leads to heterodox attachments. Not only do they sink into ruin themselves, but they also frequently mislead others;
hence it is said that their "sinking and drowning are not few."

As for the fact that when the sutras clarify the boundless virtues of the Buddhas in the Pure Lands, one dares not shift one's mind from them upon hearing their names, cherishing and never forgetting them;

yet, upon first hearing of the impure lands, one feels not a single joy in the hearts of the Buddhas there, immediately claiming they have no virtues to which one can turn and that one’s own sins cannot yet be extinguished—how can such hatred and love be so extreme?
Truly, this is insufficient for a detailed examination. Furthermore, I have heard it discussed in treatises:

The passage on "Much Treasure" (*Prabhūtaratna*) addresses those who, at another time, lead themselves into indolence while claiming their own practice is the fruit of resolute diligence; they immediately engage in worshipful recollection, yet severing conditions and cutting off turbidity is the conduct of the dull-witted and ignorant, a stubborn adherence to worldly ways.
In the next section, first, there is the attachment to both lands, giving rise to love and hatred; the first four lines concern the attachment to the Pure Land Sutra, namely the *Amitābha*.

In the *Contemplation Sūtra* and other texts, the first four lines below [the heading] disparage the defiled; "chà" (乍) means "suddenly" or "as if. Because the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and evil world are characterized by manifold sufferings and impurity, it is called a "defiled land" (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*).
The section beginning with "Hé" (何) below reproaches delusion. Next, the section beginning with "Yòu" (又) below adheres to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) as the ultimate teaching (*nītārtha*).

This passage is cited from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*; that treatise states that there are four kinds of intentions (*abhiprāya*) in the sūtras: the intention of equality (*samatā-abhiprāya*), the intention of another time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*), and so forth.
The first intention concerns the distinct meaning; the second intention concerns the inclinations of sentient beings. What is now called the "distinct time" refers to the second intention. It says:
"For example, as the sutra states, if a person recites and upholds the name of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, they will certainly never again fall back from unsurpassed bodhi.
This merely cites the case of one who is indolent to show that [the result] is accomplished at a different time; it does not mean that the Tathāgata does not accord with [the individual's capacity].

Because it was appropriate to speak [of this], he then took up this practice, asserting that it could lead to the ultimate fruit. [The Master] rebuked him in general for his turbid and inferior nature:
"Though one's habits may have persisted for a long time, they must ultimately be gradually transformed; if one does not renew oneself, an ordinary person can never become a sage.
Since he clung tenaciously to his former delusions, his sense of shame and remorse grew all the heavier. To inherit the lineage in such a manner is truly unworthy of the trust reposed in him.

In this exhortation, it is first shown that those of middle capacity can transform their station; their nature may rise or fall, and by hearing the Dharma and reforming their faults, they must ultimately begin anew.
Conversely, those who stubbornly cling to delusion and refuse to awaken are merely superficial recipients of the Buddha’s bequeathed teachings;
they are unfit to be entrusted with their transmission and preservation.
Thus we know that the pedagogical gateways are skillful in accordance with capacities: for those of deep capacity, they practice the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) without blemish;
for those of shallow capacity, they demonstrate the five burnings (*pañca-dāha*) yet possess purity.
Next, the instruction is shown; this is the first section. The first two phrases praise the establishment of the teachings, while the latter two phrases provide the actual demonstration.

The two gates are shown because they reveal the profound practice and the observation that penetrates the underlying principle; thus, they are considered shallow. The five "burnings" are presented to draw forth the mind.

Regarding the "ten afflictions" (*daśa-kleśāḥ*), these refer to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
As for "practice," this refers to the exhortation to cultivation; it must be understood through principle that all three vehicles equally sever these [afflictions].
Because contemplation is perfected through observation so as to bring about purity, it is called "without flaw.

If one follows the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, a Bodhisattva who has attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) may fully engage in the ten unwholesome actions such as killing and so forth without incurring any defiled fault; this refers to the profound stages [of the path] to illustrate the manifestation of transformative function.

As for the "ten proclivities" (*daśa-anuśaya*), they likely do not refer to the ten unwholesome actions, so this should be examined further. Regarding the "five burnings," this is from Zhi Qian’s translation of the *Amitābha*... [text fragment].

The *Sūtra of the Ten Wheels* states: "I have now become a Buddha in this world for the sake of those within the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, which constitute the most extreme suffering.
I instruct the people to abandon the five evils, to eliminate the five pains, and to remove the five burnings;
I subdue their minds and cause them to uphold the five virtues. Regarding the meaning of those five burnings and so forth, the text [states]:...

This is an extremely extensive work; now, its essential meaning is summarized to be shown to those who have not yet heard it. The first evil is when the strong subjugate the weak and kill sentient beings, leading them to prey upon one another.
The second evil is when rulers and ministers fail in their governance, fathers and sons are in discord, local communities oppress one another, and relatives engage in strife and litigation.
The third evil is committing sexual misconduct with those outside one’s kin and taking what is not rightfully one's own.

The fourth evil is the use of double-tongued speech, harsh words, slandering, deceiving the virtuous and worthy, and failing to respect one's elders and kin, while treating teachers and superiors with contempt.
The fifth evil is when the father does not care for his son and the son does not care for his father;
they indulge in wine and crave flavors, being arrogant and self-exalting, and failing to remember the kindness and virtue of their parents, teachers, and elders.
Constantly harboring evil thoughts with the intent to kill one's parents, an arhat, or a bhikṣu—these five kinds are called the five evils.
When these five evils accumulate, they can summon bitter fruits: in life, one encounters the king’s law; at death, one enters the evil realms. These are called the five pains.
Because the pain is so piercing, it is like being burned by fire; therefore, they are called the five burnings. If the five evils cease, then...
The five causes of good and evil having ceased, the fruits of suffering are no longer received; therefore, the five pains and five burnings naturally extinguish themselves.
By upholding the sutras and precepts, pure conduct manifests before one, and one is immediately reborn in a Pure Land; hence it is said that there is purity.
The pure lands are not uniform, yet they manifest according to the inclinations of beings; the Buddha-wisdom is unfathomable, meeting with conditions in accordance with the times.
The first two phrases of the subsequent section clarify that the pure lands are not uniform in order to refute emotional attachments;

the latter two phrases of the "Buddha" section demonstrate that Buddha-wisdom is non-dual to reveal its universal harmony. There are two aspects to the pure lands: first, the purity of principle (*li*), which is termed "eternal quiescence."
The light pervades both the *kṣaṇa* (moment) and all phenomena; these two aspects of phenomenal purity (*sāṃvṛta-śuddhi*) manifest differently according to the original vows of the Buddhas.
What is here called "purity of birth" refers specifically to the Western Land, which is phenomenal purity.

This is said for fear that one might mistake this purity for being identical to the *jìguāng* (Nirvana-light), and thus fail to see that it is not restricted to the West alone, but is universally perceived. Nevertheless, it is maintained that phenomenal purity is indeed localized in the West.
Because other regions lack [such purity], while the arising [of this land] is restricted, and because both the universal and the restricted are negated, it is said that they are "not one.

Thus we know that all Buddhas possess a "land of reality" (*vastu-śuddhi*) that adapts to the capacities of beings to guide and entice them; as this is specifically held within the Sage’s mind, it is said that "the Buddha-wisdom is unfathomable," and so forth.
It is like the bright moon in the sky, whose light shines upon vessels both large and small; or like the thunder within the clouds, whose sound is heard amidst both clarity and obscurity.

What is perceived depends on one's prior conditions, and its manifestations cannot be made uniform. Since the Way resides in the vessel of the individual, it is difficult for those with differing degrees of acuity to equalize their progress, as it depends solely upon the accumulation of habitual practice.

In the first section of the following analysis, two metaphors are initially presented solely from the perspective of the capacity to respond to what is heard; below, the application of these metaphors is discussed solely in terms of the faculties of the recipient.

The first two phrases apply the metaphor of thunder: the sound of thunder represents the perfect voice, while its manifestation or concealment represents the differing interpretations of sentient beings—that is, the two types of faculties, the sharp and the dull.
Those with sharp faculties perceive the principle and thereby attain the Way; those with dull faculties perceive phenomena and remain bound by their own emotions.

Therefore, they cannot be identical. The latter two lines combine the analogy of the moon: the substance of the moon represents the Buddha’s body, while the reflections in various vessels represent the diversity of what is perceived.

Those of sharp faculties perceive the Dharma-Buddha as eternally abiding in the Land of Quiescent Light, whereas those of duller capacities behold the Transformation Body, which varies according to direction—differing in the dimensions of its physical form and the distinctions between pure and impure lands. To investigate the source of this...

The wondrous essence and perfect sound are fundamentally without distinction. The *Sūtra* states: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
The *Xingshichao* states: "The initial proclamation at the Deer Park was originally for the sake of the śrāvakas, yet eighty thousand devas resolved upon the Great Way;
the final teaching on the extinction at the Twin Trees ultimately revealed the Buddha-nature, and thus the assembly attained the fruit."

To become an Arhat is itself awakening and understanding; this resides within the person and does not depend on the instructions of the teachings. When one asks about the teachings, there is but a single sound, yet those who hear it differ according to their own capacities.
Since this is not a matter of prescribing remedies for specific ailments, how can it be called "teaching according to individual dispositions"?
Viewed from this perspective, one finally understands that Śāriputra with his conch-shell topknot had his mind sealed by either defilement or purity;

thus, the blissful and the impure lands were each briefly presented in their respective aspects. Therefore, the text says: "My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitude sees it as utterly consumed by fire"—this is precisely the proof.
How could one not know that Amitābha’s land, though mixed with impurities, was likewise shown in this way to provide a universal illustration?
The three sections are divided into two parts: first, the formal elucidation of the two [types of] causes; second, the citation of examples to demonstrate them.

Regarding the first part, there is the initial clarification of the difference between the views of the two types of practitioners, as seen in the story of Śrīgupta. In that account, when Vimalakīrti was questioned by Ratnākara regarding the Buddha’s Pure Land, the Buddha said:
"Ratnākara, the class of sentient beings is the pure land of the bodhisattva," and so on, up to: "If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure [land]..."
"The land shall be purified by purifying one's own mind; as the mind is purified, so too is the Buddha-field purified.
At that time, Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, had this thought: "If the mind of a bodhisattva is pure, then the Buddha-field is pure.
When our World-Honored One was originally a bodhisattva, was his intention not pure, such that this Buddha-field is impure to this extent? At that time, the Conch...
The Brahma King Śikhin said to Śāriputra, "Do not harbor such thoughts as to consider this buddha-field impure. Why is this?
I see the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha as pure, like the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Śāriputra replied, "I see this land with its hills, mounds, ravines, and pits; yet you show me these two lands with such equanimity."

Fundamentally, the Saha world is itself the Land of Peace and Bliss, and the Land of Peace and Bliss is itself the Saha world. Śākyamuni conceals the pure and manifests the defiled for the sake of subduing beings; Amitābha suppresses the defiled and appears in the pure for the sake of gathering and receiving them. Since these are respectively methods of subduing and gathering, which of these two is primary? To show that the former is the teaching of Śākyamuni’s pure land, the text from the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "How much more so for those who have already attained the stage of non-retrogression... and so forth. How could this not be the pure land of Śākyamuni? Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Buddha’s Past Vows* says: "In the midst of the five turbidities, he attains supreme enlightenment. This is clearly the pure land of Śākyamuni. Moreover, the *Sutra on the Original Acts of the Buddha* says: "The Buddha’s land is pure and adorned with the seven jewels. This is also the pure land of Śākyamuni. Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Buddha’s Past Vows* says: "The land is level and smooth, like the palm of a hand, free from mountains, rivers, and steep precipices. This is also the pure land of Śākyamuni. Additionally, the *Sutra on the Buddha’s Past Vows* says: "The land is made of lapis lazuli, its ground is flat and even, and it is adorned with various precious flowers. This is also the pure land of Śākyamuni. The provisional observation (*jia-guan*) and the unifying observation (*rong-guan*) differ in their partiality and completeness, yet they ultimately converge in *Vijñaptimātra*. In the single observation of *Vijñaptimātra*, both the ultimate and the conventional are perfectly integrated.

If one defines them according to their specific characteristics, then "true emptiness" is conventional while "existence" is ultimate; however, these names apply across all teachings (for even the treatises of the Hīnayāna speak of the two truths).

If one distinguishes the observations according to their names, then the principle is exclusive and the phenomena are restricted, and the observation belongs to the School of Characteristics (*Faxiang-zong*), because that school observes the ultimate and the conventional separately. (Text)

The general principles for simultaneous contemplation, the ultimate goal of returning to the *dharmatā*, and the profound purport of complete cultivation are fully presented in the main body of this work.

Now, I shall attempt to seek the essence according to their names, provisionally distinguishing between the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*) by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): this nature exists only through delusion and is thus the conventional truth;

it refers to the grasping at a self and phenomena based upon the six consciousnesses. Second, the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*): this nature exists only as a provisional designation and is likewise the conventional truth; it refers to the manifestation of the eight consciousnesses as resembling sense-objects (*viṣaya*), which then appear as their own intrinsic substance. Third, the perfectly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)... [text fragment ends]
Regarding *svabhāva* (this nature is truly existent, which is the essence of the ultimate truth; it is *tathatā*, the common characteristic of both the real and the conventional):

if one approaches this from the perspective of perfect cultivation (*pariniṣpanna-bhāvanā*), the three natures and the three truths are fully encompassed within a single thought-moment, and perfect realization is likewise so.

Now, regarding the progressive abandonment that overturns those three natures to establish the three absences of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the depth and shallowness of the real and conventional differ according to their respective stages. One should not doubt that these are separate in the gate of sequential practice (*vyavasthāna-mukha*).
Furthermore, to summarize: on the stages prior to the [ten] bhūmis, one relies upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) to eliminate the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

Since the imagined nature is thus overturned into the *niṣparikalpita-svabhāva* (perfected nature), which is the emptiness of the imagined, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Because the dependent nature is manifested, it is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

As for the essence of the perfected nature, it pervades both the ultimate and the conventional; thus, it is termed "existent" or "non-existent" according to the circumstances. If one regards the imagined nature in relation to the perfected nature, then the former is the conventional.
If one regards the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) from the perspective of the non-existent, the conventional is deep and the ultimate is shallow;

if one considers it from the standpoint of those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), where they rely directly upon the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) to eliminate the dependent nature and seek the nature of non-substantiality, then that very dependent nature is turned into the nature of non-arising.

Thus, one part of this nature—namely, its non-arising—is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the other part—its provisional existence—is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is revealed as the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) because it is understood through the knowledge that realizes non-arising and emptiness.
According to principle, the perfected nature is the true emptiness beyond all dependence; since it is not an object of grasping, it fundamentally does not require overturning.

Nevertheless, because it is provisionally manifested as real in contrast to delusion, this name is established. Now, when the knowledge of non-arising emptiness manifests, it reveals one aspect of the perfected nature, which is the True [Nature].

Since the false is fundamentally non-arising, what could the true possibly be established as? Thus, both existence and emptiness are discarded, and one returns to the original absence of intrinsic nature;

therefore, it is called "the perfected nature is without nature. If one regards the perfected nature in contrast to the dependent nature through the lens of non-arising, then the true is profound while the conventional is shallow.

If one regards the perfected nature in relation to both of the preceding [natures], then both the true and the conventional are shallow, while the perfected alone is profound. This is because of the... [text fragment ends].
First, because this single meaning serves as the foundational substance for both the ultimate and the conventional;

second, because from the stage of ordinary beings to that of the sages, it is universally observed throughout the beginning and end, with no distinction between the causal and resultant stages of perfect cultivation; and third, because it is the fruit realized by sublime awakening (*miao-jue*).

If one follows the system of Ci'en, each of the two truths has four levels of depth. Regarding the four levels of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): first, the truth of provisional names lacking reality (*jia-ming wu-shi-di*). This refers to...

1. The Truth of Distinctions According to Phenomena (*vastu-vibhāga-satya*), such as the *senā*, *ghaṭa*, and *vana*; 2. The Truth of the Establishment of Categories (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*), namely the five aggregates, eighteen elements, and twelve bases; 3.

The Truth of the Provisional Establishment of Expedients (*upāya-prajñapti-satya*), namely the Four Noble Truths of suffering and so forth, which is the principle of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) realized by the two vehicles;

4. The Truth of Manifesting Reality through the Gate of the Four Reliances (*pratisaraṇa*), namely the gate of the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvi-śūnyatā*) cultivated by Bodhisattvas, which is the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*tattva-satya*). These four are the unity of essence and function.

The second, the truth of manifestation (*prabhāsa-satya*), is conventional because it is a fault of the first conventional truth. The third, the truth of the distinction between cause and effect (*hetu-phala-viśeṣa-satya*), is conventional.

The fourth, the truth of the attainment of the ultimate (*prāpti-paramārtha-satya*), is conventional. The fifth, the ultimate of ultimates (*paramārtha-paramārtha-satya*), refers to the single true *dharmadhātu*;
according to the nature of phenomena, there are five layers, but when categorized by meaning, they are opened into eight truths, encompassing both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

The "Vehicle-inclusive One Hundred Dharmas" consists of one dharma at the beginning that is exclusively conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and not ultimate (*paramārtha*), and one dharma at the end that is exclusively ultimate and not conventional.
Those in between, when viewed in relation to each other, are both conventional and ultimate; when viewed from the latter toward the former, the latter is ultimate and the former is conventional.
