"If it is said that there is no ritual and no contemplation, yet it is called 'equal ritual,' how is this so? The answer to this meaning is the same as what was explained previously in the fourth [section]. Furthermore, below...

The text states: "Regarding the question of whether one pays homage to what is not worthy of homage and so forth: you previously asked, 'If one correctly contemplates paying homage to one's own body as the Buddha without taking external objects as a condition, how can there be self and other?

The answer is: since it was said that one pays homage to oneself, one cannot avoid precluding the homage paid to others. When contemplating whether homage exists or not, how can these not be distinct?"
The Sūtra says: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way. Because the true mark is free from thought, it cannot be grasped by the mind, nor sought through signs;
it cannot be approached through prostration, nor avoided through non-prostration.

Since prostration and non-prostration, as well as offering and non-offering, are equal when the mind is settled in quiescence, this is called "equal prostration. Thus, the *Mañjuśrī-daśapraṇāma* says: "Neither arising nor..."
Because of cessation, I pay homage to that which is without an object of observation.
Regarding the initial passage of the cited scripture, it is from the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:
'By what characteristic do you observe the Tathāgata? The King replied: 'I observe the true characteristic of the body; observing the Buddha is likewise.'"
Yet it has no prior limit, no posterior limit, and no middle limit; it does not abide within the three limits nor is it separate from the three limits;
it does not abide within the five aggregates nor is it separate from the five aggregates; it does not abide within the four great elements nor is it separate from the four great elements;

even so, it is neither consciousness nor cognition, for it is the cessation of the sphere of mental activity, where the path of language is cut off, identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). By means of this, I...
The seven phrases beginning with "Contemplating the Tathāgata through his marks" re-explain the preceding scripture to establish the intent of contemplation.

Because the wondrous principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is pure by its own nature (*svabhāva-viśuddha*) and cannot be defiled by delusion, it is said to be "free from thought. As the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The essence of the mind is free from thought. That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; there is nowhere it does not pervade—the single Dharma-realm."

Phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are themselves the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body, which is beyond all comparison. Where there is a mind, thoughts arise; where there are marks, things are not truly existent.
To perform prostrations results in the confusion of subject and object; to not perform them leaves cause and effect obscure.
Now, by realizing the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), mind and marks are as one, and whether one prostrates or not, they are non-dual. [The following] concludes and demonstrates how to gather the mind.
To illuminate delusive thoughts while remaining unmoved is called "settling the mind" (*anxin*). This quiescence is the true mark (*dharmatā*).

The subsequent passage refers to the *Buddhagocaraprativiṣṭa-sūtra*, which contains ten verses; hence it is called the "Ten Prostrations. Non-arising and non-ceasing is the substance of the true mark.
If there is thought, the objective realm arises; if the mind ceases, phenomena cease. If one perceives arising and ceasing...
When performing acts of reverence, there is something to be observed; now, having realized the true mark (*dharmatā*), since the marks are eternally abiding, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Although one performs acts of reverence, there is consequently nothing to be observed. The remaining nine verses are extensive in text and are not cited here.

Regarding these latter two forms of worship, they are tranquil yet capable of penetration; by cultivating merit while practicing the Way, they cause cessation and contemplation to proceed together and the ultimate and conventional truths to operate in tandem.

Thus, the mind becomes vast and empty while the body remains subject to the conditions of worldly entanglement. For those at the level of ordinary practitioners engaged in study, these characteristics are consistent with this approach; beyond this, such practices are not undertaken.
As for the deluded habits of the inferior and ignorant, they are not worth questioning.

In the second of the two subsequent sections, the first division is divided into two parts: first, five lines that directly indicate the two minds; second, seven lines below that clarify their boundaries.
Within the first part, the initial line points to and indicates [the subject], while the following section is further divided into two:

the upper two lines cite the contemplation of principle, and the lower two lines clarify the practice of contemplation. "Quiescence" (śamatha) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) generally belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*); both are the means of observation.
Merit belongs to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the Path belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); both are the object of contemplation and the subject of contemplation.

When concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are fully integrated within a single thought-moment, then calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) proceed together; this is why one is quiescent yet capable of penetration.

When the conventional and ultimate truths are fully present as a single dharma that is the object of contemplation, then the conventional and ultimate operate simultaneously; this is why one cultivates merit while practicing the Path. Among these two [categories], the latter four phrases represent the superior.

The correct teaching is as presented above; it concludes by stating that while this understanding is subtle and wondrous, belonging only to the stage of the realized sages (*ārya*), those ordinary beings below are not unsuited to study it.
Therefore, based on the realization of the sages, it is extended to ordinary beings to demonstrate its scope:

for an ordinary person, although the principles of phenomena and reality have not yet been integrated, and though the mind understands the principle, the body remains subject to conditional constraints, the intention is to relinquish the body in order to advance in cultivation.

Regarding the phrase "the path-practice exceeds [the mundane]," the following three phrases censure those who abandon this correct contemplation to seek elsewhere externally; this is called "exceeding.
To be exhausted at the start and fail to cultivate it due to indolence is called "not practicing. Such people of inferior intelligence as these are not fit to inquire about the Way.
However, because those who follow after secondary characteristics mostly stop at mere self-understanding, the text states:

"Do not preach this sutra to ordinary people of shallow knowledge who are deeply attached to the five desires and harbor views of a self; for if they hear it and do not understand, they will increase their slander and defamation, which is better than not hearing it at all—rather, let them practice worldly merits and blessings."
Next, the first phrase of the middle section precludes those who are deluded and excessively attached to signs, failing to realize correct cultivation.

The second phrase seeks out those with the appropriate capacity, intending that future generations, upon reading these solemn warnings, will be moved to resolve their will and strive diligently in cultivation.

Therefore, the following citation of scriptural evidence from the *Lotus Sūtra* demonstrates that preaching the Dharma must respond to the capacity of the listener and must not be bestowed recklessly; this subsequently restates the intent to extend the admonition.
If hearing [this] increases slander, it is better not to hear it; instead, cultivate meritorious deeds to block the path to transgression. Chapter Nine:

Manifesting Traces through Exertion (Though diligence and indolence differ, both are forms of exertion; diligence leads to the excellence of the sages, while indolence results in the failings of the common folk).

This concludes the chapter "Explaining Exertion and Manifesting Traces. Regarding the title of this chapter: diligent cultivation of the three karmas is called "exertion," while the responsive resonance resulting from those karmas is called "manifesting traces.
In the commentary, the first two phrases clarify exertion, and the latter two phrases demonstrate manifesting traces.
Above, I have fully elucidated the characteristics of diligence and indolence; these aspects are now complete. Below, the masses are turbid and deluded, harboring many biased views;

unable to put [the teachings] into practice, they first give rise to slander and doubt. Therefore, I have set forth the various scriptures to block such rigid attachments, so that those with a sincere heart who practice may understand that my intention lies herein.
In this text, the first two phrases of the initial section refer to the eighth chapter.
Because those with many crooked views arise from the lower turbidity and follow their own emotional conceptions, they produce slander and doubt;

because such things are not the correct practice, the following section explicitly reveals the intent of this chapter by extensively citing the words of the Sages to clarify the universal application [of the teaching], thereby preventing the common and the ignorant from following their indolence.
This section encourages the common people to resolve their minds correctly and extensively reveals the reasons why;

it shows that those at the beginning of their path and later practitioners must rely upon teachers and virtuous friends, and should now take refuge in the Triple Gem, always delighting in being close to them.

In the first section of "Showing the Basis," the initial part indicates the general intent; from "Now, below... onward, it reveals the basis, namely the words of teachers and friends, which are themselves the Three Jewels.
Question: Since the contemplation-gate established previously primarily preserves the practice of the final stage, how can it be that at the end of this fascicle it is instead intended for beginners?

Answer: From the perspective of seeking a person through contemplation, the practice truly pertains to the final stage; however, from the perspective of the meaning of the text, its application is biased toward beginners. This being so—

In order to cause beginners to learn the contemplation of the Sages from others, it is necessary to provide detailed instruction on being led into the Perfect Gate, where ordinary beings and sages practice together as previously shown.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If a bodhisattva has not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-position (*dharmatā-sthiti*), they distance themselves from all Buddhas and destroy all roots of goodness."
Their faculties are submerged in afflictions; being unable to save themselves, how could they possibly save others? Therefore, one should not distance oneself from the Buddhas.

It is like an infant who does not leave its mother; one traveling on a road does not leave provisions; in the heat, one does not leave the cooling breeze; in the cold, one does not wish to leave the fire;
when crossing water, one does not leave a good boat; and when suffering from illness, one does not leave a skilled physician. This is so.
Therefore, a bodhisattva is never separated from the Buddha. Why is this? Parents, relatives, friends, kings, and celestial beings cannot benefit me in crossing the ocean of suffering;
only the World-Honored Buddha enables me to emerge from suffering. For this reason, one should always keep the Buddhas in mind and never be apart from them.

Next, within the middle section, the first part clarifies that ordinary beings practicing below [the stage of the sages] incur many faults if they do not rely upon the Triple Gem: first, because they destroy their roots of goodness and lose the benefits of the Dharma;
second, because they sink into afflictions and increase outflows (*āsrava*); and third, because they lack personal power and fail to benefit others.

As for the "Dharma-position," it refers to the ten stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) wherein one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); what is mentioned here is that this has not yet been attained.
The human testimony refers to the initial resolve; "for example" below introduces the analogy; "this is" below applies it to the dharma; and "why? below provides the explanation.

Thus, first, because the benefit provided by fathers and others is slight, they cannot deliver me; second, it is revealed that the virtues of the Buddhas are profound and capable of serving as a refuge.
Now, desiring to personally behold the Buddhas and hear the supramundane Dharma, by what skillful means should one practice the correct path?

Because ordinary beings have, from time immemorial, cultivated merit based on signs, they must likewise act based on signs to distance themselves from worldly discourse. As the *Dharmaparyāya* states:
"Since the stage prior to the Great Purity has never been a place of abiding, one first establishes a site for the Way and arranges sacred images, banners, canopies, and flowers."
There are ten aspects of making offerings of incense according to one’s capacity that constitute the roots of goodness for seeing the Buddha:

first, prostration; second, praise; third, making vows and dedicating merit; fourth, contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs; fifth, single-minded mindfulness and the cultivation of loving-kindness;
sixth, the three refuges and the ten wholesome paths of action; seventh, generating the bodhicitta; eighth, reading and reciting the sutras and precepts; ninth, making offerings...

10. Regarding the tenth point, "Venerating the Śarīra and Creating Buddha Images": this refers to the cultivation of *samyag-darśana* (right contemplation). Although the myriad practices differ, they are unified in principle. This section broadly elucidates the first sub-section;

within it, the initial part sets forth the intent, which is further divided into chapters. In the first of these, one seeks out the expedient means (*upāya*) and below that establishes the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings.
Generally, there should be the character "夫" (fú) [at the beginning]; the commentary below cites and demonstrates that one must cultivate this.
"Great purity" refers to the stage of Buddhahood. What is now termed the "unperfected stage" includes everything from the tenth bhūmi downwards, as none have yet attained complete purity;
they must still rely on non-abiding to advance to the higher stages. "Non-abiding" is synonymous with "not dwelling.

The subsequent section on the adornment of images and ritual implements follows the main text on correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*); the sub-commentary here integrates phenomena back into principle.
Now, those who practice according to the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha are all entrusted to Maitreya Buddha to realize the fruits of sainthood;
since the scriptural evidence is extensive, the principle is certainly not to be contravened. Furthermore, those who wish to be reborn in the Pure Land will likewise find no obstruction.

Since the meaning of Perfect Enlightenment is uniform in its compassionate salvation and its single intent toward liberation, once that is attained, all ends—how could there be any further discord or separation? Moreover, while Maitreya establishes the primary tenet, as for the others...
The same principle applies to the ten directions.

In the subsequent section, as one is about to cultivate the practice of correct action, it is necessary to rely upon that to which one returns; therefore, the Teacher is first presented so that the mind may have a point of reliance.
As for the Buddha of Compassion (Maitreya) being entrusted with the Dharma of Śākyamuni: at the three assemblies of the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa), he will first deliver the disciples of Śākyamuni.

Therefore, Maitreya is called "The One of Brahma-sound" in Sanskrit and "The Kindly One" (Cishi) here in Chinese; he received this name because he cultivated the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Alternatively, the following passage shows what is appropriate according to the capacities of beings. Regarding the previous statement that "being born in the Pure Land" belongs to the provisional method, the current mention of "vowing to be born" while also stating there is "no obstruction" is the answer:
since the preceding text revealed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it pointed to the Pure Land as a provisional method; now, for those at the initial stage...

Because the mind is such, it functions according to capacity without obstruction. In the "Chapter on Protecting the Dharma," it was taught that one should return to the principle-body (*dharmatā-kāya*);

here, we clarify upon what one relies when returning through transformation into a Buddha. The answer is: the previous chapter demonstrated the fundamental, and thus one relies on the *dharmakāya*; the present chapter addresses those at the initial stage of the path, and thus must rely on characteristics.
This is because the end reveals the origin, and one returns to rely on the principle-body; as this very text states: "The meaning of perfect enlightenment is identical."
(Because the Dharma-body is identical,) the ultimate salvation is one; (because the manifested forms are uniform,) one need only seek liberation without the trouble of forced differentiation;
thus it is said that "liberation is simply cessation," and so forth.
First, regarding the clarification that through prostration one obtains the vision of the Buddha:

if a practitioner prostrates to Maitreya and the Buddhas of the ten directions with a heart of utmost sincerity, a heart of straightforwardness, a heart of focused concentration, a heart of reverence, a deep heart, and a heart of faith—
just as one would revere one's own parents— they will be able to eliminate heavy obstructions and be born before those Buddhas.
Following the chapter-by-chapter explanation, the first section of the middle part is now explained. Regarding the "mind of sincerity," it is because one is free from falsehood.

Regarding the "mind of straightforwardness," it is because one is free from crookedness. Regarding the "mind of focused concentration," it is because one is not distracted. Regarding the "mind of reverence," it is because one is not frivolous.
Regarding the "profound mind," it is because one seeks the Dharma without weariness. Regarding the "mind of faith," it is because one holds it in high esteem.

Because of the great value placed upon the worthy and the good, as explained below regarding right practice, the concluding summary of the benefits is as follows: it constitutes the principle of resonance and response, which (1) can eliminate obstacles and (2) can enable one to see the Buddha.
Thus, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states: "If there are those who pay homage to Maitreya Buddha, they shall eliminate the cycle of birth and death for ten billion kalpas."
Even those with such transgressions shall, in a future life beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree, also behold the Buddha. Furthermore, it is said:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if members of the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings hear his name and prostrate themselves in worship, they will, at the end of their lives, be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

If there are men or women who have violated various prohibitions and committed manifold evil deeds, yet hear the name of this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion and cast themselves prostrate upon the ground..."

If one sincerely repents all evil karma, it shall swiftly become purified; if there are those who take refuge in Maitreya Bodhisattva, you should know that such persons will attain the stage of non-retrogression.
When Maitreya attains Buddhahood, they shall behold the Buddha’s radiance and immediately receive his prediction of enlightenment.

Next, I shall cite the scriptural evidence regarding the text on the "ascent to the higher realms," which contains many benefits and consists entirely of manifestations of spiritual resonance (*gantong*) and the display of traces.
First, one attains the eradication of sins; next, one attains the vision of the Buddha; and further, one relinquishes the retribution of this life to be reborn in heaven.

"I" refers to Śākyamuni himself. "The fourfold assembly" refers to monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. "The eight classes" refers to devas, nāgas, and so forth, as is commonly known. "Tuṣita" refers to the Tuṣita Heaven.

Conversely, contentment is the inner court of the Four Heavenly Kings where Maitreya resides. If one descends from violating the precepts, one will obtain the fruit and receive a prediction [of enlightenment] upon taking refuge.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that there are five merits in prostrating to the Buddha: first, physical excellence (because seeing the marks and signs gives rise to a sense of supreme reverence); second, obtaining a good...

1. Hearing [the name] (because at the time of seeing the Buddha, one thrice proclaims: "Namo Tathāgata, the Truly and Perfectly Awakened One"); 2. Abounding in wealth (because one makes offerings of flowers, incense, and lamps according to one's ability); 3.

Being born into a noble station (because at the time of seeing the Buddha, the mind is free from attachment, and one kneels with the right knee on the ground, joining the palms in prostration); 4. Being born in the heavens (because it is the natural law of the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha).
Second, regarding the praise of the Buddha’s virtues:
with a pure mind, one extols his verbal karma as it is described in the *Brahmā-rāja-stotra* of the *Tathāgata-buddha-sūtra*:
“The Perfectly All-Knowing One, the Honored One among two-legged beings, Is without equal in the world of gods and humans.”
The World-Honored One of Ten Powers is most rare and extraordinary; he is the unsurpassed, most excellent field of merit.
Those who make offerings to him will be born in the heavens. I prostrate to the peerless one of great diligence.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* in praise of the Buddha:
I pay homage to all Buddhas, the peerless Tamer of Men; I also pay homage to the Buddha-stūpas of the sixteen-foot true Dharma-body.

Where they were born, where they attained the Way, Where they turned the Wheel of Dharma and entered Nirvāṇa, And at every place where they walked, stood, sat, or lay—I pay homage to them all. The Buddhas are inconceivable.
The Sublime Dharma is likewise; both the ability to believe in it and its karmic fruit are inconceivable.
Those who praise the Tathāgata with this geya shall not fall into the evil realms for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
In the first section of the commentary on the praise of the Buddha’s virtues, it is first explained that the one who praises does not transcend the two types of pure karma;
this is because the "pure mind" is free from attachment, as will be shown in the initial passage cited below.

Second, the Venerable One possesses both merit and wisdom, and his excellence is precisely due to his surpassing the Three Vehicles. Next, in Mañjuśrī’s verses, the first two verses pay homage to the Buddha’s path.

Because it transcends the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there is no stage equal to it; because it is the ultimate of the three bodies (*trikāya*), there is no peer. Regarding the "six-foot" body: this admits of two interpretations.

First, the six-foot body is the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) belongs to the true [body]; thus, the six-foot body is not the Dharma-body itself, as their functions and manifestations differ. This is the teaching of the separate vehicles (*tri-yāna*).
Second, the six-foot body is itself the Dharma-body, for the original and the manifested are identical; this is the perfect fusion of the One Vehicle (*eka-yāna*).
The teaching remains today; as the latter meaning is what we revere, the phrase "the Buddha-stūpa is itself the locus of sustenance and birth" refers to the relics left by former sages.
The following verse praises the Dharma and the Saṅgha in general: the first line traces back to the virtues of the Buddha;

the second line [indicates] the extent of transformation through the Dharma; the third line identifies those capable of faith as the Saṅgha; and the fourth line collectively manifests their supreme virtues.
A single verse can summarize the merit and benefits.

As the *Bodhisattvapūrvacaryā-sūtra* states: "Even if countless billions of people were to become pratyekabuddhas, and someone were to provide them with the four requisites for a hundred years—the merit from such an act would be very great, yet it would not equal that of a person who, with a heart of joy, [offers] a single..."

Verses of praise extol the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata; furthermore, as stated in the *Sujāta-sūtra*, the merit of offering the treasures of the four continents to the Buddha and the merit of praising the Tathāgata with a sincere heart are equal and without distinction.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that by even once uttering the name of the Buddha, "Namo Buddha," one enters nirvāṇa through this root of goodness.
The realms are inexhaustible.
Regarding the "threefold manifestation of vows and dedication":
among the three types of vows and dedications, the first is designated as "manifesting vows" (*praṇidhāna*), because karma arises from the mind; thus it is called "manifesting."
One should pray with sincere resolve, saying: "I vow to turn back from what I have previously done and to turn toward the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Because the power of a practitioner's roots of goodness is weak, they must be supported by vows; it is like a blind person walking on level ground who would fall over without them.
Therefore, vows and practice must be mutually dependent, like two wheels traveling a long distance. One should speak these words: "May [the merit of] my past lives and this present body..."
May all roots of goodness cultivated be dedicated together with all sentient beings toward the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, so that they may be born before Maitreya and hear the pure Dharma,

awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). May it be their wish that at the time of death, their minds shall be free from hindrances and afflictions, and by the power of these roots of goodness,
they may attain birth with sovereign ease before all Buddhas.
In the first section of the commentary, it is first stated that the mutual requirement of aspiration and practice is like the relationship between eyes and feet, or like wheels and wings;

when these are mutually required and complete, there is no destination too far to reach. Below this, the actual characteristics of the practice are clarified. First, the text on dedication is explained:

although the roots of goodness of the past and present are numerous, they do not exceed the two types of practice—merit and wisdom. Furthermore, the meaning of "past and present" implicitly includes the future.
To bestow upon sentient beings is to turn oneself toward others; to dedicate toward the Buddha-way is to turn delusion toward enlightenment and to turn from the false into the true.

Next, the arising of vows is clarified: first, the vow to be born before Maitreya as one who has attained the patience of non-arising—this refers to those from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) onward who know that all phenomena are non-arising.
Second, the vow to be free from affliction at the end of life. Third, the vow to follow [the path].
One delights in being reborn there.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are those who cultivate small meritorious deeds; hearing of a blissful place, they constantly vow to be reborn there, and upon the end of their lives, each is born therein.
Furthermore, the task of adorning a Buddha-field is so great that it cannot be accomplished by practicing virtues in isolation.

To achieve accomplishment, one must rely on the power of aspiration; just as a bull, though strong enough to pull a cart, requires a driver to reach his destination, so too is the purification of a buddha-field brought to fulfillment through the guidance of aspiration.
By the power of aspiration, merit increases, remains undiminished and indestructible, and because one constantly beholds the Buddhas, [the goal] is attained.
In the citation of scriptural evidence, first it is shown that one with little merit who possesses aspiration is immediately reborn;

furthermore, below this, it is shown that one who has practice but lacks aspiration cannot reach the fruit, as illustrated by the following analogy. "Pure" refers to the dharma; "the strength of the ox" corresponds to practice; and "the driver" corresponds to aspiration.
Fourth, regarding the practice of contemplating the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Buddha:

the practitioner, with single-minded devotion, sits upright in a quiet room with right mindfulness directed toward the physical form of the Tathāgata. Whether eyes are closed or open, the image appears with perfect clarity.
Those with heavy karmic offenses may require a long time before seeing it; by means of this contemplative visualization, one comes to know whether one's evil karma is heavy or light.

Regarding the first section of the commentary on the four aspects of mindfulness of the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*): first, it indicates the subject who practices mindfulness; next, it indicates the object of mindfulness;
finally, it clarifies both subject and object together, showing that only when one's meritorious practice is perfected can one clearly perceive [the Buddha].

Question: When this teaching speaks of "seeing the Buddha," does it mean seeing one's own Buddha or seeing another Buddha? Answer: This teaching is for those at the stage of the initial mind; furthermore, it is not yet based on principle-contemplation (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), but merely follows conventional conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
The mind perceives other Buddhas as well.
Both are equally products of deluded thought; yet the distinction between good and evil realms is inconceivable. Birth and death press upon people so urgently that one cannot afford to be negligent.

If one has not habitually cultivated focused attention, then when encountering a grave illness later on, one will become frantic and distressed, with no ground upon which to rely the mind. Everything!

Since evil karma arises from the mind, how can one eliminate it if there are no seeds of goodness? If one has long cherished goodness and constantly recollects the Buddha, then according to the state of that mind, what must be seen will indeed be seen.

Regarding the three initial phrases of the section on "Exhorting the Cultivation of Goodness," these follow upon the preceding discussion of mental conceptions to demonstrate that both good and evil are equally false imaginings.
They are considered "evil" because the mind conditions sensory objects, and through the accumulation of such causes, delusion is formed;

they are considered "good" because the mind recollects the Buddha and, by stilling its thoughts, brings forth wisdom. Since only a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the fundamental principles of the workings of good and evil karma, [the text proceeds as follows].
It is said: "It is inconceivable. This establishes the principle following the preceding statement and further encourages [the practice of] karma arising from the mind;

the mind is precisely the eight consciousnesses, and their seeds are the seeds of volition (*cetanā*). Alternatively, since both thought and recollection possess seeds, one might ask: "If volition and the like inherently possess their own seeds, why do you say they do not exist? The answer is:
because the original seeds are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and have not yet produced good or evil, and the new seeds have not yet been perfumed (*vāsita*).

It is said that [the Buddha] does not exist; however, since one now conceives of him as virtuous, one immediately perfumes the seeds of goodness. Therefore, when one beholds the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they manifest in accordance with the mind.

Thus, the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, those disciples of mine who abandon evil and clamor, speak little, and simplify their affairs, will—throughout the six periods of day and night, even for a mere moment—contemplate my white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) with clarity and without distraction. (Note)
If one’s mind does not cease [from distraction] when seeing these extraordinary marks, or even if one does not see them,

this person shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over ninety-six billion *nayuta* of *Ganges-sand* atoms of *kalpas*. Furthermore, if there is another person who merely hears [of the white tuft] and their heart is not startled or doubtful,
but instead receives it with joy and faith, this person likewise shall eliminate the [sins of] birth and death for eighty billion *kalpas*.

The Buddha said to the offender: "The merit of the eighty-four thousand marks and secondary characteristics of a Tathāgata does not equal even a small fraction of the merit of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa).
Therefore, I shall now for the sake of future generations explain the method of contemplation on the Great Wisdom Light of the White Tuft of Hair, which eliminates evil.

If there are wicked people who, upon hearing this contemplation of the hair-tuft, give rise to anger and resentment, the light of the white tuft of hair will nevertheless protect them and eliminate [their offenses]."
After the retribution for the three types of karmic offenses, one is born before a Buddha.

Regarding the demonstration of merit and benefits, the superior explanation states that the marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) collectively encompass eighty thousand; however, what is shown in this present sutra specifically reveals only the mark of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa).

Although they are identical in their efficacy, there is a distinction of excellence between them. First, the section beginning with "Expedient Means" explains mindfulness; below that, it demonstrates right visualization. If...

The first part of the initial section on manifesting merit and benefit clarifies that because one practices contemplation, one eliminates deep transgressions numbering in the *nayuta*—a count of ten billion.
The second part clarifies that even hearing the name [of this teaching] to extinguish sin is inferior to the Buddha’s further manifestation of superior merit.

Regarding "the light of great wisdom" (*mahā-prajñā-āloka*): wisdom arises from the mind; when the mind is pure, wisdom is luminous. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "the radiance of wisdom."
Regarding the "radiance like the sun," as for the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair), the *Jingshu* (Commentary on the Sutra) states:

"The Tathāgata has a white *ūrṇā-kośa* mark between his eyebrows, resembling a conch shell or snow. It is one zhang and five chi in length; the hair has eight facets and its circumference is five cun.
The interior of this hair is hollow and it curls to the right like a tube of lapis lazuli. From this, light is emitted, illuminating all things."
Judging by this, one can say that the light of the ūrṇā-kośa mark is able to illuminate sentient beings throughout the ten directions;

because its merit in enabling them to leave suffering and attain happiness is most vast, it transcends all other marks. Even if those of base or evil character harbor anger and resentment, they likewise obtain the removal of their transgressions.
This is due to the fact that great compassion is impartial.
To single-mindedly recollect the Buddha’s virtues and cultivate compassion among the five sciences is called true offering.
The fifth heading states that "recollecting the Buddha’s virtues" is for the sake of contemplating how to repay his kindness, and "cultivating compassion" is for the sake of rescuing sentient beings;
because these practices involve seeking the supreme above and transforming those below, their merit and conduct are most profound, and thus this heading is designated as "true offering."
The practitioner, with a pure and profound mind, at all times recollects the Buddha’s great kindness as if remembering one's parents,

who nourish one for a single lifetime in this physical body; yet the Buddha’s kindness is far more profound and heavy, for he enters the prison of the three realms of existence for the sake of all sentient beings,
diligently instructing and admonishing them to cultivate correct practice so that they may attain liberation from the sufferings of countless kalpas.
I now constantly recollect the Buddha’s grace; how much more so when, through the act of recollecting the Buddha, the seeds of goodness and the fruits of merit produced are inexhaustible.

Within the initial section of the detailed explanation of the virtues of recollection, the first point concerns the capacity for recollection: the purity of the mind that dedicates its grace is the same as previously described.

This demonstrates that one should contemplate the Buddha’s kindness by considering how he enables one to transcend birth and death. Because the Buddha possesses this kindness, one must be mindful of it;
furthermore, one should reflect on the Buddha’s kindness as that which has enabled me to escape from birth and death.

As for the comparison between the two kinds of kindness mentioned below, first, the *Lotus Sūtra* shows that the kindness of parents is shallow, whereas the kindness of the Buddhas shown below is profound. Those who are imprisoned within the three realms of existence... [The *Lotus Sūtra*].

The Sūtra says: "To diligently exhort sentient beings so that they may strive to escape from the prison of the triple world" is also the diligent application of skillful means found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Therefore, the subsequent summary and demonstration—whereby those who obtain benefit possess the seeds of goodness—is the cause, while the retribution received is the fruit.
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* states: "The karmic retribution for performing deeds toward the Buddha is boundless.

In the preceding section of this citation, the primary intent was specifically to contemplate the Buddha’s grace; now, these various passages are cited to demonstrate the attainment of benefits and the principle of spiritual resonance (*gantong*).
As the texts are all easily understood, I shall explain them according to their difficulties.
Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* states: "The Buddha is a treasure among humanity, bringing abundant benefit and merit;
even those who merely hear his name, pay homage to him, or make offerings to him obtain a weighty reward—how much more so for those who focus their mindfulness on the true marks of the Buddha!"

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who diligently cultivate various merits, whose majestic deportment is unimpaired, who sweep stupas and smear the ground with plaster, who offer flowers and incense, who practice various samādhis, and who read and recite the sūtras—such persons, though they have not severed their fetters, shall obtain the six supernormal powers;
they should maintain constant mindfulness, contemplate the image of the Buddha, and invoke the name of Maitreya."

If one receives the eight precepts for even a single moment of thought and cultivates various pure deeds, at the time of death, one will immediately be reborn within a lotus pedestal in Tuṣita Heaven.
There, one will immediately behold the light from the Buddha’s *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair between the brows), thereby transcending the sins of birth and death for ninety billion kalpas.
In accordance with one's past affinities, the Buddha will preach the wondrous Dharma, enabling one to attain non-retrogression.

In the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realms*, the practices of recollecting the Buddha’s physical form, sweeping stupas, smearing the ground with plaster, and observing the eight precepts are all auxiliary means for cultivation.
The *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* states:
"If one resolves to restrain the mind and recollects the merit of the Buddha, even scattering a single flower into the air [is sufficient]."
In future ages, the merit of the various devas and Brahmā kings shall not be exhausted; because it is inexhaustible, they will ultimately attain nirvāṇa.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If sentient beings commit evil through the three karmas but, at the moment of death, recollect the merits of the Tathāgata, they will certainly leave the evil realms and be reborn in the heavens.
Even an extremely wicked person, by virtue of mindfulness of the Buddha, may likewise attain rebirth in heaven."
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha for even a brief moment, the light of wisdom will extinguish the darkness of delusion.

Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because a bodhisattva always loves to mindfully recollect the Buddha, they encounter all Buddhas whenever they cast off this body and receive another."
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Suppose the three-thousandfold world system were filled with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,

and someone were to provide them with every kind of pleasant requisite for an entire kalpa, even continuing such offerings after their parinirvāṇa by erecting stupas and making offerings throughout their own lifetime—

the merit from this, though vast, is not equal to that of someone who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, gives rise to a single thought of pure faith and contemplates it with faith and understanding."
The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable; by means of these roots of goodness, it surpasses the former beyond compare. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s merits, great kindness, great compassion, and the fivefold Dharma-body are immeasurable and unimpeded; thus, his realm is inconceivable.
If there is respectful service and sustenance toward him, that too is inconceivable; therefore, the karmic retribution is also inconceivable.

In the latter section of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, two sages are cited to compare their relative merits. First, it is shown that making offerings to those of the Two Vehicles does not equal the contemplation of the Buddha’s wisdom;
this serves as the basis for the formal comparison of their merits. Following this, it is demonstrated through inquiry that the wisdom of the Dharmakāya is an inconceivable realm;
yet, by now being able to believe, understand, and make offerings to it, one attains inconceivable fruits.
This is the deliberation.
Next, one practices the four immeasurables of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in accordance with the teachings.

Regarding the cultivation of the four immeasurables as indicated by "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), these—compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—pervade the entire realm of sentient beings. This...
Fourth, because loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is primary, it is specifically mentioned as will be further explained later.

Why is this so? Because the mind of all Buddhas is what is called "great loving-kindness"; if one does not now cultivate and practice it, one cannot become equal to the Buddhas and has no way to see them.
Therefore, when recollecting the Buddha, one practices the contemplation of loving-kindness.
In the first section of the main exposition, the first phrase poses a question, which is then explained below.

That "the Buddha’s mind is great compassion" means that the Buddha has no other minds, but takes only great compassion as his mind. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The mind of compassion is itself the Buddha-mind.
What follows below uses a reductio ad absurdum to exhort [the practitioner] to cultivate it.

When a practitioner first wishes to cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they sit upright in a secluded place and fix their mindfulness upon all sentient beings of the ten directions, regarding them all as their own kin, free from thoughts of anger or obstruction.

By providing the four requisites with the most sublime excellence—whether for a single moment of thought, or for a period of one day—they are able to generate merit; for this merit is immeasurable, corresponding to the scope of their resolve.

In the first section of the "Clarifying the Arising of Conditions through Cultivation," first it clarifies the preliminary application (*upāya*). Having already explained the mental cultivation according to the instructions below, because one's own kin are most immediate and intimate, they are cited as an analogy.
Since enemies are treated like kin, there is no obstruction of anger; this is compassion (*karuṇā*), which is able to extract suffering.
The four requisites are provided as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which bestows happiness. This, then, takes sentient beings as its object and is thus mundane.
This joy is called "compassion conditioned by birth" (*upapattipratyaya-maitrī*), which, by taking what is near to illustrate what is distant, reveals its merit and benefits.
The following passage clarifies its immeasurable meaning.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "If one who cultivates compassion should reach the time of death, they will see the Buddhas of the ten directions placing their hands upon the crown of their head."
Because they were touched by [the Buddha's] hand, their minds became peaceful and joyful, and they immediately attained rebirth in a pure buddha-land.

This is the first of the four benefits clearly explained in the section on the "Initial Response" (*gànbào chūkē*). First, at the moment of death, one sees the Buddha; next, one is touched by the Buddha’s hand;
then, one receives the Buddha’s touching of the crown of the head; and finally, the three points—mind becoming peaceful and joyful, and immediately attaining rebirth in a pure land—are established.
I have observed that those whose worldly nature and conduct are gentle and supple die with composure, peace, and mastery over their faculties;

yet those whose nature is coarse and harsh die in a state of confusion and agitation. Their eyesight fails first, they lose their voices and cannot speak, and even when given kind instructions, they do not comprehend them.
Judging by this actual fact, practicing compassion is the ultimate duty; that you now fail to do so is simply due to your evil karma and lack of a compassionate heart.
Because one must inevitably cast oneself into the evil realms, the Sūtra says: "By practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in this way, one beholds immeasurable Buddhas.

In the first section, it is shown that through compassionate compliance, one attains a good death; in the subsequent section, it is shown that coarse and negligent conduct leads to a chaotic and frantic death.
Thus, the following section follows upon these matters to exhort practice, while the subsequent section demonstrates the faults of non-cultivation, and the final section cites scriptural authority.
This further confirms that those who practice loving-kindness see the Buddha, while those who do not practice it are proven by this to sink into the evil realms.
If one practices the objectless and non-objective loving-kindness, one will possess the four immeasurables and attain the Way of the Buddha.
Next, to clarify the two types of compassion, the *Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* (*Guānxīnlùn shū*) states:

"To perceive the suffering of birth and death within the six realms and, out of pity, to extract them from it and bestow upon them the bliss of emptiness and *nirvāṇa* is called 'compassion with a dharma-condition' (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).

To perceive the suffering of dualistic discrimination and, out of pity, to extract them from it and bestow upon them the bliss of the Tathāgata’s middle-way *dharmakāya* is called 'unconditioned compassion' (*anālambana-maitrī*). This is the sequential extraction [of beings from suffering]."
Although suffering and pleasure take the Tathāgata as their condition, they are not of the same substance because there is no [reciprocal] conditioning; thus, this is a matter of conceptual thought.

Now, observing the nine realms as being precisely the Buddha-realm, and observing the realm of the Tathāgata without losing the nine realms—where flourishing and decay are both illuminated—is the true treasury of the Great Nirvāṇa.
According to this principle of conditions, one might otherwise obtain only a small fruit; now, we proceed from the ultimate perspective.
Because one reaches the Buddha-way, it is said that one "attains Buddhahood.
Sixth, regarding the clarification of receiving the three refuges and bowing to the ten wholesome precepts:
this is because all monastics and laypeople who possess discernment must take refuge in the Three Jewels and request their protective empowerment to obtain [the fruits].

The merit is immeasurable. Regarding the seven classes of practitioners, since they have already received the refuge according to their respective precepts, it does not hinder receiving it again; receiving it repeatedly brings about the non-informative (avijñapti) merit.

Since this applies to both good and evil, the same principle extends to the precepts as well. If one has not yet received the precepts, one may simply receive the inverted refuge from heterodox paths;
one should receive it at each of the six periods of the day as the occasion arises, manifesting refuge in the Triple Gem and vowing not to turn back.

In the separate explanation of the Three Refuges within the first section of the ten wholesome precepts, the first four lines clarify that those who must receive them include both monastics and laypeople, thereby encompassing the seven assemblies.
The term "those with consciousness" broadly includes the four modes of birth, as all five destinies are capable of receiving the Dharma.
The following two lines demonstrate the merit and benefits for the seven assemblies; the subsequent passage explains the meaning of receiving the precepts again, according to the text.

According to the underlying principle, this encompasses multiple aspects, as the following passage states: "Receiving [the precepts] at each of the six periods of the day according to the time" clarifies the sense of repetition by referring to receiving them separately at each distinct time.
Furthermore, this same text states: "The seven assemblies [of the Sangha] regarding the precepts;
although one has already received the refuge, it does not hinder receiving them again. This refers to the sequential repetition of receiving both the refuge and the precepts.
It is repeated to clarify its gravity. Furthermore, the *Platform Sūtra* states: "Precepts have nine grades; the lower are superior.
This is because it takes the inferior as the superior to clarify their gravity. However, this doctrine is extensively found in the sacred words [of the Buddha].

There are those who wish to discard it in favor of describing the ancestral instructions. To properly explain this, one cites examples: performing good deeds results in heavy karma of feeling, which constitutes gravity.

The principle that committing evil brings retribution, and that the gravity of the act determines the severity of the suffering received, is now clearly established; since there is no such thing as "not acting," this logic is self-evident.

Furthermore, when the following section reveals how one accords with the capacities of beings to receive the gravity of the precepts at any of the six periods of the day, the meaning of this gravity becomes even more manifest. Because one establishes a resolve and sets a specific deadline for fulfillment, it is called a "self-vow."

Regarding the reception of the Dharma, one says: "I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha" (reciting these words with single-minded devotion toward the Buddha;

repeating this three times as above is called obtaining the refuge). "I, [Name], have taken refuge in the Buddha for as long as life lasts; I have taken refuge in the Dharma for as long as life lasts;
I have taken refuge in the Saṃgha for as long as life lasts" (having thus recited these three times, the self-vow of reception is completed).
As the *Sujāta-sūtra* states: "If a person receives the three refuges, the resulting karmic reward is inexhaustible.
For example, even if the people of an entire nation were to transport out the four great treasuries of jewels for seven years, they would not exhaust them;
yet the merit of one who receives the three refuges exceeds that, being beyond all calculation."

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Comparing Merits* states: "If one were to provide offerings throughout their entire life to all those who have attained the fruits of the Two Vehicles within the four continents, and even go so far as to erect stupas for them, this would not equal the merit obtained by a man or woman who speaks these words:
'I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. This is because among all blessings, the Triple Gem alone is supreme."
If one gives rise to slander and defamation, the resulting transgression is boundless; for good and evil are analogous in their consequences.

Just as Jīvaka and Devadatta both drew blood from the Buddha, it was because of the goodness or wickedness of their respective intentions that they experienced longevity or the suffering of a shortened life.

In the cited evidence, at the beginning of the subsequent passage, four analogies for the four continents (*caturdvīpa*) are presented; these do not correspond to the actual phenomena [of the dharmas] but are employed to manifest their superior function.
If one were to apply them to the categories of good and evil, they would clarify matters such as those concerning Jīvaka and others, as seen in the *Hufa* (Protecting the Dharma) section.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyuktāgama* states: "Those who associate with Sudatta are led to receive the Three Refuges and are reborn in the heavens at the end of their lives.

If there are women who are pregnant, he causes the fetus to receive the Three Refuges; once born, they receive them again. Later, when they attain knowledge and vision, he further teaches them the Three Refuges.
Even if male or female slaves or guests are pregnant and give birth to children, he likewise instructs them in this way. If one purchases slaves, [he does so] for this purpose."
One must first receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts before purchasing [a slave]; one cannot fail to purchase them [without this].

Even when begging, lending, or taking interest, one must require the recipient to accept the Three Refuges before giving [the goods]. If there are those who give offerings to the Triple Gem, they shall hear the World-Honored One recite the names and offer prayers for their merit, whereby they shall attain rebirth in heaven.
The Buddha said, "Excellent! The Tathāgata possesses unsurpassed knowledge and vision; this is indeed certain."
One knows that by employing skillful means, all may attain rebirth in heaven.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Sudatta is called "Vimalakīrti" in the language of the Brahmans, which here is translated as "Gijukud" (also known as "Shanshi," meaning "Good Giver").

Because this elder harbored pure faith within and externally protected the Triple Gem, all those with whom he associated—whether acquaintances, relatives, or those to whom he lent money, slaves, or servants—[were likewise benefited].
All pregnant women were instructed to take refuge; this was also the speech with which Sudatta exhorted others.
The passage following "The Buddha" clarifies that the Buddha’s prediction regarding what the elder said was not erroneous.
Thus, the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* states that the Buddha addressed Maitreya in verse: "Those people of your three assemblies are those whom I previously [taught]."

Next, those nine hundred and twenty million people who received my three refuges—some reciting "Namo Buddha" once—attained the fruit of their refuge as described in detail in the *Sūtra on Right Mindfulness*: they were reborn in the heavens, experiencing the signs of celestial bliss.

Next, the practice of receiving the ten wholesome laws (daśa-kuśala-dharma) is explained: this refers to the three wholesome actions of body, four of speech, and three of mind. These ten karmic paths constitute the fundamental principle of the precepts of goodness.
The ten wholesome laws are the standard established by the Great Sage, the Wheel-Turning King; there is nothing that exceeds them, save for the three poisons and the seven [unwholesome paths].

The prohibitions and precepts established by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles do not transcend these [three categories]; therefore, they are called the "Pinnacle of Preceptual Goodness" (*śīla-kuśala-mūla*).

Nowadays, most rely on the superficial characteristics [of the precepts], and those who actually receive them are rare. Recently, there have been some foolish people who refuse to accept them, claiming that merely refraining from evil is itself what constitutes goodness.
This is not so; first, one must make a vow and prayer not to commit any evils, and then, based on that vow, one must initiate actual practice.

There must be something to rely upon as a standard; if one does not prepare in advance but suddenly gives rise to goodness, there will be no internal discipline or restraint. Consequently, when encountering conditions for transgression, one will create evil without ceasing.
Because there was no prior aspiration, one has produced manifold evils. The Great Sage, knowing the capacities of beings, therefore causes them to receive goodness.
If you say, "I do not commit evil, so this [goodness] is mine," then since you do not perform good, it should likewise be evil. Thus it is.
If one does not kill oxen, horses, donkeys, or mules, is that necessarily virtuous? This state is neutral (*avyākṛta*);
because it lacks the karma of either merit or demerit, one must give rise to a thought that is focused, sincere, and profound for it to constitute a full course of action (*karmapatha*).

In the first section of the "Direct Clarification," the initial part refutes non-acceptance while simultaneously revealing the [opponent's] views. Now, in the passage beginning with "I say," it demonstrates that acceptance is necessary.

First, the phrase "indicating the intent of the Great [Vehicle]" reveals the emergence of the noble mind, showing that this is not a mere fabrication. Then, the passage beginning with "If... serves as a reprimand against the deluded and ignorant, establishing the principle of restraint and observance.
Furthermore, the section using "evil" as an analogy for "good" shows that neither position can be established; finally, the passage beginning with "As below... cites the example of keeping livestock.
This clarifies that because one does not receive retribution for [actions] below this level, they are taken away;

therefore, one must necessarily undergo [the results] from this level downward. Thus, the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra* states: "The lower grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to a single moment of thought; the middle grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to the duration of a single meal;
the upper grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to the period from dawn until noon. During this time, one contemplates the ten wholesome actions in the mind and brings them to rest."
Because of ten evil deeds, a jackal thought of the ten wholesome actions for seven days and did not eat; it was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings wish to be born in the fourth heaven, they should, from the first day to the seventh day, fix their mindfulness upon that heaven, uphold the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, contemplate the ten wholesome actions, and practice the path of the ten wholesome deeds."

Dedicating these merits, one vows to be reborn before Maitreya Buddha; regarding the phrase "seven days," this is spoken merely from the perspective of the near term—if even this brings about rebirth in that heaven, how much more so will a single lifetime not surely achieve it?
In the section on citing questions to manifest merit, the first part—“Never before has such a virtuous portion been seen”—is divided into three sections, the textual structure of which is clear.
The term *yǎngān* (野干) should be read as *jiàn* (豻); the *Jīng yīnyì* (經音義) states that its form is like that of a dog.

[The commentary] asks: "How can a foolish beast recollect virtue? This statement serves to clarify the phrase "seven days" found in the sutra. The point made below is that it explains this expression from the scripture.
Question: The superior rewards in the heavens are inconceivable; how is it that one can experience such great merit within seven days? Answer:

Although a virtuous cause may be minute, the fruit obtained can be exceedingly great. Just as a small fire can burn a massive mountain, so too a single good deed, though subtle, can destroy great evil.
Furthermore, when one harbors a single moment of wrong view and slanders the Mahāyāna, although the time is extremely brief, one will suffer for long kalpas.
The principle of the causes and effects of suffering, as well as karma, are inconceivable and cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.
Within the questions and answers, the question can be understood by using the cause to clarify the effect, and the answer can be comprehended by using evil as an analogy for good.

Next, the method for receiving the precepts is explained: whether one receives them from a teacher or takes the vow of self-ordination, as described above, after having performed the threefold refuge and the threefold self-refuge, one speaks these words aloud:
"I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, shall give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and benevolence toward all sentient beings and shall not give rise to a mind of killing.
As with the subsequent nine wholesome precepts, this should be applied by analogy; there is no need for further prolixity.

Within the dharma of receiving [the precepts], first showing the formal conclusion indicates the emergence of the essence of the reception; subsequently, the characteristics are shown, mentioning only non-killing, while the remaining nine are to be understood by analogy.
Seventh, the clarification of generating the bodhicitta.
*Bodhi* means awakening; because one awakens oneself and awakens others, one is called a Buddha.

In the first section of the seventh explanation, the initial phrase translates the name, while the following portion explains the meaning. There are three meanings of "awakening," but in this text there are only two;
the single character "Buddha" (佛) signifies the fulfillment of awakening.

Since the practitioner already dwells within the Buddha-dharma, they possess the seeds of Buddhahood; they must therefore arouse the aspiration for awakening and apply mental attention (*manasikāra*) to practice contemplation.

This is the bridge for proceeding toward the fruit of Buddhahood and the root from which the myriad practices arise. It is like space containing all phenomena or the ocean receiving the hundred rivers;
if one does not first establish this mind before initiating practice, one will inevitably become lost and submerged.

In the section "Explaining the Intent and Manifesting Virtue," first, regarding the "Buddha-seed": because it continues the lineage of the Sage, one must generate the Buddha-mind once one has become a seed of the Buddha;
"Buddha" means awakening. Hereafter, the virtues are manifested: because it can ferry one to the other shore, it is like a bridge or raft;
because it can give rise to the myriad practices, it is the root; because it is vast and all-encompassing, it is likened to space and the ocean; [it is] suffering... [end of fragment].
The following passage demonstrates the fault of not generating the resolve; "jian" (建) means to establish.

As for the characteristics of this bodhi: if one now wishes to generate the resolve, there must be both principle (li) and practice (xing), which exist in relation to conditions—these two aspects are comprehensive in meaning.
Otherwise, if the ultimate (zhen) and the conventional (su) diverge, it is not the meaning of the True Dharma.

In the first section of the main explanation of the aspects of practice, the first two phrases investigate the present state; the subsequent portion clarifies that these aspects are twofold: principle (*li*) and practice (*xing*). Below, they are harmonized:

according to principle, one accords with the mind; as for practice, one must confront phenomena. Phenomena must be integrated by means of the mind, and the mind must be integrated by means of phenomena;
only when mind and phenomena are perfectly interfused does one conform to the correct path. If this were contrary to the true and the conventional, it would not be so.
It is not appropriate to cultivate [this] in a circular manner.

What is called "the arising of principle" refers to the fact that the five aggregates and all phenomena of one's own mind are fundamentally without self; to deeply realize this essential point is named the bodhicitta.

In the first section of the initial principle explained separately, the first phrase establishes the premise. This is followed by the formal explanation that "mind" refers to the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The five aggregates and all phenomena are provisionally existent through dependent origination; they are the objective portions (*nimittabhāga*) of consciousness, which is the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Sentient beings, through delusion and inversion, conceive of these as real, thereby giving rise to the view of self (the self of persons and the self of dharmas), which is the nature of universal imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Their fundamental nature, however, belongs to the realm of principle (*tattva*).

That is, by realizing that all phenomena are originally without self, one now enters the nature of perfected accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) based upon the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

furthermore, by understanding that all phenomena are one's own mind and that there is truly no object produced through conditions, one enters the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda-svabhāva*) based upon the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
and finally, by understanding that the original nature of all phenomena is spontaneously true, neither defiled nor pure, one enters the nature of perfected accomplishment.

The nature of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is profound; the concluding summary below shows that these three absences of intrinsic nature constitute the true principle. Because one is able to know this essential point, it is called *bodhi*.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Quiescence is *bodhi*, because it is free from all marks; the provisional name is *bodhi*, because it is merely a designation."
Because it is empty, as stated in the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra*: "The characteristic of bodhi is that which transcends the three realms, surpasses mundane dharmas, and cuts off all speech;
the non-arising of all arisings is called the arousal of the bodhicitta. Thus, according to these various sūtras, one arouses the mind by means of dispelling both characteristics and the mind itself.
Therefore, it is called "arousing the mind."
In the citation of scriptural authority, first, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* quotes Vimalakīrti speaking to Maitreya:
"Do not entice these devaputras with this Dharma; in reality, there is no one who has set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
Because bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind; it is simply quiescence."
This bodhi is because it extinguishes all marks; one does not contemplate this bodhi because it is free from all conditions...
up to "this bodhi is a mere provisional name" because names are empty. That passage is extremely extensive; I have cited its essentials here.

Furthermore, the subsequent text explicitly states in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*: "Those who transcend the three realms are those who are free from fetters and have passed beyond the mundane."
The Dharma has no marks of existence, therefore language is cut off; names are empty, therefore it is based on objects that the mind arises.
Thus it is said that all arisings do not cling to the mark of arising, which is why it is called "non-arising," as summarized below.

This means that because the essence of this mind is fundamentally pure, one realizes this principle and brings about purification through practice; therefore, "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*) is itself called "practice.

Among these three [sections], the first sentence provides a general indication of the principle-essence, while the subsequent sentences explain how the gates of practice arise from that principle-essence. Thus, "mind" refers to the eight [consciousnesses].
The substance of consciousness is itself the true reality, inherently pure and penetrating the three natures as explained above.
Examining the arising of practice below, it is based upon this rational nature; since the nature is fundamentally pure, the characteristics of the karma performed are also pure.

Therefore, the following section concludes by showing that practice arises from principle and principle is established through practice. Because practice is subsumed within principle, it is so stated.
Principle is itself practice.

As for practice: having established the mind in stillness as described above, one generates the great aspiration, thinking, "I shall enter the Buddha-way to extensively deliver all sentient beings," and dedicates all roots of goodness cultivated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Next, regarding the first section of the middle practice, the first two phrases are based on correct principle to give rise to the great aspiration for right practice.
This "mind of great desire" is precisely the bodhicitta. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The root of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is desire;
even 'wholesome desire' is the initial arousal of the mind toward the Way, the very root of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Therefore, I say that desire is the root. My entry into the Buddha-way is the practice of self-benefit, while the extensive deliverance of sentient beings is the practice of benefiting others.
What has been set forth below is the general dedication of these two benefits toward Bodhi;
based on this practice, I take principle as the foundation.

Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a person resolves their mind, saying, 'I shall certainly become a Buddha,' they have already transcended all worlds and should receive supreme offerings.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a person resolves their mind to seek Buddhahood without ceasing or resting, even if someone were to lift them up with a finger..."
It is not difficult for the trichiliocosm to abide through the kalpa of emptiness; however, if one makes a vow saying, "I shall become a Buddha," such a person is rare.
Why is this? Because the minds of worldly people are inferior and lack great resolve.
The *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* states that there are ten great right vows to which one should constantly aspire and practice.

Because it clarifies the precepts of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-śīla*), this initial section on the great vows consists of two fascicles; therein it is explained that these ten vows are all for the purpose of generating the bodhicitta.
First, I vow that the roots of goodness planted by me in previous lives and in this present life shall be bestowed upon all sentient beings and dedicated to the Buddha-way,
so that this vow of mine may increase with every thought-moment, never be forgotten throughout successive births,
and be protected by *dhāraṇī*.
In the first of the separately explained vows, the initial clarification of the two benefits cultivated is dedicated toward Bodhi; this is followed by the actual formulation of the vow.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "Total Retention" (*zongchi*).
The second vow is that by means of these roots of goodness, wherever he is born, he may encounter a Buddha and always receive offerings, never being born in a land where no Buddha resides.
The third vow is that he may be born in a Buddha-land.
The fourth vow is that he may draw near to all Buddhas, attending them at their left and right like a shadow follows a form; having attained such proximity, [he may...]
I have taught that the accomplishment of the five supernormal powers constitutes the third vow:

to draw near to the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and attain thorough awakening (the treatise indicates that this arousal of the mind belongs to the stage of Dry Wisdom, yet it results in the realization of the five supernormal powers).

The fourth vow is to thoroughly penetrate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and its provisional designations so as to disseminate [the teaching], and to realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and attain the wisdom of the True Dharma.
The fourth [vow] relies on conventional truth to disseminate the ultimate truth; thus, with both the true and the conventional flowing together, one attains that correct wisdom.
The fifth vow is to preach, instruct, benefit, and gladden sentient beings with an insatiable mind, causing them all to attain understanding;
that is, the fifth is to preach the Dharma without weariness so as to cause people to attain understanding.
The sixth vow is to reach all worlds throughout the ten directions by means of the Buddha's spiritual power to make offerings to all Buddhas,
listen to and receive the True Dharma, and extensively gather in sentient beings.
This sixth [vow] relies on the power of all Buddhas to make offerings to all Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and gather in sentient beings.
Seventh, may all sentient beings who follow the pure wheel of Dharma, who hear my teaching or hear my name,
immediately attain the abandonment of all afflictions.
Seventh, to follow the pure wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas above and transform sentient beings below, causing them to be liberated from afflictions.
Eighth, to follow and protect sentient beings, bestowing happiness upon them, sacrificing body, life, and wealth to uphold the True Dharma and eliminate that which is unbeneficial.
The eighth is to manifest through provisional means to transform others, uprooting their suffering and bestowing upon them happiness.

The ninth is the vow: "Though I practice the True Dharma, my mind shall neither engage in anything nor refrain from anything; yet, in order to transform sentient beings, I shall not abandon the right aspiration."
Ninth, I benefit sentient beings through the Dharma without seeking any karmic retribution.
Tenth, may these ten great vows of mine pervade the realm of sentient beings and encompass all vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
even if the realm of sentient beings were to come to an end, my vows would then end, yet because the realm of sentient beings can never be exhausted, so too shall my great [vows] never end.
Vows, too, are inexhaustible.
The tenth is the perfect arousal of ten vows that pervade the realm of sentient beings; because these ten vows serve as the king among vows, encompassing all infinite vows without exception.
If one examines the characteristics of the tenth vow in detail below, they will be seen to be inexhaustible.

Upon careful examination, there are slight differences between this treatise and the text [of the *Abhidharmakośa*]. The treatise divides the "hearing of the Dharma from one who is near the Buddha" into three or four categories, whereas the present text combines them into three;
the manner in which they are expanded according to the treatise is self-evident.

Once the practitioner has thus made these correct vows, they next receive the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-koṭi-śīla*). As the text is easy to understand, it is not provided here in full;
those who wish to see it should consult the lower fascicle of the *Zhengxing yi* (The Ritual of Correct Practice).

In the section on receiving the precepts, the text also refers to the *Bodhicittotpādana-vidhi* (The Ritual for Generating the Bodhicitta), specifically the *Śrāvakayāna-samyak-pratipatti-paścāt-tāpa-vidhi* (The Ritual for the Right Practice and Repentance of the Śramaṇa School) composed by the Great Master [Śāntarakṣita]. Alas, this text has now been lost;
the essential points for receiving the precepts are silent and unheard—how lamentable!

the term "true scriptures" (*sūtra*) is used in the eighth heading to distinguish them from external (non-Buddhist) texts.
This Mahāyāna scripture of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) proclaims the profound and pure Dharma of emptiness, as it has been taught by the Tathāgata.
