The pure and empty dharma is precisely the Mahāyāna’s ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
That which flows from the Dharma-body is traced back to its source to reveal the capacity for exposition.
Thus, the practitioner, with a pure mind, cherishes and honors the Mahāyāna, upholding, reciting, copying, and making offerings to it;
furthermore, because all sūtras belonging to other vehicles are likewise outflows of the Mahāyāna, they too are upheld by me as being without marks (*animitta*).
Because they do not contradict this, they are able to see the Buddhas.
Next, regarding the recitation of the middle [section]: first, one merely recites the Mahāyāna; subsequently, one universally propagates all the teachings.

That which flows from the Mahāyāna constitutes the establishment of provisional means for the sake of ultimate reality (*upāya-kauśalya*). Those who receive and uphold it without contradiction understand that the provisional is itself the real (*prajñā*).
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "If there are those who receive and uphold the words of the *Prajñā*, draw near to them, read, recite, remember, transcribe, and preserve them,

and perform various kinds of offerings, they shall not fall into the evil destinies, shall constantly behold the Buddhas, and shall travel from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, likewise making offerings to the Buddhas."
In the cited passage, the first "Great Chapter" refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Its clarification of the benefits of merit consists of six sections according to the text:
(1) the section on upholding the name; (2) reciting it closely; (3) reciting the main text; (4) recollecting its meaning and principle;
(5) transcribing it; and (6) making offerings to it. The subsequent sections do not conclude with a summary of the benefits.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If, for the sake of fear, or for the sake of gain and merit, one writes out even a single verse of this sūtra, one will be born in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*).

If, desiring blessings and benefit, one reads and recites the sūtra for a single day, or personally gives one's own wealth and treasures to the Dharma-preacher, or if one is able to hear, write, uphold, and read and recite the secret treasury of all Buddhas, then one will be born [there]."
Regarding the Akṣobhya realm:
according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, if one upholds even a single verse of this sutra out of fear, for the sake of profit, or for the sake of merit, one will be reborn in the Akṣobhya realm;
the rest of the text is easy to understand.

Furthermore, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "If there are those who, upon briefly hearing of the Buddha’s supreme wisdom, rejoice with a profound heart and do not give rise to slander, they shall not fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
wherever they are born, they will encounter a Buddha, and even by recollecting the merits of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, their virtues will be boundless."
The ninth [section] clarifies the making of Buddha images as an offering to the *śarīra*.
The ninth heading mentions *śarīra*, which here is translated as "sacred bone.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "Because the Buddha saw this benefit, he entered the Vajra-samādhi and shattered his body into pieces like mustard seeds."

There are those who obtain the Buddha’s *śarīra* and make offerings according to their capacity; such persons will receive happiness among devas and humans, even until the end of suffering, yet their merit will not be exhausted.

In this section of the *Śāstra*, the first part indicates the Buddha’s original vow, the section beginning with "If" indicates the mode of practice, and the section beginning with "This" concludes the benefits.
Furthermore, the *Anuttaraśraya-sūtra* states: "Suppose the Sahā world were ground into fine dust, and every one of those particles were a person who, throughout their entire life,

would not equal that of a man or woman who takes a Buddha-relic the size of a mustard seed and constructs a stupa the size of an *āmala* fruit."
If one fashions a needle-sized canopy, a jujube-leaf-sized image, or an image as large as a grain of wheat,
this merit surpasses the former by an immeasurable and inconceivable amount. Even if one does not dedicate it toward the Unsurpassed Way,

the accumulation of this merit could not be fully exhausted even if it were used to become the king of the six heavens of desire or a Wheel-Turning Sage King for as many times as there are atoms in the Sahā world.

Next, the *Anuttaraśrayasūtra* (The Sutra on the Supreme Reliance) consists of two fascicles; the term "āmala," a small fruit from India, is used here as a small example to illustrate the greatness of its meritorious benefits.

This refers to the Pure Land, which is eternally adorned and unmoved by the three calamities.

The general heading of "Right Contemplation" (Zhèngguān) is annotated as follows: "Although the myriad practices differ, they are based on a single principle.

This first point excludes false understandings, such as those of external paths (*tīrthika*), for although they also cultivate meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), these are not truly right contemplation. Thus, the text below states: "Only the Buddha-way possesses it; other paths do not.

Question: Since the principle is pervasive throughout the One Vehicle, how does it differ from *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only)? Answer: The distinction between subject and object will be clarified below. Question:

Since both Emptiness and Consciousness are equally profound, which constitutes the ultimate truth? Answer: The principle of *Vijñaptimātra* is profound, yet the merit of the two-fold emptiness is great; thus, [the latter] reaches the ultimate.
The great merit is manifest and the profound principle is ultimate; since the principle is inexhaustible, how could the merit ever be exhausted?

To lead one to the source of the mind is precisely the two bodies of Principle and Wisdom (*dharmatā-kāya* and *jñāna-kāya*). To clarify it in this way is no different from the "Sevenfold Rites of Right Contemplation," as will be explained in detail below.
The ultimate truth of the absolute limit does not transcend the two emptinesses of person and phenomena; it exists only in the Buddha-way and is absent in other paths.
Through the two emptinesses of person and phenomena, the two types of grasping are severed, and thus all afflictions have no cause by which they can arise.

In the general summary of the explanation of the meaning, there are three parts. First, the initial two lines provide a general indication. Second, the following two lines, beginning with "only," distinguish and clarify.

Third, the four lines beginning with "by means of" explain the merit. Regarding the first part: the upper line reveals the profundity of the principle, while the lower line clarifies the subtlety of contemplation.

As for the phrase "the ultimate truth is truly supreme," according to the three vehicles [of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas] below, all must employ these two contemplations; if within one's own vehicle, they are likewise required.

To speak of the ultimate principle (*tattva*) is none other than the true pinnacle. Now, based on the perfect cultivation and the correct application of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) to reveal the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), it is stated directly that the ultimate principle is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the essential substance of the nature of sentient beings.
Because it exhausts the principle and fully realizes the nature, it is called the "ultimate principle. Since this principle is fundamentally without delusion, it is termed "true."

That to which the three vehicles return is called the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*). Although this principle is truly ultimate, it is obscured by delusion and thus not manifest. Delusion consists of the person and phenomena;
the function of discarding these two attachments relies upon the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). When the two kinds of emptiness are established, the ultimate principle is revealed.

Thus, one knows that consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is not [the ultimate] apart from the two kinds of emptiness, yet the two kinds of emptiness are not complete apart from consciousness-only. One must abandon this [dualistic] practice.
Since there are no faults that can surpass this gate, it is said that one does not "transgress the two emptinesses. Based on this, these are the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*).
Next, ordinary beings and non-Buddhists turn their backs on these two emptinesses and constantly cling to the reality of a person and phenomena within body and mind;

thus, regarding the principle of emptiness, they have nothing to attain and merely hear of it. Even if they practice worldly meditations (*dhyāna*), they merely follow perverse conceptions. Among the three [categories], the first is as follows:
The first two lines are able to destroy the two attachments, while the latter two lines are able to sever the two obstacles.
Thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All noble beings are named after the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This means that although there are differences in depth and shallowness among the noble ones of the three vehicles, when it comes to entering realization, it depends solely upon the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

In the first section of the initial clarification, the scripture is first cited from the Wei translation. Below this, the intent is shown by distinguishing the capacities of the vehicles into Great and Small, thereby proving that there are hierarchical differences.

Thus, the depths of the three vehicles differ; although their stages and positions (*caryā-bhūmi*) vary, they all realize the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), and thus the realization of the fruit consists solely of the two emptinesses.
Question: It is generally said that the Lesser Vehicle does not penetrate the emptiness of phenomena.
Now, as for who provides the response: if we consider the provisional methods of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), it is indeed as the Tathāgata asked.

Because the Buddha first opened the teaching by primarily addressing those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), he spoke only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and not of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); therefore, the single contemplation of the emptiness of persons is what is appropriate to that specific teaching.
Now, according to the *Xing-shi chao*, it says: "At the Deer Park, when the fundamental [teaching] was proclaimed, eighty thousand devas immediately [realized it]."
To give rise to the Great Path is precisely the universal resonance of the Perfect Sound, which reaches both those of dull and sharp faculties alike;

thus, even those of the Lesser Vehicle attain the two contemplations of penetration and clarity. Within the various divisions of the Lesser Vehicle, there are twenty schools comprising six sects (the six sects are detailed elsewhere).

Only the Vātsīputrīya school asserts the existence of a self (that is, the school that maintains the co-existence of both self and dharmas); all other schools maintain non-self. This is because the Buddha had not yet...

In the world beyond, there are various non-Buddhists who each speculate that there is a self (*ātman*), either identical to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) or separate from them, whether large or small, white or yellow;
they designate this presiding entity within the body as the "divine self" (*puruṣa-ātman*).

Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, in order to refute these speculations, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for those of the Hīnayāna, stating that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*).
When various minor schools contemplate the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), they see only the form produced by the aggregation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

how could there be a divine self (*ātman*) acting as a sovereign? It is merely the illusory conceptualization of one’s own mind—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the false construction of the conditions of karmic momentum.

Because these accumulated delusions serve as the cause, one undergoes the fruit of suffering. Now that the deluded causes of origination (*samudaya*) are understood, they cease of their own accord; thus, one's arbitrary calculations come to rest.

In this regard, I ultimately have no self as a knower; this absence of a personal self is called "emptiness of persons. However, regarding the phenomena (*dharma*) upon which they each rely, their attachments differ:
some hold that all three time periods exist; others hold that the past and future do not exist; some hold that both the coarse and the subtle are real; others hold that both are conventional;

some hold that the coarse is conventional while the subtle is real; and others hold that the coarse is real while the subtle is conventional. Since these attachments differ, their contemplations [also differ].
The characteristics [of these views] also differ; for now, based on this region, I shall provisionally present two interpretations—real and conventional—to clarify their differences.

The Sarvāstivāda school, which maintains that dharmas are substantially real, asserts that the phenomena of the three categories exist in all three time periods, and that both the coarse and the subtle are real; thus they hold the doctrine of "dharmas exist, but the self does not.

That school contemplates the emptiness of dharmas, yet it is only the coarse aspects that are empty; as for the subtle aspects of form and mind, they are perceived through the power of contemplative wisdom.

Because they are inferior, [the Vaibhāṣikas] further grasp them as being the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); since these coarse, substantial dharmas can be refuted, they are also called "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
However, although name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) are empty by nature, this does not obstruct their own reckoning of them as being truly ultimate.

The Dharmaguptaka school is designated as the "School of Provisional Names" (i.e., the school that all dharmas are merely names, or alternatively, the school whose view encompasses both the provisional and the real), which reckons the three categories of phenomena.

The aggregates (*skandha*) are designated as real (because each of the five aggregates—form and the four mental factors—possesses its own intrinsic nature), while the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are designated as conventional (because they are formed by aggregating the aggregates and thus lack an intrinsic nature of their own).
Regarding the establishment of this contemplation, it follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, which states that the cessation of three types of mind is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

These are: the mind of conventional designation (*prajñapti-citta*), the mind of dharma-nature (*dharma-svabhāva-citta*), and the mind of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-citta*). As for the mind of conventional designation, there are two types: first, the conventional person (*pudgala-prajñapti*); second, the conventional phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*). "Person" refers to the self (*ātman*), and "phenomena" refers to the elements and bases. The person is a false conceptualization; phenomena are conventionally established based on the aggregates. Both lack an intrinsic nature and are collectively termed "conventional designations. Because one clings to these names...

[The three types of mind are: (1) the mind of provisional names (*prajñapti-citta*); (2) the mind of real dharmas (*dharma-citta*)—that is, the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates: form is the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), and mind is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Because they can serve as the substratum for all phenomena, they are called "real dharmas"; because one clings to these [aggregates] as being without reality, it is called the "mind of real dharmas";

(3) the mind of emptiness (*śūnyatā-citta*)—this refers to using the wisdom of emptiness to extinguish the mind of real dharmas. Although the mind of real dharmas is extinguished, the wisdom of emptiness still remains. Question: How are these three minds extinguished? Answer:

The mind of provisional names is extinguished either by the wisdom resulting from the condition of extensive learning (*bahu-śruta*), or by the wisdom resulting from the condition of reflection (*cintā*).

The wisdom that extinguishes phenomena functions within the stages of *uṣmagata* and so forth; by means of the wisdom of emptiness, one extinguishes the mind of emptiness and enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
At the time of extinguishing suffering and entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and at the time of severing the continuity [of existence], one extinguishes [phenomena].

This passage serves as proof that a practitioner’s initial mind cultivates both contemplations simultaneously: by means of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, one earnestly seeks the non-existence of a provisional person within the five aggregates.

One perceives that the self (*ātman*) consists merely of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), and provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*). (Thus, the *Jingye shu* says: "Observing and analyzing in relation to the self, one sees only these as objects.

By means of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*), one contemplates these gross elements and observes that they aggregate the aggregates (*skandha*) to form a body; they themselves lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and exist only as provisional names.

Since provisional phenomena are empty, how could provisional names exist? Thus, one is able to dismantle the coarse marks of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This begins from the initial stage of the path.

Upon reaching the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*), one immediately understands this principle; because it can extinguish this mind of provisional names, one enters the preparatory stages (*prayoga-avasthā*) such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Within these stages, one still clings to the subtle dharmas of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*)—the five aggregates—as being truly existent (as the *Yejie shu* says:

"When seeking them within the aggregates, there are only name-and-form"). Based on this, in the preparatory stage of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-nairātmya-prayoga*), one primarily [contemplates] name...
Form is the object of contemplation, and the wisdom of the "emptiness of mind" is the subject of contemplation;

this continues until the stage of the Sage, when both form and mind are empty, and one contemplates the principle of the twofold emptiness solely through the wisdom of emptiness. At this point, the subtle marks of the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) are utterly extinguished.
When the mind that clings to phenomena is extinguished, the self-mind does not arise, and the subtle marks of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) are also utterly extinguished.
Thus we know that although one attains the two kinds of emptiness during the preceding stage of the Requisites (*sambhāra-avasthā*), it is not yet ultimate;

only upon reaching this point where the two types of grasping are completely extinguished can it be called the true, ultimate principle of the two emptinesses. (Therefore, the *Jieshu* says: "Seeking persons and seeking dharmas, they are utterly unobtainable—this is emptiness. Thus the Treatise says:

"First, by means of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one does not perceive a self (*ātman*) within the five aggregates; subsequently, by means of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)."

Within the five aggregates, one does not perceive the nature of form, nor does one perceive the nature of consciousness up to the end of the list. Furthermore, it is said there are two kinds of contemplation:

the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of non-self. Regarding the contemplation of emptiness, one does not perceive conventionally designated sentient beings, just as a person sees that a jar is empty because it contains no water;
if one does not perceive dharmas, this is called the contemplation of non-self. It is further said that this is because of the emptiness of dharmas.
To see the extinction of the substance of form, up to the extinction of the substance of consciousness, is called the wisdom of emptiness and non-self. It is further said:
"As long as the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas) persist, my mind will not necessarily be ultimately severed, because causes and conditions are not empty.

Only when the five aggregates are extinguished is it then called the perfection of the characteristic of emptiness. This is further illustrated by the analogy of a tree that is cut down, burned, and reduced to ashes.

When the charcoal is completely consumed, the perception of trees is extinguished. Although the two schools mentioned above differ regarding the conventional and the real, as far as entering into realization is concerned, it lies solely in the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).

(The above refers to the Śrāvaka-yāna; although the causes and conditions of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna differ, what they ultimately realize does not go beyond the two emptinesses. Question: In the commentaries on the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), it is said that the nature of phenomena is empty and there is no self (*anātman*);
now you speak of the "two emptinesses. Are these the same or different? Answer: The emptiness of nature and the absence of self are precisely...

There are two kinds of emptiness. Furthermore, there are two natures: first, the nature of attachment (which is the *ātman*), and second, the essential nature (which consists of the five aggregates and the two dharmas of name-and-form).

If one empties the nature of attachment, it is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); if one empties the essential nature, it is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Thus, the *Shishi yaoyong chao* states:

"All dharmas" (the objects of observation), "nature" (the attachments to be subverted, namely the nature of attachment and the essential nature), "emptiness" (the emptiness of persons), and "non-self" (the emptiness of phenomena). This is explained in detail as follows.
The preceding discussion has resolved any doubts regarding the two lesser bodhisattvas who clarify the two emptinesses.

As for "emptiness of persons," it is the same as before. Regarding the contemplation of the "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*): one directly contemplates the fundamental nature of all phenomena as empty; they exist only because of deluded perceptions of the mind.

Thus, their illusory characteristics are known to be without substance, and form and emptiness are naturally integrated. Emptiness does not depend on being dissected or cut apart before it is realized. This concludes the section on the three greater bodhisattvas.

Regarding the two types of emptiness realized by the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, this is roughly the same as previously shown: it means that through profound contemplation of the fact that self-nature is fundamentally devoid of both persons and dharmas, these two attachments perish, and the three bodies are perfectly realized.
This will be explained more extensively later. Question: Since both the Mahayana and Hinayana schools speak of the two types of emptiness, upon what sutras and teachings are they based?
Answer: The various treatises of the Hinayana all take the *Āgamas* as their primary authority; this is recorded in the Master’s catalog of internal scriptures.

It is said that what is subsumed under the Sautrāntika school must necessarily be based upon the *Catur-āgama*; this is the case for the "lesser bodhisattvas," whose principles must be investigated in detail.

However, while the discourse on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is found throughout the various Mahāyāna sūtras, there are distinctions between the partial and the perfect regarding emptiness, as well as differences in depth and shallowness.
Now, by citing the various schools to determine the standard of their teachings, one can know that if a practitioner’s stage belongs to the partial or lesser vehicle, then...

In various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and other scriptures, the initial Mahāyāna practitioners are specifically taught that the characteristics of the causes and conditions of all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent;
this is precisely the foundational scripture of this school. Guifeng said:

"The Fully Pure Awakened One, appearing in the world of humans, first taught the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing to enable them to realize suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."

To eliminate the grasping at a self without yet having realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one must first exhaust the root of the illness before discussing Prajñā. Master Ci'en said:
"The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths to bring about knowledge of the emptiness of the self, while maintaining that only phenomena exist.

When Kauṇḍinya and others first attained the Way, they heard that 'phenomena exist' and consequently clung to the notion that all phenomena are ultimately existent; thus, they were attached to the lesser fruit and did not seek the Great."
The Buddha, as a skillful means, further taught the emptiness of dharmas to eliminate attachment to existence;
therefore, during the subsequent period, he spoke of the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, stating that the fundamental characteristics of all dharmas are empty.

Subhūti and others, turning their minds toward the Great Vehicle, asserted that the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are entirely non-existent. The Four Teachings of Tiantai state that bodhisattvas of dull faculties see only this.
"One-sided emptiness does not see non-emptiness," and so forth, up to the statement that "Prajñā within the Vaipulya section" refers to the *Sādhāraṇaprajñā* (Common Prajñā) and others;

this is precisely this teaching. (The *Yuanren lun* states: "Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva established two kinds of Prajñā: first, the common, and second, the uncommon. The common is heard and understood by the Two Vehicles alike, serving to destroy their attachment to the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
The uncommon is understood only by Bodhisattvas, revealing the Buddha-nature. Based on these various texts, the school takes the *Prajñā* as its primary principle; such is the practitioner.
It is said: "One merely understands the emptiness of phenomena but has not yet exhausted the root of the mind; because this is inferior to the subsequent Great [Vehicle], it is called 'Small.
Because its name is the Way (*mārga*), and its contemplation flows as a dual stream, and its compassion is widely extended—surpassing the two previous vehicles—it is termed a Bodhisattva.

Question: It is said that the four divisions of the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*) constitute the teaching for Small Bodhisattvas. What is the meaning of this? Answer: The four divisions are established according to their meanings and according to their schools. Although the person...

Generally speaking, regarding the temporal and doctrinal limitations that confine the Small Vehicle and the lesser Bodhisattvas, both the *Shu* (Commentary) and the *Chao* (Sub-commentary) clearly state that these two vehicles are distinct in their heavenly realms and that the contemplative practices and principles of the Sūtras and Śāstras are divergent.

One should investigate the texts of the Patriarchs and refrain from making groundless judgments. Furthermore, some say that while [the vehicle] is small in terms of doctrine, it is great in terms of the person; this refers to Dharmamitra.

Since Virtue has already understood the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and further feels weary of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he directs his mind toward the Great Vehicle with the aspiration for the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

Furthermore, since the *Chao* (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*) clearly judges this school as Mahāyāna, and since the mental contemplation (*citta-bhāvanā*) therein is universal, how could he not be a Bodhisattva? Moreover, this is not so;

since he aspires to the Buddha-vehicle and ultimately aims for the Single Reality (*eka-tattva*), he is indeed a Great Bodhisattva. How then could the practices for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood be categorized as "Small"?

Regarding the stages used to suppress the great mind, there are those that refer collectively to those in the forty minds, as well as those that refer specifically to the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth—not a few.
I have not had the leisure to discuss them here. If this is so, what are the characteristics of the stages of a small bodhisattva?

The answer is that in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the stages beginning from the "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood encompass the three vehicles and comprise ninety-two stages.
This stage is that of the Small Bodhisattva, the fruit of realization which is not [limited to] any single level;
it is explained extensively in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and the *Śrāvaka-viniścaya-śāstra*. The *Zongjinglu* states:

"The reason all the Sages have transmitted their teachings is to ensure that the blind-born ordinary beings do not cling to birth-and-death (or the realms of humans and devas), and to ensure that the 'one-eyed' followers of the Two Vehicles do not dwell in nirvana."

(Threefold Canon) At night, one observes the minor bodhisattvas and causes them to relinquish the provisional vehicle; (Shared Teaching) one observes the distinct bodhisattvas and causes them not to cling to the path of the teaching;
(Distinct Teaching) when both attachments to persons and phenomena have perished, the single path of constant radiance manifests of itself; (Perfect Teaching).
The practitioner who trains and studies should rely on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, which states:
"One who practices the Dharma relies upon a body that is empty and tranquil, does not travel about, maintains silence in speech, speaks little, sleeps little, and remains awake much;

always eats in a single sitting, does not consume mixed foods, contemplates all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata as being neither existent nor non-existent, and through that knowledge, causes all dharmas to be universally penetrated and attained."
Well understood.

In the first section of the "Demonstrating Right Practice," although the distinctions between the characteristics of the Great and Small Vehicles were initially presented based solely on the Sūtras, since that approach was general and intended to establish the primary meaning of the present text, it now cites the *Ārya-śāstra* (the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra*) to demonstrate right practice; from this, one can fully understand the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

This correctly reveals Consciousness-Only. The first two lines establish and manifest the fundamental tenet of the treatise. Below, the text cites passages to demonstrate the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which is divided into two parts:

first, clarifying the preparatory means (*upāya*); second, demonstrating the actual contemplation. This latter part is further divided into three sections: the first three lines show how understanding arises based on the teachings;

"deliberation" (*cintā*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), which, according to the meaning, corresponds to the two types of wisdom—listening (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*). "That which is taught" refers to the teaching itself, namely the Mahāyāna *Abhisamaya* (Realization).

The meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures is that all dharmas are objects; these are the mundane and supramundane, contaminated and uncontaminated, and the primary and secondary environments (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) as explained in the sūtras.

Their essence permeates the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). To know that they are neither existent nor non-existent is precisely the contemplative characteristic (*vipaśyanā-lakṣaṇa*) elucidated in the sūtras.
This occurs through hearing (*śruta*), which leads to reflection (*cintā*); because of reflection, one knows the meaning that they are neither existent nor non-existent. The details are as follows:
The following three phrases explain how practice arises based on understanding; the first two phrases cite wisdom confronting its objects to establish correct practice;
the final phrase uses wisdom to illuminate the teachings so as to abandon false attachments. "Universal" (biàn) means observing all three natures simultaneously;

"pervasive" (tōng) means understanding and penetrating existence and non-existence. [Question: When one asks about all phenomena, they are the objects [of cognition], and since these objects pervade the three natures, how should one apply contemplation?

Knowing that there is neither existence nor non-existence: first, one contemplates that the false conceptualization of all phenomena as a self or a person is the nature of pervasive imagination (the coarse aspect of persons and phenomena).

Because this nature is truly non-existent, it is called "not existent" (the initial aspect of the two emptinesses). Next, one contemplates that all phenomena are transformations of consciousness-only, which is the nature of dependence on others (the subtle aspect of the two attachments).
Because this nature exists only conventionally, it is called "not non-existent. Finally, one contemplates all [phenomena]...

The intrinsic purity of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); because this nature is truly existent, it is "neither existent nor non-existent" (i.e., True Suchness as revealed by the correct contemplation of the two emptinesses).

The first [of these three] is the contemplation of reality (*tattva-vipaśyanā*), the second is the contemplation of the conventional (*saṃvṛti-vipaśyanā*), and the third is the contemplation of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-vipaśyanā*).

If one contemplates the former two separately without contemplating the latter one, it belongs merely to the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*) and does not accord with perfect cultivation. If [one contemplates] only...
If one contemplates only the latter [the ultimate] and not the former two [the conventional and the middle], then it belongs exclusively to the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*);

to judge the stages based on names would likely distance the beginner. Now, contemplating a single dharma through its three natures—where the conventional is the ultimate and the single object is the three truths—it is neither before nor after.
Thus, it reaches upward to the ultimate sages and connects downward to the beginner, as has already been clarified; therefore, you should properly adopt this understanding.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "That all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent is the primary ultimate truth. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas reveal the Middle Way; although they teach that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, they do not remain fixed [in that negation].
Because they arise from conditions, they are called 'existent,' and because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are called 'non-existent.'"
The *Wú fóxìng lùn* (Treatise on the Absence of Buddha-nature) states: "The two truths cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said to be non-existent; they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Therefore, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it cannot be said to exist because there is no grasping at persons or phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-abhiniveśa*);

it cannot be said to be non-existent because it manifests the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is likewise: it cannot be said to exist because it is of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."
It can be said that because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists, it cannot be said that it is non-existent (and so forth).
By means of this passage as proof, a practitioner must understand that when observing one's own mind, it has been primordially pure by nature;

it is neither empty nor existent, neither defiled nor pure, and is free from all conceptual discrimination. It is only due to deluded imagination (*vikalpa*) that there appear to be "is" and "is not."
The causes of gain and loss, as well as demerit and merit, increase by means of this; now that one has reached the original nature, it may be called "returning to the source.

Constantly performing this contemplation, one does not perceive persons or phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*); this is precisely reaching emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since emptiness is fundamentally formless, how could delusions arise?

Thus, regarding all such karmic activities—whether moving the body or directing the thoughts—one must not lose mindfulness. As clarified above, this is the true contemplation; other names are merely conventional designations.

This is a superficial understanding. Regarding the meaning, the establishment of the "Middle" (Madhyamaka) is based on a thorough examination of the original treatise (*śāstra*), which states: "One merely contemplates all phenomena. Now, to contemplate one's own mind seems to differ from that treatise;

however, the Great Master [Xuanzang] wished to demonstrate the perfect integration of phenomena and principle, fearing that others might interpret the treatise’s statement "one merely contemplates all phenomena" as referring only to the formation of phenomena.

Because it is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the true mind is directly pointed out as the object of contemplation; this reveals that when contemplating all phenomena (*dharma*) within the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, one is simultaneously contemplating their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Now, in contemplating the intrinsic nature, one does not depart from all phenomena, for the ultimate and conventional are presented alternately, and essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are fully encompassed.

Within the text, the first two lines admonish people according to the teachings, while the subsequent section correctly clarifies the aspects of practice. Furthermore, there are five [sections], the first of which consists of six [lines].

The establishment of the contemplation through the verses consists of two parts: the first verse line indicates the object of contemplation, and the subsequent five lines clarify the characteristics of the contemplation.

The two characters "contemplating" (*guānchá*) belong to the wisdom that performs the contemplation; the two characters "one's own mind" (*zìxīn*) belong to the nature that is the object of contemplation, namely the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature).

When this nature follows conditions to manifest as all phenomena, its celestial truth remains unchanging and is not defiled by delusion; therefore, it is free from the two attachments to persons and phenomena.

Question: Regarding the statement that "the nature of one's own mind is pure," if this purity of the mind's nature can be known, is it possible to speak of the purity of the self-nature of all phenomena?
Answer: All phenomena lack inherent nature; this very absence of nature is the nature of one's own mind.

Since the entire substance of the mind's nature constitutes its phenomenal appearance (*lakṣaṇa*), and since this nature is fundamentally pure, how could its appearances be defiled? Thus, one knows that both persons and phenomena are entirely appearances.
The nature of these [phenomena] is that defilement and purity are non-dual; being primordially true and quiescent, it is said that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is pure.

Thus, one should know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the very intrinsic nature of the mind. It is essential to understand this well and not deviate from the relationship between the ultimate and the conventional truths. Question:

The previous explanation of the treatise’s text, by generally employing the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to clarify that they are neither existent nor non-existent, has already made its meaning manifest. Now, you directly clarify the [intrinsic nature] itself.

"Regarding the meaning of 'the nature is neither dual,' I wish to hear its essential purport. The answer was: "In order to bring about contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one must rely on skillful teachings for clarification.

Now, seeking the meaning through reasoning, I shall briefly present two interpretations. Because the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is truly eternal and endowed with all virtues, it is said to be 'not empty' (this refers to the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*).
Because its nature is inherently natural and fundamentally devoid of deluded phenomena, it is said to be 'not existent' (this refers to the empty *tathāgatagarbha*). From this..."
Because it is not existent, it manifests as not empty; precisely because it is not empty, one knows it is not existent.

Furthermore, the previous statement "not existent" means that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is truly non-existent and thus empty; however, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the emptiness that is naturally and inherently pure, rather than the emptiness of the non-existence of the imagined nature. Therefore, it is called "not existent. As for the previous statement "not empty," it refers to... [the perfected nature].

Emptiness exists because it is dependently originated and appears as if it were existent; thus, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is an eternally abiding, ultimate existence, whereas it is not an existence of dependent, provisional characteristics.
Therefore, it is said to be "not existent. By negating the existence of emptiness, the existence of emptiness is revealed.

One must carefully contemplate how the ultimate and conventional truths are observed together, being perfectly interfused and mutually penetrating. Furthermore, its characteristics are formed through conditions as delusion.

This mind appears to be defiled, yet because it is not truly defiled, it is said to be "non-defiled. By employing contemplation to treat delusion until delusion is exhausted and emptiness is seen, this is called "purity.
Since this nature is fundamentally pure and does not require cultivation or treatment, it is said to be "non-pure.

Thus one should know that all dharmas are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately level and equal.

When one practices this contemplation by becoming equidistant from all names, signs, and various conceptual discriminations, one then knows that persons and phenomena are fundamentally empty and the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure.
Because persons and phenomena are empty, the perfected contemplation is revealed; because the nature of the mind is pure, the ultimate principle is manifested.

What was previously called "reaching the ultimate truth" and "the true ultimate meaning" is seen here. There are those who suppress the Great Master’s establishment of the "contemplation of phenomena."
Seeing this, one should seek repentance for oneself; thus the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "How should the nature of reality (*tathatā*) be known?

It should be known by means of the teaching of the four kinds of purification. This nature is one: first, it is the primordial purity of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), signlessness (*animitta*), and the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The commentary states: "By virtue of this, its intrinsic nature is original."

"Because it is pure from the beginning and because all sentient beings equally possess it, all dharmas are called the Tathāgatagarbha," and so forth, up to the four kinds [of purity], as stated in the treatise (*śāstra*).
Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Verses) states: "One must recognize that the fundamental mind is the principle of the Mahāyāna;
from the very beginning, its self-nature is the pure Buddha-nature. The *Lun* (Treatise) states: "The essence of the nature of differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is eternally non-existent, yet its substance exists while lacking reality;
the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exists as both existence and non-existence, being the suchness (*tathatā*) whose essence is neither existent nor non-existent.

Furthermore, it is said that "Buddha-nature" is precisely the suchness revealed by the two-fold emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*). Moreover, it is said that what is known in the world consists of only two kinds: first, persons; second, phenomena.

If one can thoroughly penetrate these two kinds of emptiness, then one will eternally attain that which corresponds to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), up to and including the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*);

this is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Since delusions are fundamentally non-arising and the pure mind does not engage in grasping, this is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) (and so forth).
All the aforementioned treatises represent the ultimate and most profound discourse of the Mahāyāna, and they all employ the two kinds of emptiness.
This reveals that those who cling to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as being either dualistic emptiness or mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) perceive this [text] as a single awakening.
Next, the following four lines show that delusion arises from the false [imagination];

herein, one relies on the two natures as they are conceptualized, and by relying on these natures, one manifests one’s own mind. Third, the following five lines concern the cultivation of delusion into awakening.
By means of this, the two attachments are dispelled; the original nature is the source, and for delusion to arise from the truth is to follow the current.

Now, having reversed the flow to return to the source and restore the fundamental purity, it is called "returning to the source. This contemplation is precisely right contemplation. Once right contemplation is perfected, the two attachments are severed;
thus it is said that one does not perceive persons or phenomena. When the contemplation is accomplished and attachment is exhausted, the true principle is revealed.

Because it manifests, it is called "penetrating emptiness. This emptiness is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); the essence of the pure mind is that which is revealed as the supreme principle.

The five phrases following the four types of emptiness reveal its virtues and admonish against delusion. Because one realizes that one’s own mind is originally true and pure, it is said to be "formless.
Since the truth is formless, from what could delusion arise? Thus, the true mind is fundamentally non-existent [as a substantial entity].

Because of these false attachments, the practitioner, at all times and in all places—whether with a single glance, a single prostration, a single flower, or a single incense—should constantly perform this contemplation through physical movement and mental application; therefore, it is said that one must not lose mindfulness.

The five [points] below, the last three phrases, serve as a concluding demonstration. The character "ultimate" (至) refers to the True Ultimate (真極), which does not transcend the text concerning the two kinds of emptiness. Question:
If the two kinds of emptiness (dvi-śūnyatā) are used to refute attachment and reveal the principle, why is it necessary to further clarify the two contemplations of the ultimate and the conventional?

Answer: The two contemplations of the ultimate and the conventional do not transcend the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness; their methods must be mutually required and cannot be separated from one another. The objects contemplated are the conventional and the ultimate; that which is refuted is the attachment to persons and phenomena;
and that which reveals them is the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness. This is precisely what is revealed by the truth of Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra-tattva).

This principle is the application of the wisdom of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) to contemplate the objects of the two truths (*satya-dvaya*), thereby destroying attachment to persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) and revealing the single true reality.
It is also the principle employed within the contemplation of Consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Therefore, in the preceding section, the contemplation of the body as selfless and the contemplation of the mind as unattached both perfectly manifest Consciousness-only through the two emptinesses; the subtle essence of this lies in the thorough understanding that transcends what can be expressed by pen.
Commentary:

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "To observe that all phenomena, sentient beings, and the world of lands are entirely quiescent, with a mind that has no dependence and is free from conceptual construction—this is called correctly recollecting the Buddha’s Bodhi. It further states: "If one wishes to attain the wisdom of a Buddha, one should..."
Free from all deluded thoughts, one thoroughly penetrates both existence and non-existence, swiftly becoming a Teacher of Gods and Humans.

Regarding the two verses from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that together testify to the two kinds of emptiness: the first verse’s first two lines provide a general indication; the third line reveals the principle;
and the fourth line provides the conclusion. In the subsequent verse, the first line concerns the arousal of the mind to seek the Way, while the second line offers an exhortation.

One who is free from the two attachments, whose three phrases perfectly manifest right contemplation, whose four phrases perfectly realize the ultimate fruit, and who is a teacher of gods and humans— this is the Buddha.
When a practitioner cultivates this contemplation, the merit in a single moment and a single thought is boundless.

Therefore, the *Kāśyapa Sūtra* states: "The merit possessed by all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm is not equal to that of a person who cultivates the dharma of seclusion, whose pure mind corresponds with the realization that all phenomena are empty, neither coming nor going;
such a small measure of merit through patience cannot be reached even by analogy."
In the first section of the "Exhibiting Merit and Further Inducing" passage, the matter of King Mimi is not clearly explained, and thus it is not correlated with the formal practice below.
Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* states: "If there are those who, during the six periods of day and night, pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and recite Mahāyāna sūtras..."

To contemplate the ultimate truth of the profound dharma of emptiness for even the duration of a single finger-snap eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges-sands of kalpas. One who practices this dharma is truly a child of the Buddha, born from all Buddhas;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions serve as their preceptors. Such a person is said to be one who is fully endowed with the bodhisattva precepts.
One must perform the *karmavācanā* (ritual action) so that it may be spontaneously accomplished and one may receive the offerings of all humans and devas.
In the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, the practice of prostrating to the Buddha and reciting the sutras is cited as evidence for this.

To contemplate the first principle (*paramārtha*) according to the text below is to realize the ultimate truth; because this principle is profound and subtle, it is called "extremely deep," and its nature is fundamentally natural and true.

Therefore, it is said: "The dharmas are empty" (1). This concludes the section praising the benefits of the merit. Question: Above, it was stated that after one has generated the right vows, one next receives the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*).

Now, you say they need not be conferred through *karma* (ritual procedure) but are spontaneously accomplished. How do you respond? Answer: The previous statement was based on the formal ritual procedures and, according to the teachings, required formal reception.

The present explanation clarifies that when one realizes the principle through right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), the precepts must be understood as being naturally attained. This is like the case of those of high intelligence who attain realization individually.
Awaiting Admonition and Instruction.

Chapter Ten: On the Vessels of Capacity and Traces of the Past (Explaining the manifestation of the mind through the observation of forms; bathing in the Way through internal reflection on one’s own ailments; entrusting words to events to give rise to discourse).

An explanation of the chapter titled "Exhibiting Traces" (*Zhongcheng shi ye*). The title "Exhibiting" (*shì*) indicates that what is presented here is the author’s own intent. "Traces" (*qì*) refers to the manifestations of conduct described throughout the various chapters;
these are all intended to reveal the author's inner intent and set forth the traces of the teaching to be bequeathed to the future, so as to jointly propagate the Buddha-way.

Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "I venture to exhibit my capacity for the present," and so forth. Furthermore, "exhibiting" (*chéng*) may also be understood as "anticipating" (*qī*) or "aiming toward."
"Limit" (*yan*) refers to the karmic retribution of the physical form; "array" (*chen*) refers to the sequential narration; and "traces" (*ji*) refers to the characteristics of the teachings.
Since the Great Master composed this text only when his years had advanced into late life, he established this chapter to record the sequence of time.

Regarding the phrase "clothing and vessels," it is also said to mean recording the "vessels of one's progress. The intended meaning of "sequence of time" is that the celestial number was nearing its end and the conditions for retribution were limited.

It is said: "To 'measure the capacity' (chéngqì) means to follow the circumstances of the situation in accordance with the feelings of those who come; to 'present the traces of the teaching' (chénjì) refers to the manifestation of the teachings.

In the commentary, the first two phrases—'examining and urging form and mind'—correspond to the meaning of measuring capacity; the latter two phrases—'relying on events to establish words'—correspond to the meaning of presenting traces."
My years have advanced like the *púliǔ* tree; I await my end day by day. Since this is not a matter of worldly adornment, why should it concern others?
The first two lines of the initial section of the original text state that the retributive form is finite, which carries the meaning of a limited term.

The *púliǔ* is a weak plant among grasses and trees that withers first when autumn arrives; this serves as a metaphor for its lack of longevity. The subsequent two lines [address] the mind whose afflictions and karma have not yet been purified.
While striving to cultivate one's own practice, before it is yet perfected, how can one find the leisure to describe past deeds? Thus, the *Commentary on the Treatise* states: "I am old;
I fear that merely shifting the passage of time and recklessly impairing my primary effort by indulging in useless words will only cause me to waste my finite life.
This is truly not permissible."

Furthermore, regarding the composition of these works on the characteristics of practice, their followers are indeed numerous; they provide comprehensive summaries to address immediate needs as they arise.

Among the traces left behind, the first section clarifies what was composed—namely, the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the Vinaya, as well as various biographies and records—while the subsequent section clarifies their benefits and efficacy.

Now, having traveled through various regions and followed the Way, I have frequently sought out those who could provide guidance; yet in these degenerate times, ordinary people regard formal ritual respect as paramount.
When they encountered me, they were intent on recording my deeds for use as admonitory inscriptions, which I found unbearable and distressing, and thus I have once again set forth this narrative.
In the first section of the following analysis, the initial part clarifies the formal invitation. The first two lines identify the person who makes the request;
the subsequent lines indicate the Dharma being requested, which constitutes the ritual of reverence. "Ling" (領) means to receive; "zhēn" (箴) means to admonish;
and "míng" (銘) means to enshrine. Because he granted their petition, he composed this text.
Of these ten chapters, only three remain; they propagate the Buddha-way above and gather in self and others below. The wording is most earnest, and the meaning lies in the elimination of attachment.
It is hoped that those who read them will understand their intent. Should there be any deficiencies, I pray you will wait for my correction and instruction.
In this summary, this constitutes the third section, the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding dedication). The preservation of the three activities demonstrates correct practice:

propagating the Buddha-way above is the practice of self-benefit; gathering oneself and others below is the practice of benefiting others. The earnestness of the phrasing demonstrates the literary form;
the preservation of the rejection of attachments demonstrates the intent of cultivation. May those below be encouraged to have faith as follows.
*Shiqian*. *Shimen guijing yi tongzhen ji*, Scroll Lower (End).
My Patriarch.

The *Gujingyi* (Ritual of Homage) composed by the Holy Master of the Southern Mountain has long been in existence; it is truly the fundamental source for contemplative practice and reveals the ultimate perfection of both phenomena and principle.
Although there have been commentaries on it since antiquity, they have not clarified the contemplation of principle.
The Vinaya Master Abhāva composed this record to elucidate [the text], such that its literary meaning is radiant and its underlying principles are profound.
Now, his disciples wish to carve it into woodblocks to propagate its transmission and have requested me to proofread and verify it; thus, I have merely recorded the date and composed this preface.
Recorded on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the year of the Great Fire (the Year of the Horse), the third year of the Kaixi era of the Great Song, by Mukan (Rujiao),
Abbot of the Zhaokai Jitan Monastery within the jurisdiction of Shaoxing Prefecture, who transmits the teachings and contemplations of the Nanshan school.
